rajasthan-738.name: Battle of Rajasthan
significance: Stopped Arab expansion into India, saved Hindu civilization
casualties: Heavy Arab losses, minimal Rajput casualties
tactics: Guerrilla warfare in desert terrain, coordinated Rajput alliance
rajasthan-738.story:
## The Battle of Rajasthan — How the Arab Advance Beyond Sindh Was Checked

*The Arab raids are recorded in al-Baladhuri's ninth-century* Futuh al-Buldan *and in Indian inscriptions, chiefly the Navsari grant of the Chalukya prince Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin (739 CE) and the later Gwalior prashasti of the Pratihara king Mihira Bhoja; Bappa Rawal's part rests on much later Mewar tradition, and "the Battle of Rajasthan" is a modern label rather than the name of a single recorded battle.*

The phrase "Battle of Rajasthan" appears in many popular histories, usually with the date **738 CE** and the claim that a confederacy of Rajput kings under **Bappa Rawal** and **Nagabhata I** destroyed an Arab army in one great engagement. The real history is less tidy and more interesting. What the sources describe is a series of raids and counter-attacks across western India over roughly fifteen years, in the 720s and 730s, which ended with the Arab governors of Sindh confined to the lower Indus. No contemporary text names a single decisive battle, gives its location, or records the numbers engaged. The date 738 is a modern convention, drawn from the approximate time of the Chalukya victory recorded in Gujarat.

### Background: Sindh and the Umayyad frontier

In **712 CE** Muhammad ibn Qasim, a general of the Umayyad Caliphate, conquered Sindh after defeating Raja Dahir. Sindh and Multan became the easternmost province of an empire that stretched to Spain. Under the Caliph Hisham, the governor **Junayd ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Murri** (c. 723–726) reasserted control and sent expeditions beyond Sindh.

Al-Baladhuri lists the places Junayd's commanders attacked: Marmad (often identified with Marumandala, the Marwar region), Mandal, Dahnaj, Barwas (Bharuch), al-Baylaman (probably Bhillamala, modern **Bhinmal**), Jurz (the Gurjara country) and Uzayn (**Ujjain**), with raids reaching as far as Malibah, possibly Malwa. These were plundering expeditions rather than conquests: the Arabs took booty and some forts but did not hold them. Baladhuri then states that under Junayd's successor, **Tamim ibn Zaid al-Utbi**, the Muslims withdrew from several parts of India and did not return to them, and that the next governor, **al-Hakam ibn Awana**, had to found a new garrison town, al-Mahfuza ("the protected"), because the Muslims had no safe place of refuge.

### The Indian response

Western India in this period had no single dominant power. Gurjara clans held the country around Bhinmal and Mandor; the **Chalukyas of Lata** in southern Gujarat were a branch of the Chalukyas of Badami; the Maitrakas still ruled Valabhi; and in Mewar the Guhila clan held a modest principality. The resistance that the inscriptions record came from several of these powers.

The clearest evidence is the **Navsari copper-plate grant of 739 CE**, issued by Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin, the Chalukya governor of Lata. It says that the "Tajikas" (Arabs), having destroyed the Saindhava, Kachchhella, Saurashtra, Chavotaka, Maurya and Gurjara kingdoms, advanced to conquer the Deccan, and that Pulakeshin defeated them near **Navsari**. His overlord, Vikramaditya II, honoured him with titles such as "Repeller of the Unrepellable". This battle on the Gujarat coast is the only engagement of the period whose place and approximate date are firmly documented.

**Nagabhata I**, founder of the imperial Gurjara-Pratihara line, ruled from about **730 to 760**, probably from Bhinmal at first and later from Ujjain. The Gwalior inscription of his descendant Mihira Bhoja, composed more than a century later, praises him as a form of Narayana who crushed the large armies of a powerful "mlechchha" ruler. Most historians accept that this refers to the Arab raids, and that Nagabhata's defence of Malwa and Marwar was the foundation of later Pratihara power. The inscription gives neither a date nor a place.

### Bappa Rawal: tradition and history

**Bappa Rawal**, the celebrated founder of Guhila power in Mewar, is the figure most associated with the "Battle of Rajasthan" in popular retelling. Mewar tradition credits him with taking Chittor from its Mori (Maurya) rulers and with driving foreign invaders westward. These stories survive in inscriptions and chronicles written centuries later, such as the fifteenth-century Kumbhalgarh prashasti and the khyats. Historians including R. C. Majumdar have suggested that Bappa may have fought the Arabs alongside the Pratiharas, and the Navsari grant's mention of a "Maurya" kingdom overrun by the Arabs makes Chittor's involvement plausible. But no contemporary document names Bappa in connection with the Arab wars, and a formal alliance between Bappa and Nagabhata is a modern reconstruction.

### Forces, course and tactics

No source gives the size of either side. The figures and detailed guerrilla tactics in popular versions are not drawn from any source. What can be inferred is limited: the Arab expeditions were cavalry raids moving fast through Marwar, Malwa and Gujarat, and they were defeated by local rulers fighting on their own ground, sometimes in pitched battle, as at Navsari.

### Outcome and consequences

The result was real, if gradual. After about 740 Arab rule was confined to Sindh and Multan, and the frontier stayed close to that line for nearly three centuries. The Caliphate itself was in crisis: the Berber revolt of 740, defeats in Central Asia and the Abbasid revolution of 750 drained resources from its distant Indian frontier. Later Abbasid raids by sea brought no lasting advance inland.

The chief beneficiaries were the **Gurjara-Pratiharas**. The ninth-century Arab merchant Sulaiman described the king of "Juzr" as the greatest enemy of the Muslims in India, with the finest cavalry in the land. That reputation began with Nagabhata I.

### How sources differ

Arab authors record the raids and the retreat but say little about their opponents. Indian inscriptions celebrate victories but give no numbers. Mewar tradition, written down centuries later, places Bappa at the centre. Popular modern accounts claim "minimal Rajput casualties" and say the battle "saved Hindu civilisation"; neither claim can be supported from the sources. The fairer conclusion is that several regional powers, largely independently, made Arab expansion beyond Sindh too costly to continue.

### Key points
- **Not a single battle.** "Battle of Rajasthan" is a modern name for Arab raids and Indian resistance between roughly 725 and 740 CE; 738 is a conventional date.
- **Best-documented victory.** The Navsari grant of 739 records the Chalukya prince Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin defeating the Arabs in southern Gujarat.
- **Nagabhata I.** The Gwalior inscription credits the Pratihara founder with crushing a mlechchha army, laying the base of Pratihara power.
- **Bappa Rawal.** His role is a strong Mewar tradition but is not attested in contemporary records.
- **Result.** After about 740, Arab rule stayed confined to Sindh and Multan for nearly three centuries.

mount-abu-1008.name: Battle of Mount Abu
significance: Successful regional resistance that disrupted Ghaznavid movement through the Aravalli range and secured western Rajasthan routes during Mahmud’s western India campaigns
casualties: Several thousand Ghaznavid soldiers lost due to ambushes, terrain-related attrition, and supply disruption; Rajput losses comparatively limited
tactics: Mountain warfare, ambush tactics, control of passes, disruption of supply lines, attritional defense
mount-abu-1008.story:
## The Battle of Mount Abu — A Battle the Sources Do Not Record

*No contemporary Persian chronicle (al-Utbi, Gardizi, and later Ibn al-Athir) and no Paramara inscription records a battle at Mount Abu in 1008 CE; this account sets out what is actually known about Mahmud of Ghazni's campaigns of that year, the Paramaras of Abu, and Mahmud's march through Rajasthan to Somnath in 1025–26, the one occasion when his army passed near the Abu hills.*

Popular lists of Rajput battles include a "Battle of Mount Abu" in **1008 CE**, in which the Paramara chiefs of Abu are said to have trapped a Ghaznavid army of 12,000–15,000 men in the passes of the Aravallis and forced it to turn back. The story is told with confident numbers and detailed tactics. It cannot be supported. The surviving sources for Mahmud of Ghazni's campaigns — al-Utbi's *Tarikh-i Yamini*, written in Mahmud's lifetime, Gardizi's *Zain al-Akhbar* of about 1050, and later compilations such as Ibn al-Athir's — place his army of 1008 hundreds of kilometres to the north, and no Indian inscription or chronicle describes a battle at Abu in that year. The figures for armies and casualties in the popular version have no source behind them.

### What Mahmud actually did in 1008

**Mahmud of Ghazni** (r. 998–1030) raided India repeatedly, usually in the cold season. His campaign of **1008–09** was directed against **Anandapala**, the Hindu Shahi ruler of the Punjab. Anandapala gathered a large army, and al-Utbi and later writers say that contingents came from other Indian kingdoms to support him. The battle was fought near **Waihind** (Udabhandapura), on the Indus, or between Waihind and Peshawar. After a hard struggle, in which Anandapala's elephant is said to have panicked and turned, the Shahi army broke. Mahmud then went on to sack the temple-fort of **Nagarkot** (Bhimnagar, in Kangra), carrying off great treasure.

Neither of these places lies anywhere near Mount Abu. Some later writers, Firishta among them, list the rajas of Ujjain, Gwalior, Kalinjar, Kannauj, Delhi and Ajmer as Anandapala's allies, but that list is probably an embellishment and in any case concerns a battle in the Punjab, not in the Aravallis.

### The Paramaras of Abu

The hill country around **Mount Abu**, with its capital at **Chandravati**, was ruled in this period by a branch of the **Paramara** clan. Its known rulers include **Dharanivaraha** in the late tenth century and, in the early eleventh, **Mahipala** and his son **Dhandhuka**. The Abu Paramaras were usually feudatories of the **Chaulukyas (Solankis) of Anahilavada** in Gujarat, though at times they leaned towards their powerful kinsmen, the Paramaras of Malwa, whose most famous king, **Bhoja**, ruled from about 1010 to 1055. Abu itself was a natural stronghold: a high granite plateau rising out of the plain, with limited approaches, guarding one of the routes between Marwar and Gujarat.

### The Somnath campaign of 1025–26

The only time a Ghaznavid army certainly passed near Abu was during Mahmud's most famous raid. In late **1025** he marched from Ghazni to Multan and then crossed the Thar desert, his chroniclers say with tens of thousands of camels carrying water and supplies. He reached **Anahilavada**, which its king **Bhima I** abandoned, and in January **1026** sacked the temple of **Somnath** on the Saurashtra coast.

For the return journey, Ibn al-Athir reports that Mahmud learned that a great Indian king, named as **Paramadeva**, was waiting to intercept him on the road he had come by. Rather than fight, Mahmud returned by a different route, through Kachchh and the Sindh desert to Mansura, losing men and animals to thirst and to attacks by Jats along the way. Historians have identified "Paramadeva" variously with Bhoja of Malwa or with Bhima of Gujarat; some suggest a gathering of Paramara and other forces in the region between Abu and Malwa. Whatever its exact identity, this is the event closest to the popular "Mount Abu" story: an Indian force that did not defeat Mahmud in battle, but made him avoid the Aravalli road.

### After the raid

Local politics continued to turn. Jain sources record that Dhandhuka of Abu displeased Bhima I and took refuge with Bhoja; Bhima then placed **Vimala**, his minister, as governor (dandanayaka) at Chandravati. In **1031** Vimala built the first of the celebrated marble **Dilwara temples** on Mount Abu, a sign that within a few years of Mahmud's raid the region was stable and prosperous. The Paramaras were later restored at Abu as Chaulukya feudatories and ruled there until the early fourteenth century.

### How sources differ

Persian chroniclers record Mahmud's victories in detail and rarely admit setbacks, so a minor reverse in the Aravallis could have gone unmentioned. On the other hand, Paramara inscriptions are generous in praising their kings, and none mentions a victory over the Turks at Abu in 1008. Without evidence, the honest position is that the "Battle of Mount Abu, 1008" is a later construction, possibly a blending of the 1008 Shahi campaign with Mahmud's 1026 avoidance of the Rajasthan route. The claims of several thousand Ghaznavid dead and limited Rajput losses, and the description of weeks of mountain warfare, are not drawn from any historical record.

What is historical is the wider pattern: the Rajput and Gurjara kingdoms of western India could not stop Mahmud's swift raids, but he never attempted to hold territory south of the Punjab and Multan, and his successors lacked the strength to try.

### Key points
- **No recorded battle.** No contemporary Persian or Indian source mentions a battle at Mount Abu in 1008 CE.
- **Mahmud in 1008.** That year he fought Anandapala of the Hindu Shahis near Waihind on the Indus, then sacked Nagarkot in Kangra.
- **The Paramaras of Abu.** A branch of the Paramara clan ruled from Chandravati, usually as feudatories of the Chaulukyas of Gujarat.
- **The real near-miss.** Returning from Somnath in 1026, Mahmud avoided a king called Paramadeva and went home through Kachchh and Sindh.
- **Aftermath.** Vimala's Dilwara temple at Abu, built in 1031, shows the region's quick recovery.

tarain-i.name: Battle of Tarain I

significance: Major defensive victory that temporarily halted Ghurid expansion into northern India and exposed the limitations of steppe cavalry in direct engagement

tactics: Massed Rajput heavy cavalry and infantry assault versus Ghurid mounted archers and light cavalry
tarain-i.story:
## The First Battle of Tarain — Prithviraj Chauhan's Victory over Muhammad of Ghor

*The battle is recorded in Minhaj-us-Siraj's* Tabaqat-i Nasiri *(c. 1260), the nearest Persian account, and retold with additions by Firishta around 1600; the contemporary Sanskrit* Prithviraja Vijaya *breaks off before these events, and the much later* Prithviraj Raso *of the Chauhan bards mixes memory with legend, including its claim that Prithviraj defeated Ghori many times.*

In the winter of **1191 CE** (some historians prefer 1190–91), on the plain of **Tarain** — modern Taraori, near Karnal and Thanesar in Haryana — the army of **Prithviraj III**, the Chauhan (Chahamana) king of Ajmer, routed the forces of **Muhammad of Ghor** (Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad ibn Sam). It was one of the clearest defeats the Ghurid sultan ever suffered, and for a year it seemed to have closed northern India to him.

### Background

The **Ghurids**, from the mountains of central Afghanistan, rose in the second half of the twelfth century under two brothers: Ghiyath al-Din, who ruled from Firozkoh, and his younger brother Mu'izz al-Din, who governed Ghazni and directed the Indian campaigns. Muhammad of Ghor took Multan and Uch in 1175. In 1178 he attempted to invade Gujarat through the desert and was soundly defeated near Mount Abu by the Chaulukya army of the young king Mularaja II, led by the queen mother Naikidevi. After that, he turned to the Punjab, and in **1186** he captured Lahore and ended the last Ghaznavid line.

The **Chauhans of Shakambhari** (Sapadalaksha), with their capital at Ajmer, were then the strongest power in the eastern Punjab and Rajasthan. Delhi was held by a Tomara family as Chauhan feudatories. Prithviraj, who came to the throne as a boy around 1177–78, had already fought the Chandelas of Bundelkhand, the Bhadanakas and the Chaulukyas of Gujarat.

In **1190–91** Muhammad of Ghor seized the fortress of **Tabarhindah**, usually identified with **Bathinda**, which lay on the Chauhan frontier. He left a garrison of about 1,200 horsemen under Qazi Zia-ud-din Tulaki and was preparing to return home when news came that Prithviraj was advancing with a large army. He turned back to meet him.

### Forces and commanders

The sources give no reliable figures. Firishta, writing four centuries later, credits the Rajput side with 200,000 horse and 3,000 elephants, numbers that historians regard as greatly inflated. What is clear is that Prithviraj had a larger army, made up of his own forces and those of allied and feudatory chiefs, with cavalry, infantry and war elephants. Among his commanders was **Govindaraja** (Govind Rai), the ruler of Delhi, whom Firishta calls Prithviraj's brother. Muhammad of Ghor led an army built around mounted archers and armoured cavalry, smaller and more mobile.

### The course of the battle

According to Minhaj, the Rajput army attacked and the wings of the Ghurid force gave way, enveloped by the larger Indian line. The sultan's centre held for a time. Muhammad of Ghor then rode forward against Govindaraja, who was mounted on an elephant. In the most vivid incident of the battle, as later told by Firishta, the sultan struck Govindaraja in the mouth with his lance, knocking out several teeth, while Govindaraja hurled a javelin that wounded the sultan badly in the upper arm.

The wounded sultan nearly fell from his horse. A young Khalji soldier is said to have leapt up behind him, held him in the saddle and carried him off the field. When his troops did not see their leader, they assumed he was dead, and the Ghurid army broke and fled. It regrouped only some distance away, where the sultan was found and carried to safety on a litter.

### Outcome and consequences

The victory was decisive on the field. Prithviraj did not, however, pursue the retreating army into the Punjab. He turned instead to recover Tabarhindah, which Qazi Zia-ud-din defended for about thirteen months before surrendering on terms. Some historians count the failure to pursue as a strategic mistake that allowed Muhammad of Ghor to rebuild his army; others note that a long chase into Ghurid territory would have been risky, and that recovering the frontier fort was the normal aim of such a war.

Firishta says that the sultan, on returning to Ghazni, punished the officers who had fled by making them march around the city with nosebags of grain hung around their necks. Whether or not that detail is true, Muhammad of Ghor spent the following year preparing to return, and he did so in 1192, with very different results.

There are no reliable casualty figures. The sources agree only that the Ghurid army was routed and its commander gravely wounded.

### How sources differ

Minhaj's account is brief and focuses on the sultan's personal courage. Firishta adds the dramatic details of the lance and the teeth, which may come from earlier sources now lost. Prithviraj's court poet Jayanaka, whose *Prithviraja Vijaya* was written in the king's lifetime, does not cover the battle in its surviving portion. The *Prithviraj Raso*, attributed to the bard **Chand Bardai** but largely composed much later, claims that Prithviraj defeated Ghori many times and released him each time; historians do not accept these repeated victories, though the first Tarain battle itself is well established.

### Key points
- **Date and place.** Fought in 1191 (or 1190–91) at Tarain, modern Taraori in Haryana.
- **Cause.** Muhammad of Ghor had seized Tabarhindah (Bathinda) on the Chauhan frontier.
- **Decisive moment.** Govindaraja of Delhi wounded the sultan, who was carried from the field; his army fled.
- **Aftermath.** Prithviraj recovered Tabarhindah after a siege of about thirteen months but did not pursue the Ghurids.
- **Sources.** Minhaj and Firishta are the main narratives; the *Prithviraj Raso*'s tales of many victories are legend.

tarain-ii.name: Battle of Tarain II
tarain-ii.rajputSide: Prithviraj Chauhan and Rajput warrior clans
significance: Battle won only after exhausting and breaking one of the most ferocious warrior societies of medieval India through deception and prolonged warfare
casualties: Massive Rajput losses after relentless combat; Prithviraj Chauhan captured after severe injuries; Ghurid losses heavy but tactically managed
tactics: Night attacks, exhaustion warfare, feigned retreats, mounted archery against direct Rajput shock charges
tarain-ii.story:
## The Second Battle of Tarain — The Defeat That Opened North India

*The main accounts are Persian: Hasan Nizami's* Taj-ul-Maasir *(written in the early thirteenth century), Minhaj-us-Siraj's* Tabaqat-i Nasiri *(c. 1260) and Firishta's history (c. 1600); coins struck at Ajmer and later Sanskrit works such as the* Hammira Mahakavya *add details, while the* Prithviraj Raso's *story of Prithviraj blinding and killing Ghori in Ghazni is legend.*

In **1192 CE**, a year after his defeat on the same ground, **Muhammad of Ghor** returned to **Tarain**, near modern Karnal in Haryana, and destroyed the army of **Prithviraj III Chauhan**. The battle ended the Chauhan kingdom of Ajmer as an independent power, gave the Ghurids a base in the Indo-Gangetic plain and led, within fifteen years, to the founding of the Delhi Sultanate.

### Background

The First Battle of Tarain in 1191 had been a rout: the sultan was wounded and carried off the field, and Prithviraj went on to recover the frontier fort of Tabarhindah (Bathinda). Muhammad of Ghor spent the following year rebuilding his army in Ghazni. Prithviraj, by contrast, is criticised in some later traditions for complacency, though there is little contemporary evidence about how he spent that year. Later legend links this period to his elopement with **Sanyogita**, daughter of Jaichand of Kannauj, but that story comes from the *Prithviraj Raso* and is not supported by contemporary sources.

### Forces and commanders

Minhaj says the sultan brought **120,000** armoured horsemen; Firishta gives Prithviraj 300,000 horse, 3,000 elephants and the support of some 150 Rajput chiefs. Both sets of figures are certainly exaggerated, but the sources agree that both armies were very large and that Prithviraj again had the larger force, including many elephants and contingents of allied rulers. His leading commander was again **Govindaraja** (Govind Rai) of Delhi. The Ghurid army relied on disciplined mounted archers and a reserve of heavy cavalry, under commanders including **Qutb-ud-din Aibak**, a slave officer who would later found the Delhi Sultanate.

### Diplomacy and surprise

Firishta records an exchange of letters before the battle. Prithviraj, confident after his earlier victory, offered to let the sultan withdraw unharmed. Muhammad of Ghor replied that he was only acting for his elder brother and needed time to seek instructions, implying a truce. According to this account, the Rajput camp relaxed, and the sultan attacked before dawn, while many in the Indian army were not yet ready for battle. Minhaj does not mention the ruse, and some historians treat it with caution, but the story fits Ghurid practice.

### The course of the battle

Minhaj describes the sultan's plan clearly. He left his baggage and heavy troops in reserve and divided his light cavalry into **four divisions of about 10,000 mounted archers** each. These were sent to attack the Rajput army from the flanks, the rear and the front, shooting arrows and then withdrawing whenever the Indian line charged. The Rajput army, built for close fighting with elephants, infantry and heavy cavalry, could not catch them.

The harassment continued for hours. When the Rajput formation was tired and broken by repeated charges, the Ghurid centre made a **feigned retreat**, drawing the pursuers out. Then the sultan threw in his reserve of about **12,000** heavy cavalry, which struck the disordered Indian army and broke it. Govindaraja was killed; Firishta says his body was recognised by the broken teeth from the lance blow of the previous year.

### The fate of Prithviraj

Prithviraj left the field on horseback and was captured near **Sarsuti** (perhaps Sirsa). Here the sources diverge. Minhaj says he was taken prisoner and put to death soon afterwards. Hasan Nizami says that he was allowed to return to Ajmer as a tributary ruler, was later accused of plotting against the sultan, and was executed. Coins have been found bearing Prithviraj's name on one side and the name of **Muhammad bin Sam** on the other, which supports the idea of a brief period as a vassal.

The *Prithviraj Raso* tells a different story: that Prithviraj was taken to Ghazni and blinded, and that, with the help of his bard Chand Bardai, he killed Muhammad of Ghor with an arrow aimed by sound alone (shabdabhedi baan). This is a powerful legend, but it is not history. Muhammad of Ghor lived for another fourteen years and was assassinated at **Damiak**, on the Jhelum, in **March 1206**, by Khokhar rebels or Ismaili assassins.

### Outcome and consequences

The victory opened the way to the Indo-Gangetic plain. Prithviraj's young son **Govindaraja IV** was installed at Ajmer as a Ghurid vassal; when Prithviraj's brother **Hariraja** rebelled and took Ajmer, Govindaraja withdrew to **Ranthambore**, founding the Chauhan line there that later produced Hammir Dev. Qutb-ud-din Aibak occupied **Delhi** in 1193, and it became the Ghurid headquarters in India. In **1194** the sultan defeated Jaichand of Kannauj at Chandawar. On Muhammad of Ghor's death in 1206, Aibak became the first ruler of what is known as the Delhi Sultanate.

### How sources differ

There are no reliable casualty figures; the sources agree only that the Rajput losses were very heavy and that many chiefs fell. The idea, common in popular accounts, that the Rajputs were beaten only through deception oversimplifies matters: the Persian sources describe a well-planned use of mobile cavalry against an army organised for a different kind of war. The Rajput side of the story survives mainly in later bardic literature, which preserves the grief of defeat but adds much that is legend.

### Key points
- **Date and place.** Fought at Tarain, near Karnal, in 1192 CE, a year after the first battle.
- **Tactics.** Four divisions of mounted archers harassed the Rajput army, followed by a feigned retreat and a charge by 12,000 heavy cavalry.
- **Prithviraj's fate.** He was captured near Sarsuti and executed, either at once or after a brief period as a vassal.
- **Legend.** The *Prithviraj Raso*'s tale of Prithviraj killing Ghori in Ghazni is not historical; Ghori died in 1206.
- **Consequences.** Delhi fell to Aibak in 1193, and the way was opened for the Delhi Sultanate.

chandawar-1194.name: Battle of Chandawar
significance: Decisive victory that destroyed the Gahadavala kingdom and enabled firm Ghurid control over the Ganga–Yamuna heartland
casualties: Heavy Rajput losses; Jaichand killed in battle; Ghurid casualties moderate but sustainable
tactics: River-based engagement, mobile cavalry warfare, encirclement, exploitation of political isolation
chandawar-1194.story:
## The Battle of Chandawar — The Fall of the Gahadavalas of Kannauj

*The battle is recorded mainly in Persian and Arabic works, chiefly Hasan Nizami's Taj al-Ma'athir and Ibn al-Athir's al-Kamil, written from the Ghurid side, and in later Persian histories; Gahadavala copper-plate inscriptions document the dynasty itself. The image of Jaichand as a traitor who invited the invaders comes from much later bardic literature such as the Prithviraj Raso and is not supported by the contemporary record.*

### The kingdom of Kannauj

In the twelfth century the most extensive kingdom of the Ganga plain belonged to the **Gahadavala** dynasty. Its founder, **Chandradeva**, had taken **Kannauj** and **Varanasi** around the 1090s, and his grandson **Govindachandra** (r. c. 1114–1155) made it the leading power of northern India, ruling a territory stretching from the Yamuna into Bihar. Dozens of Gahadavala copper-plate land grants survive, showing a settled state that endowed Brahmins and temples and patronised Sanskrit learning. The poet Shriharsha, author of the Naishadhiyacharita, is associated with the Gahadavala court.

**Jayachandra**, known in popular memory as **Jaichand**, came to the throne around 1170. His inscriptions show him ruling from Kannauj and Varanasi over a wide and wealthy realm. Ibn al-Athir, writing in distant Mosul, called him the greatest king of India, with the largest territory and a huge army that included many elephants.

### After Tarain

In **1192** **Muhammad of Ghor** defeated **Prithviraj III Chauhan** at the Second Battle of Tarain. Ajmer and Delhi passed under Ghurid control, and the sultan left his general **Qutb al-Din Aibak** in India to extend his conquests. Northern India had no single power capable of uniting the remaining kingdoms. The Chauhans and the Gahadavalas had been rivals, and there is no evidence that Jaichand sent help to Prithviraj, or that Prithviraj had expected it.

The later bardic story turns this rivalry into a personal drama. The **Prithviraj Raso**, a poem that grew over several centuries, tells how Prithviraj carried off Jaichand's daughter **Sanyogita** from her svayamvara, and how the humiliated Jaichand then invited Muhammad of Ghor to destroy him. Historians regard this as legend. No contemporary source mentions Sanyogita or any alliance between Jaichand and the Ghurids, and Jaichand himself died fighting them two years after Tarain. In north Indian speech, however, the name "Jaichand" came to mean a traitor, an example of how a late literary tradition can overwhelm the record.

### The campaign of 1194

In **1194** (590 AH), Muhammad of Ghor returned to India with a large cavalry army. Aibak led the vanguard. The aim was the Gahadavala kingdom, whose wealth and position in the Doab made it the natural next target.

The Ghurids advanced down the Yamuna and met Jaichand's army at **Chandawar**, near modern **Firozabad** and **Etawah** in Uttar Pradesh. The Persian writers give very large figures for the Indian army, especially its elephants. Such numbers are a familiar feature of victory literature and cannot be trusted, but there is no doubt that the Gahadavala host was large and that its elephants were an important arm.

### The battle

The Ghurid sources describe the fighting only in general terms. The Ghurid army relied on horse archers and well-drilled cavalry divisions, the same arm that had won at Tarain, and these could harass a slower army, withdraw, and strike again. The Gahadavala army, in contrast, depended on infantry, heavy cavalry and elephants massed around the king.

According to Hasan Nizami, the battle was hard fought and for a time undecided. It turned when Jaichand, directing the fight from his elephant, was struck by an arrow and killed. His fall broke the army's resistance, and the Ghurids won the field.

Ibn al-Athir adds a detail often repeated later: the king's body lay unrecognised among the dead until it was identified by his teeth, which had been fastened with gold wire. The Ghurids captured a great many elephants, which the sources count as a large part of the spoils.

### After the battle

From Chandawar the Ghurid army moved on the Gahadavala treasury at the fort of **Asni** and then to **Varanasi**. The Persian chroniclers boast of the plunder taken and of many temples destroyed there; these claims are written in a triumphal style but match the pattern of the campaign.

Chandawar did not end the Gahadavala dynasty at a stroke. A copper-plate grant of 1197 shows Jaichand's son **Harishchandra** still issuing land grants and using royal titles in the region of the present Jaunpur and Mirzapur districts. Kannauj itself appears to have been finally secured by the Delhi Sultanate only in the time of **Iltutmish**, in the early thirteenth century. Some later Rajput clans, including the **Rathores** of Marwar, claimed descent from the Gahadavalas of Kannauj, though historians debate that link.

In the longer view, however, the battle was decisive. With the Chauhans and Gahadavalas both defeated within two years, no strong kingdom remained in the Ganga–Yamuna Doab. Aibak's conquests in the following years laid the base of the **Delhi Sultanate**, which he founded in 1206.

### Why the Gahadavalas fell

Modern historians stress several causes. The northern Indian kingdoms were rivals and fought their wars separately; the Ghurids met them one at a time. The Ghurid army had a mobile, professional cavalry trained in mounted archery, against armies built around elephants and the presence of the king. When the king fell, as at Chandawar, the whole army often lost its command. The legend of personal betrayal offers a simpler moral story, but the evidence points to these political and military causes rather than to the treachery of one man.

### Key points
- **Date and place.** Fought in 1194 at Chandawar on the Yamuna, near modern Firozabad, between Muhammad of Ghor and Jayachandra (Jaichand) of Kannauj.
- **The kingdom.** The Gahadavalas were the largest power of the Ganga plain, ruling from Kannauj and Varanasi.
- **The battle.** Jaichand was killed by an arrow while fighting from his elephant, and his army broke.
- **Aftermath.** The Ghurids took the treasury at Asni and plundered Varanasi; Jaichand's son Harishchandra kept a reduced realm for some years.
- **Legend and record.** The story of Sanyogita and Jaichand's treachery comes from the later Prithviraj Raso, not from contemporary sources.

## The Siege of Ranthambore — Hammir Dev and the Price of Refuge

*The siege is described by the court poet Amir Khusrau, who accompanied Alauddin Khalji, and by the later historians Ziauddin Barani and Isami; the Rajput side is remembered chiefly in Nayachandra Suri's Sanskrit poem Hammira Mahakavya (fifteenth century) and in later Hindi and Rajasthani ballads. Details of betrayal, of Hammir's last fight and of his family come mostly from these later poetic sources.*

### Ranthambore and its ruler

The fort of **Ranthambore** stands on a high, isolated hill in the forests of eastern Rajasthan, surrounded by ravines and ridges of the Vindhya and Aravalli ranges. After the fall of **Prithviraj III** at Tarain in 1192, a branch of the **Chauhan** family made it their seat, and for a century they held out against the rulers of Delhi. Iltutmish and Balban both campaigned against it; Jalaluddin Khalji besieged it in 1291–92 and withdrew, reportedly saying that the fort was not worth the lives of his men.

**Hammir Dev** (Hammira) came to the throne around **1283**. His inscriptions and the Hammira Mahakavya show him as an active, expansionist ruler who raided neighbouring kingdoms, including Malwa and Mewar, and performed royal sacrifices. By the 1290s he was the most powerful Hindu ruler left in the region between Delhi and Malwa.

### The cause of the war

The immediate cause lay in an incident of **1299**. Alauddin Khalji's army, returning from the conquest of Gujarat under **Ulugh Khan** and **Nusrat Khan**, quarrelled over the division of plunder. A group of "New Muslim" Mongol soldiers mutinied, killed several officers, and fled. Two of their leaders, **Muhammad Shah** and his brother **Kehbru**, took refuge with Hammir Dev, who gave them land and protection. Alauddin demanded their surrender; Hammir refused. In the Hammira Mahakavya and later ballads this refusal becomes the heart of the story: a Rajput king who would not give up those who had sought his shelter. The Persian writers simply treat it as defiance.

### The first campaign

Late in 1299 Ulugh Khan and Nusrat Khan advanced, took the town of **Jhain**, and laid siege to Ranthambore. During the siege Nusrat Khan was struck by a stone from a mangonel fired from the fort and died a few days later. Hammir's forces then made a sortie and drove Ulugh Khan back. The defeat was serious enough that Alauddin decided to come in person.

### The sultan's siege

Alauddin arrived in **1300** and took personal command. The fort could not be stormed easily, so he settled down to a long siege. Khusrau and Barani describe how his men built a **pashib**, a great ramp of sacks filled with sand, to bring troops and siege engines up close to the walls, while stones from the fort's engines fell among them.

The siege lasted many months and was hard on the besiegers. While Alauddin was at Ranthambore, his nephew **Akat Khan** tried to assassinate him during a hunt at Tilpat; two other nephews rebelled in Badaun and Awadh; and an officer named **Haji Maula** seized Delhi for a time. Alauddin crushed each revolt without lifting the siege, and these crises later led him to tighten his control over his nobles. That he stayed shows how much he wanted the fort.

Inside, the defenders suffered more. Khusrau writes that food ran so short that a single grain of rice was bought for two gold pieces; the image is poetic, but famine clearly set in. The Hammira Mahakavya says two of Hammir's commanders, **Ratipala** and **Ranamalla**, went over to the sultan, weakening the defence. This detail is not confirmed by the Persian sources, and the poem, written about a century later, may shape events to its moral purpose, but desertions are not unlikely in a long blockade.

### The fall of the fort

The fort fell in **July 1301**. Khusrau, in a passage often cited as the earliest Persian description of jauhar, writes that the Rai lit a fire and cast the women into it, and then came out with his remaining men to fight. The Rajput tradition names Hammir's queen **Ranga Devi** as leading the women into the fire. Hammir Dev was killed in the final fighting. Jauhar was a terrible act carried out by women facing capture and enslavement; it should be understood in that context, not as something to be admired.

The Mongol refugee Muhammad Shah fought beside Hammir and was found wounded. According to later accounts, when Alauddin asked him what he would do if his wounds were healed, he replied that he would kill the sultan and place Hammir's son on the throne; Alauddin had him executed. Whatever the exact words, the story shows how the refuge given by Hammir was remembered on both sides.

Ranthambore was placed under Ulugh Khan, and the Chauhan dynasty of Ranthambore came to an end.

### Memory and meaning

The fall of Ranthambore opened the way for Alauddin's campaigns against **Chittor** in 1303 and against Siwana and **Jalore** in the following years. In Rajput memory Hammir became a symbol of stubborn honour; the phrase "Hammir hath" (Hammir's obstinacy) passed into proverb, and works such as the Hammir Raso and Hammirayana retold his story. Historians caution that these later texts add speeches, omens and characters that cannot be checked, but the core events — the shelter given to the rebels, a long siege, the death of Nusrat Khan, a jauhar and the death of Hammir in 1301 — are attested by Khalji-period writers.

### Key points
- **Ruler.** Hammir Dev Chauhan ruled Ranthambore from about 1283 and was the strongest Hindu power between Delhi and Malwa.
- **Cause.** He sheltered Mongol rebels from Alauddin's army and refused to give them up.
- **First campaign.** In 1299 the Khalji generals were repulsed and Nusrat Khan was killed by a stone from the fort.
- **Siege.** Alauddin besieged the fort in person, holding on despite revolts and an attempt on his life.
- **Fall.** The fort fell in July 1301 after a jauhar; Hammir Dev died fighting.

## The Siege of Chittorgarh, 1303 — History and the Legend of Padmini

*The siege itself is recorded by Amir Khusrau, who was present in Alauddin Khalji's camp and wrote of it in his Khaza'in al-Futuh, and more briefly by Barani and Isami; Mewar's own inscriptions, such as the Kumbhalgarh inscription of 1460, name the defenders. The story of Rani Padmini, the mirror, and Gora and Badal comes from Malik Muhammad Jayasi's Awadhi poem Padmavat (1540), later Rajasthani versions, and James Tod; most historians regard it as literature rather than record.*

### Chittor and Mewar

**Chittorgarh** stands on a long, steep-sided plateau above the plain of the Berach and Gambhiri rivers in southern Rajasthan. By the late thirteenth century it was the capital of the **Guhila** rulers of **Mewar**, a dynasty that traced its line back to the seventh century. The senior branch bore the title **Rawal**. A junior branch held the village of **Sisoda**, and would later give its name to the Sisodia dynasty.

In 1302 **Ratnasimha**, remembered as **Rawal Ratan Singh**, succeeded his father **Samarasimha**. An inscription of that year confirms his accession. He had ruled for barely a year when the Delhi army arrived.

### Why Alauddin came

**Alauddin Khalji** had already taken Gujarat in 1299 and **Ranthambore** in 1301. Chittor was the strongest fort in Rajasthan and controlled routes between Delhi, Malwa and Gujarat. Its capture fitted the pattern of his reign: an ambitious sultan subduing the strong Rajput forts that could threaten his communications and refuse tribute. The Persian writers give no other reason, and none is needed to explain the campaign.

### The siege

Alauddin left Delhi on **28 January 1303** and camped between the Berach and Gambhiri. Khusrau describes the sultan holding court on a nearby hill, the camp spread across the plain, and mangonels hurling stones at the walls. The rains came during the siege, and the operations dragged on for about eight months. Khusrau gives few details of the fighting, but he makes clear that the fort could not be taken quickly.

On **26 August 1303** the fort was taken. According to Khusrau, the Rai came out and submitted, and was spared; afterwards the sultan ordered a massacre of the common people of the area, and Khusrau gives a figure of thirty thousand killed. Large numbers in such texts are often exaggerated, but there is no reason to doubt that the conquest was brutal.

Mewar's own tradition, recorded in the Kumbhalgarh inscription more than 150 years later, says that **Lakshmasimha** (Rana Lakha) of Sisoda died defending Chittor together with several of his sons. The fate of Ratan Singh is uncertain: Khusrau implies he survived, while later Mewar tradition has him die in battle. Historians generally note that the sources cannot be reconciled with certainty.

Contemporary Persian writers do not clearly describe a jauhar at Chittor in 1303, though Khusrau describes one at Ranthambore two years earlier. The jauhar of Chittor in this siege is firmly established in Rajput tradition and later literature, and it may well have happened, but the record for it is weaker than for the later sieges of 1535 and 1568.

Alauddin renamed the fort **Khizrabad** and gave it to his son **Khizr Khan**. Within about a decade the Sultanate's direct hold weakened, and the fort was entrusted to **Maldeva**, a Songara Chauhan chief allied to the sultan. Sisodia power under **Hammir Singh** later recovered Chittor, probably in the 1320s or 1330s.

### The Padmini legend

Today the siege is best known through the story of **Rani Padmini** (Padmavati). In Jayasi's **Padmavat**, written in **1540**, more than two centuries after the siege, Ratansen, king of Chittor, wins Padmavati, princess of Sinhala (Sri Lanka), after a long quest guided by a talking parrot. A banished Brahmin describes her beauty to Alauddin, who besieges Chittor to win her. In the poem Alauddin glimpses her reflection in a mirror, takes Ratansen captive by deceit, and is outwitted when **Gora** and **Badal** smuggle soldiers into his camp in palanquins and rescue the king. Ratansen later dies fighting another king, his queens burn themselves on his pyre, and when Alauddin finally enters Chittor he finds only ashes.

Jayasi was a Sufi poet, and he ends his poem with an allegory in which Chittor is the body, Ratansen the mind, and Padmavati wisdom. Later Rajasthani poets, such as Hemratan in his *Gora Badal Padmini Chaupai* (1589), reshaped the story as a Rajput heroic tale, and in the nineteenth century **James Tod** published it in his Annals as history. From there it entered school books, plays and films.

Most historians, beginning with scholars such as Gaurishankar Hirachand Ojha, have concluded that the Padmini story cannot be confirmed: Khusrau, who was present, does not mention it, though some scholars read a veiled allusion in one passage. The legend still tells us much about how Rajput society later remembered the siege and about the values of honour and loyalty that the bards wished to celebrate.

### Significance

The fall of Chittor in 1303 was the first of the three great sieges of the fort, followed by those of **1535** under Bahadur Shah of Gujarat and **1567–68** under Akbar. Together they made Chittor a symbol of resistance in Rajput memory, and the jauhar and saka (the final sortie of the men) became central to how those sieges are remembered. Jauhar should be understood in its historical setting: a desperate act by women facing capture and enslavement, not something to be glorified.

### Key points
- **Date.** Alauddin Khalji besieged Chittor from January to 26 August 1303, about eight months.
- **Defenders.** Rawal Ratan Singh ruled; Mewar tradition says Lakshmasimha of Sisoda and his sons died defending the fort.
- **Aftermath.** Khusrau records a massacre; the fort was renamed Khizrabad and given to Khizr Khan.
- **Ratan Singh's fate.** It is uncertain: Khusrau suggests he submitted, later tradition says he died fighting.
- **Padmini.** The story of Padmini, the mirror and Gora–Badal comes from Jayasi's Padmavat (1540) and is regarded by most historians as legend.

## The Siege of Jalore — Kanhadadeva and the End of the Songara Chauhans

*The Persian record of the Khalji conquest of Jalore is brief, found mainly in Isami, Barani and the later Firishta. The fullest account is the Old Gujarati poem Kanhadade Prabandha, written by the poet Padmanabha in 1455 for a descendant of the Chauhans, together with Muhnot Nainsi's seventeenth-century Khyat. These Rajput sources are rich in speeches, omens and romance, and their details should be read as tradition.*

### Jalore and the Songaras

The fort of **Jalore** crowns a granite hill in south-western Marwar, overlooking the valley of the Sukri river on the routes between Gujarat and the north. Its old name was **Suvarnagiri**, the "golden hill", which in local speech became **Sonagir**; the branch of the **Chauhans** who ruled it were therefore called **Songaras**. They had held Jalore since the late twelfth century, when **Kirtipala** founded the line, and had survived earlier attacks from Delhi.

**Kanhadadeva** (Kanhad Dev) became ruler in the 1290s. In the time of Alauddin Khalji he was the strongest Rajput ruler left in Marwar after the fall of Ranthambore in 1301 and of Chittor in 1303.

### Earlier tensions

According to the Kanhadade Prabandha, the conflict began in **1299**, when Alauddin's army under **Ulugh Khan** set out to invade Gujarat. The poem says Kanhadadeva refused to let the army pass through his territory. After the army sacked the temple of **Somnath**, Kanhadadeva's forces are said to have attacked it on its return, freed captives, and recovered fragments of the sacred image, which he enshrined in his own lands. The Persian sources do not confirm this episode, though they record the troubles of the returning army and the mutiny in its ranks that led to the Ranthambore war.

Firishta adds a different story, that Kanhadadeva had at one point accepted the sultan's authority and attended the court at Delhi, but left offended when the sultan boasted that no Hindu raja could stand against him. Both stories may reflect real friction; neither can be checked in detail.

### The fall of Siwana

Before Jalore, Alauddin attacked its neighbour **Siwana**, held by Kanhadadeva's kinsman **Sataldeva**. Siwana fell in **1308** after a hard siege; Sataldeva was killed, and the fort was renamed **Khairabad**. Jalore was now isolated.

### The siege of Jalore

The campaign against Jalore was conducted by Alauddin's generals rather than by the sultan in person. The Prabandha describes several rounds of fighting over more than one season, in which the Chauhans at first defeated the Sultanate troops and raided their camps, before Alauddin sent reinforcements. The decisive commander named in the Persian sources is **Malik Kamaluddin Gurg**, a senior officer who had fought at Siwana.

The siege followed the familiar pattern of the period: blockade, mangonels against the walls, and a slow wearing-down of the garrison's food and water. Jalore's hill was well defended, and the Prabandha speaks of many assaults beaten back.

The poem says the fort fell through betrayal. A **Dahiya** Rajput named **Bika** (Vika), angered at his treatment or tempted by reward, is said to have shown the besiegers a hidden path into the fort. In the tradition his own wife, ashamed of his act, killed him. The episode is famous in Marwar, but it comes only from the Rajput poetic sources.

### The end of the fort

When the fort could no longer be held, the Prabandha says, the women of Jalore performed **jauhar**, and Kanhadadeva led the men out in a final fight in which he was killed. His son **Viramadeva** carried on the resistance briefly and died soon after. Jalore fell in about **1311**; some historians place it in 1310. Jauhar was an act of despair by women facing capture and enslavement; it is recorded here as part of the history and memory of the siege, not as an ideal.

The Prabandha also tells a romance in which a daughter of Alauddin, named **Firoza** or Sitai in different versions, falls in love with Viramadeva, who refuses her, and after his death she carries his head to Delhi and takes her own life. This is a literary invention with no historical support, though it remains popular in Rajasthan.

### Aftermath and memory

With Jalore and Siwana taken, the Delhi Sultanate controlled the main Chauhan strongholds of Marwar. Its hold was not permanent: after Alauddin's death in 1316 Khalji power declined, and Jalore later passed to other rulers, including a line of Afghan governors who held it in the fifteenth century.

For the Rajputs of Marwar and Gujarat, Kanhadadeva became a hero of resistance, and the Kanhadade Prabandha is an important early work in the region's literature as well as a source for the customs, weapons and society of the time. Historians use it with care: it was written a century and a half after the events, for a patron who claimed descent from the Songaras, and it shapes the story to show the honour of the Chauhans.

What is clear from both sides is the outline: a strong Rajput fort that held out for years against the Delhi Sultanate, the earlier fall of Siwana, and the conquest of Jalore around 1311 with the death of its ruler.

### Key points
- **Fort.** Jalore, on the hill of Suvarnagiri (Sonagir), was the seat of the Songara Chauhans.
- **Ruler.** Kanhadadeva was the strongest Rajput ruler left in Marwar after Ranthambore and Chittor fell.
- **Prelude.** Siwana fell to Alauddin's forces in 1308, isolating Jalore.
- **Fall.** Jalore was taken around 1311 under Malik Kamaluddin Gurg; Kanhadadeva died fighting and his son Viramadeva soon after.
- **Sources.** The main account is Padmanabha's Kanhadade Prabandha (1455); its betrayal by Bika and the romance of Alauddin's daughter are tradition.

## Chittor under Hammir Singh — The Sisodia Recovery and the Tughlaq Challenge

*No Persian chronicle of the Delhi Sultanate records a Tughlaq siege of Chittor or a defeat by Mewar. The story of Hammir Singh's recovery of Chittor and his victory over the sultan's forces comes from Mewar's own inscriptions, such as the Kumbhalgarh prashasti of 1460 and the Chittor inscriptions of Rana Kumbha, from later Mewar chronicles, and from James Tod. Its date and details are uncertain; the year 1326 given here is traditional.*

### Chittor after 1303

After **Alauddin Khalji** took Chittor in 1303, he renamed it **Khizrabad** and placed his son **Khizr Khan** there. The direct hold of the Sultanate did not last. Within a few years the fort was handed to **Maldeva**, a **Songara Chauhan** chief of the Jalore family who had made his peace with Alauddin, and who governed it as a client of Delhi. After Alauddin's death in **1316**, the Khalji state fell into confusion, and in **1320** the **Tughlaq** dynasty came to power under Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq. His son **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** succeeded in **1325**.

### Hammir Singh of Sisoda

The senior **Rawal** line of the Guhilas had been broken by the conquest of 1303. The junior branch, the Ranas of **Sisoda**, survived. According to Mewar tradition, **Lakshmasimha** of Sisoda and most of his sons died defending Chittor in 1303; one son, **Ari Singh**, also fell, but his son **Hammir** survived as a boy.

Hammir grew up in the hill country of Mewar, where the Sisodias kept their following. Tradition says he built up power by raids from the hills around Kelwara, gathering Rajput and Bhil supporters and wearing down the authority of the Songara administration in the countryside. The chronicles add a famous story: Maldeva, seeking to bind the young chief to himself, offered Hammir his daughter in marriage. She was said to be a widow, which was intended as an insult, but she became Hammir's ally and helped him win over the garrison, so that Chittor passed to him with little fighting. The story is told by Tod from Mewar sources and cannot be checked.

What is reasonably clear is that Hammir recovered Chittor from the Songaras in the first half of the fourteenth century. Dates proposed by historians range from about **1326** to the 1330s. With this, the **Sisodia** dynasty began its rule from Chittor, and Hammir took the title **Rana**, which his successors kept.

### The conflict with the Tughlaqs

According to Mewar tradition, Maldeva's son **Jaisa** (or Banbir) fled to Delhi and asked the sultan for help. An army sent by **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**, or according to some versions led by the sultan himself, marched into Mewar. The armies met at **Singoli**, and the Rajputs won. The later chronicles add that the sultan was captured and held prisoner for three months, and released only after paying a huge ransom and surrendering Ajmer, Ranthambore, Nagaur and other places together with a hundred elephants.

Historians treat this account with great caution. Muhammad bin Tughlaq's reign is well documented by Barani, by the traveller **Ibn Battuta**, who served at his court, and by others, and none of them mentions any such defeat or captivity. The territorial claims are also impossible to reconcile with the Sultanate's later hold on Ajmer and Ranthambore. The sultan was certainly beset by rebellions at this time, among them the revolts of his cousin Bahauddin Gurshasp in the Deccan in 1326–27 and of Kishlu Khan at Multan in 1327–28, and he could not easily spare forces for Rajasthan. Many historians therefore suggest that the battle at Singoli was a real clash with Sultanate troops, perhaps under a provincial commander and supported by the Songaras, which later tradition enlarged into a victory over the sultan himself.

The Kumbhalgarh inscription, written about a century later, praises Hammir for victories over Muslim armies and gives him the epithet *vishama-ghati-panchanana*, "a lion in difficult passes". That supports the idea of real fighting against Sultanate forces, without confirming the details of the later story.

### Hammir's achievement

Whatever the details, Hammir Singh's reign marked a turning point. Within a generation of the disaster of 1303, Mewar had a new ruling line, its capital back at Chittor and its independence in practice restored. Tughlaq power in Rajasthan, never firm, faded as Muhammad bin Tughlaq's reign ran into crisis after crisis, and the Sultanate itself broke up after **Timur's** sack of Delhi in 1398.

Hammir is remembered as a restorer who built up Mewar's power by patience and local alliances rather than by single dramatic battles. His successors, **Kshetra Singh** and **Lakha**, extended Mewar's territory, and in the fifteenth century **Rana Kumbha** and later **Rana Sanga** made it the strongest Rajput state in north India.

### Reading the sources

The story of 1326 shows the problem of Rajput history in this period. The Persian chronicles record the deeds of the sultans and are silent on events that did not concern Delhi or that did not flatter it. The Rajput sources, mostly written much later, preserve memories of local events but enlarge them in praise of their heroes. The careful conclusion is that Hammir recovered Chittor and resisted Sultanate forces with success, while the capture of Muhammad bin Tughlaq belongs to tradition.

### Key points
- **Background.** After 1303 Chittor was held for Delhi by Khizr Khan and then by the Songara chief Maldeva.
- **Hammir Singh.** A survivor of the Sisoda branch, he built up power in the hills and recovered Chittor, traditionally around 1326.
- **New dynasty.** His recovery began the rule of the Sisodia Ranas from Chittor.
- **Singoli.** Mewar tradition says he defeated and captured Muhammad bin Tughlaq; no contemporary Persian source confirms it.
- **Legacy.** Mewar regained practical independence and later grew into a leading Rajput power.

## The Battle of Khanwa — Rana Sanga's Last Stand Against Babur

*Babur's own memoir, the Baburnama, which reproduces his victory proclamation (fathnama), is the main contemporary source for Khanwa. Later Persian histories and the Mewar chronicles add detail, while bardic tradition supplies much of the colour around Rana Sanga's wounding and the betrayals in his camp.*

### Background

When **Zahir-ud-din Muhammad Babur** defeated Ibrahim Lodi at **Panipat** in April 1526, he won Delhi and Agra, but not northern India. The strongest power left standing was **Rana Sangram Singh of Mewar**, remembered as **Rana Sanga** (r. c. 1508–1528). Over two decades he had fought the sultans of Malwa, Gujarat and Delhi, extended Mewar's influence towards Bayana and the Chambal, and gathered most of the leading Rajput houses around him.

Babur later wrote that Sanga had promised to help him against Ibrahim Lodi and then failed to move; Rajput sources say the opposite. Whatever the truth, both men now saw each other as the obstacle. Sanga expected the Timurid adventurer to plunder and go home, as Timur had done in 1398. When Babur stayed, a confrontation became unavoidable.

### The forces and commanders

Sanga's army was a confederacy rather than a single command. Alongside the Sisodias of Mewar came contingents from **Marwar**, **Amber** (under Prithviraj Kachwaha), the Hadas, the Jhalas, and **Medini Rai of Chanderi**. Two important Muslim allies joined him: **Hasan Khan Mewati**, lord of Mewat, and **Mahmud Lodi**, a brother of the dead Ibrahim who claimed the Delhi throne. Babur put Sanga's strength at 200,000; modern historians treat this as a victor's exaggeration, though the Rajput host was certainly much larger than Babur's.

Babur's army probably numbered somewhere in the low tens of thousands. Its strength lay in organisation: Central Asian mounted archers trained in the **tulughma** flanking manoeuvre, matchlockmen, and field guns under **Ustad Ali Quli** and **Mustafa Rumi**. As at Panipat, he used the Ottoman-style tactic of carts chained together (**araba**) with gaps for guns and cavalry, ditches in front, and protected positions for musketeers.

### The road to Khanwa

The campaign opened badly for Babur. In February 1527 Sanga took **Bayana** and mauled a Mughal advance force near it. Babur records that his men were badly shaken; an astrologer predicted defeat, and some officers wanted to retreat to Kabul. Babur answered with theatre and policy. He publicly renounced wine, had his gold and silver drinking vessels broken and given to the poor, remitted a trade tax (*tamgha*) for Muslims, and declared the campaign a holy war. He then made his soldiers swear on the Quran to stand. He chose ground at **Khanwa**, about sixty kilometres west of Agra, and spent days entrenching.

Sanga, by most accounts, gave him that time. He lingered at Bayana for several weeks — a delay later writers blame on overconfidence or the slow assembly of allies.

### The battle

The armies met on **16 March 1527** (some calculations give 17 March). The Rajput cavalry attacked with great force against both Mughal wings. Babur's right came under heavy pressure and had to be reinforced from the centre. For several hours the fighting was close and its result uncertain; Babur himself admitted it was the hardest battle he had fought in India.

The Mughal guns and matchlocks firing from behind the carts inflicted steady losses on massed horsemen who could not break through the barricade. Babur then sent his flanking columns round both ends of the Rajput line in the tulughma manoeuvre, and pushed his centre forward with the guns. Packed together and attacked from front and sides, the confederate army began to lose cohesion.

The turning point came when **Rana Sanga was wounded** — struck on the head, according to most accounts, possibly by an arrow — and fell unconscious. His attendants carried him off the field. Tradition says that **Jhala Ajja** took up the royal insignia so that the army would think the Rana was still fighting, and fell under them. Some sources also say that **Silhadi**, the chief of Raisen, went over to Babur during the battle; historians are divided on whether this happened. Either way, once news spread that the Rana was gone, the confederacy broke apart.

### Outcome and consequences

The losses were heavy. Hasan Khan Mewati was killed, along with many Rajput chiefs, including Ratan Singh Rathore of Merta and Ramdas of Ajmer according to the chronicles. Babur raised a tower of skulls near the field and took the title **Ghazi**.

Rana Sanga came to at **Baswa** and is said to have sworn not to return to Chittor until he had beaten Babur. He gathered troops again and marched towards Chanderi, where Babur was besieging his ally Medini Rai, but he died at **Kalpi** in January 1528. Several sources claim his own nobles poisoned him because they did not want another war. Chanderi fell to Babur that same month.

Khanwa settled more than Panipat had. Panipat removed a dynasty already in trouble; Khanwa broke the only coalition that could have pushed the Timurids out of the Ganga–Yamuna plain. The Rajput states were not conquered — Mewar would fight the Mughals for another ninety years — but never again did a Rajput leader command such a broad alliance aiming at Delhi.

### How the sources differ

Babur's account is vivid but partisan: he inflates the enemy's numbers, frames the war in religious language, and says little about his own losses. Mewar's chronicles and the bards make Sanga's defeat the result of betrayal and bad luck rather than of tactics, and give Silhadi a central villain's role that the Persian record does not clearly support. Modern historians generally agree on the essentials — Sanga's delay at Bayana, Babur's fortified position, the effect of guns and flanking attacks, and the collapse after the Rana's wounding — and treat precise numbers on either side as unknowable.

### Key points
- **Date and place.** Fought on 16 March 1527 at Khanwa, west of Agra, about a year after Panipat.
- **Two kinds of army.** A large Rajput–Afghan confederacy under Rana Sanga faced Babur's smaller army of horse archers, matchlockmen and field guns.
- **Babur's preparation.** After a setback near Bayana he rallied his men with a vow against wine and a call to holy war, and fortified his position with carts and ditches.
- **Turning point.** Rana Sanga's wounding and removal from the field, not a single charge, led to the confederacy's collapse.
- **Consequences.** Babur's hold on the north was secured; Sanga died in January 1528, and no comparable Rajput coalition ever formed again.

## The Siege of Chittorgarh, 1567–1568 — Jaimal, Patta and the Fall of Mewar's Citadel

*The siege is unusually well documented: Abul Fazl's Akbarnama, Akbar's own victory proclamation (the Fathnama of 1568), Badauni and Nizamuddin Ahmad all describe it, and the Mewar chronicles and later writers such as James Tod preserve the Rajput memory. The bards add details — especially about Jaimal and Patta — that cannot be checked against the Persian record.*

### Background

By the mid-1560s **Akbar** had secured Malwa and won over the Kachwahas of Amber through alliance and marriage. Mewar, ruled by **Maharana Udai Singh II** (r. 1537–1572), was the most prestigious Rajput state still outside the Mughal system, and it had sheltered Baz Bahadur of Malwa and other men Akbar regarded as rebels. Its great fort of **Chittorgarh**, on a long mesa rising some 150 metres above the plain, controlled the routes between Agra, Malwa and Gujarat. Chittor had already fallen twice — to Alauddin Khalji in 1303 and to Bahadur Shah of Gujarat in 1535 — but it remained the symbol of Sisodia sovereignty.

In September 1567 Akbar marched on Mewar in person and arrived before Chittor in **October 1567**.

### The forces and commanders

Udai Singh did not stay to defend the fort. On the advice of his council he withdrew with his family and treasure into the hills to the west, leaving the defence to **Jaimal Rathore** (Jaimal Mertiya, of the Merta branch of the Rathores, who had lost Merta to Mughal arms) and the young **Patta (Fateh Singh) Sisodia** of Kelwa. Later writers have argued fiercely over this decision — Tod called it cowardice, others see sound strategy that kept the dynasty alive. Its consequence is clear: Mewar's ruler survived to keep fighting, and his son Pratap inherited an unbroken claim.

According to Abul Fazl the garrison numbered about **8,000 Rajputs**, and some **40,000 peasants** had taken refuge inside the walls. The Mughal army was much larger, with heavy guns, musketeers and large numbers of labourers; Akbar directed operations himself. Reliable totals for the besieging force do not survive, and the large figures in later accounts are estimates.

### The course of the siege

Akbar ringed the fort with camps and batteries, but early assaults achieved nothing. Mughal engineers then began two methods at once: **mines** dug towards the base of the walls, and **sabats** — covered trenches roofed with timber and hide, wide enough for horsemen to ride through — pushed up the slope under fire.

In **December 1567** two mines were fired. The first exploded and opened a breach; Mughal troops rushed in just as the second, its fuse burning longer, went off beneath them. Hundreds of attackers were killed, along with defenders on the wall. The garrison repaired the gap during the night. Through the winter the Rajputs fought back with sallies, musket fire and constant rebuilding of damaged sections, while the Mughals brought up larger guns and extended the sabats.

On the night of **22–23 February 1568** the decisive moment came. Akbar, watching from a raised firing post, saw a figure directing repairs by torchlight at a breach and shot him with his own musket, which he called *Sangram*. The man was Jaimal. Rajput tradition, which differs slightly, says Jaimal had already been wounded in the leg, and that his kinsman **Kalla Rathore** carried him on his shoulders so that both could fight in the final battle.

### Jauhar and the final assault

With Jaimal dead or wounded and the walls breached, the defenders knew the end had come. That night fires were seen in several places inside the fort. Abul Fazl records **jauhar** in three houses, including those of Patta and Jaimal: the women of the garrison chose death by fire rather than capture. The tradition is remembered in Mewar as one of Chittor's three great jauhars, and it must be understood as the grim outcome of a war in which captivity meant enslavement.

At dawn on **23 February 1568** the men, in saffron, fought the **saka** — the final battle to the death. The Mughals entered through the breaches with elephants among the assault troops. Patta was killed; the Persian sources say he was trampled by an elephant. Jaimal fell in the fighting near the gates. Memorial chhatris to Jaimal and Kalla still stand inside the fort.

### Outcome and consequences

The fall of Chittor was followed by a massacre. Abul Fazl, Akbar's admiring biographer, states that about **30,000 people** were killed, most of them the peasants who had taken refuge in the fort, because they had joined in the resistance. Akbar's Fathnama presents the war in harsh religious terms. Historians count this among the darkest episodes of his reign, and it contrasts with the more conciliatory policy he soon adopted towards Rajputs.

Akbar also honoured his opponents in his own way. He had statues of Jaimal and Patta mounted on stone elephants set up at a fort gate; the French traveller Bernier later described such statues at the entrance of the Delhi fort.

Strategically Chittor was a hollow prize. Udai Singh never returned to it; he developed **Udaipur** as his new capital and died at Gogunda in 1572. Ranthambhor surrendered in 1569 and Kalinjar the same year, so Chittor's fall did weaken Rajput resistance elsewhere. But Mewar itself did not submit: under **Maharana Pratap** it continued the war, and Chittor stayed in Mughal hands until the treaty of 1615 under Jahangir returned it on condition that it not be refortified.

### How the sources differ

The Persian accounts focus on engineering, Akbar's personal courage and the scale of the victory; they are frank about the massacre. The Rajput tradition centres on Jaimal, Patta, Kalla and the jauhar, turning the defeat into a story of loyalty. Points of disagreement include exactly how Jaimal died, whether Udai Singh's withdrawal was prudent, and the numbers — both the 30,000 dead and later claims of far larger armies.

### Key points
- **Dates.** Akbar besieged Chittor from October 1567; the fort fell on 23 February 1568.
- **Commanders.** Udai Singh II withdrew to the hills; Jaimal Rathore and Patta Sisodia led a garrison of about 8,000.
- **Siege methods.** Mines and covered sabat trenches, backed by heavy guns, slowly broke the walls.
- **The end.** Jaimal was shot, jauhar was performed in the fort, and the garrison fell in a final saka.
- **Aftermath.** Abul Fazl records about 30,000 deaths; Mewar moved to Udaipur and fought on, and Chittor returned only in 1615.

## The Battle of Haldighati — Maharana Pratap Against the Army of Akbar

*The best contemporary witness is the historian Abd al-Qadir Badauni, who rode with the Mughal army; Abul Fazl's Akbarnama and Nizamuddin Ahmad add the imperial view. Mewar's later chronicles, Tod's Annals and popular ballads supply the stories of Chetak, the attack on Man Singh's elephant and Jhala Man's sacrifice — some well grounded, some legend.*

### Background

When **Maharana Pratap Singh** succeeded his father Udai Singh II in 1572, Chittor had been in Mughal hands for four years and most Rajput rulers had entered imperial service. **Akbar** sent a series of envoys — Jalal Khan Qurchi, Raja **Man Singh of Amber**, Raja Bhagwant Das and Raja Todar Mal — between 1572 and 1573 to persuade Pratap to attend court and accept Mughal overlordship. Pratap received them courteously but would not come in person. Later legend tells of a quarrel at a dinner with Man Singh; the contemporary sources do not mention it.

In 1576 Akbar ordered a campaign to force the issue. He gave command to Man Singh, a Rajput himself, with **Asaf Khan** among the senior officers. The army moved from Ajmer to **Mandalgarh** and then towards Pratap's base at Gogunda in the Aravalli hills.

### The forces and commanders

Badauni gives the Mughal army as about **5,000 horsemen**; other estimates go up to 10,000. It included Kachwaha, Barha Sayyid and Central Asian contingents, with war elephants and some matchlocks. Pratap's force was smaller, perhaps **3,000 horse**, with elephants, and a body of **Bhil** foot soldiers and archers under **Rana Punja**, who knew the hills intimately.

Pratap's army was not purely Rajput. His vanguard was led by **Hakim Khan Sur**, an Afghan of the Sur family, whose followers had their own reasons to resist the Mughals. Beside him fought **Ram Shah Tanwar**, the exiled ruler of Gwalior, with his three sons; **Bida Jhala** (Jhala Man) of Bari Sadri; and the chiefs of Salumbar, Bedla and other Mewar houses.

### The battle

The armies met on the morning of **18 June 1576** (some reckonings give 21 June) near the narrow **Haldighati** pass, named for its turmeric-yellow soil, and on the more open ground at Khamnor below it. Pratap chose to attack rather than wait.

The opening charge was a success. Hakim Khan Sur and the Rajput vanguard struck the Mughal advance guard and left wing so hard that, in Badauni's words, those troops fled several miles. The Mughal position might have collapsed had not the commander of the reserve, **Mihtar Khan**, rallied the fugitives with drums and the false cry that Akbar himself was arriving with reinforcements.

The fight then became a close, confused struggle among the rocks and ravines. Badauni admits he could not always tell friendly Rajputs from hostile ones, and that he was advised simply to shoot, since a dead Rajput on either side was no loss to the empire — a remark that shows the cold attitudes of the time. The war elephants played a large part. Mewar's elephant **Lona** fought the Mughal elephant **Gajmukta**; then Mewar's prized **Ram Prasad** was captured after its driver was shot. Akbar later renamed it Pir Prasad.

At the height of the battle Pratap, it is said, charged **Man Singh's elephant** on his horse **Chetak**. The ballads tell of Chetak rearing so that his hooves rested on the elephant's head, of Pratap's lance killing the mahout while Man Singh ducked in the howdah, and of the elephant's tusk-sword wounding the horse's leg. The episode is part of Mewar memory and is carved on later reliefs; the Persian sources describe intense fighting round the commanders but not this exact scene.

Pratap himself was wounded. As Mughal pressure grew, **Bida Jhala** took the royal parasol and insignia, drawing the enemy to himself while the Maharana withdrew; he was killed. Ram Shah Tanwar and his sons also fell. Tradition says that Chetak, badly wounded, carried Pratap across a stream and then died; a memorial at **Balicha** marks the spot. Chetak's role is not mentioned in contemporary Persian works, but the story was established in Mewar tradition early on.

### Outcome and consequences

By midday the Mughals held the field. Badauni reports about **150 dead** on the Mughal side and around **500 Rajputs** killed; later bardic tradition inflated the totals into the tens of thousands. The Mughal troops, exhausted by heat and fearing an ambush in the hills, did not pursue. Pratap regrouped at Kolyari.

Man Singh occupied **Gogunda** but found his men short of food in hostile country, and soon withdrew. Akbar was displeased that Pratap had escaped, and for a time Man Singh and Asaf Khan were kept away from court. Akbar then went to Mewar himself in late 1576 and sent further expeditions under Shahbaz Khan and others, which took Kumbhalgarh in 1578 but never captured Pratap.

So Haldighati was a **Mughal victory** in the military sense: the enemy army was driven off, an elephant was captured and the Maharana's capital taken. But it did not achieve the campaign's purpose. Pratap remained free and turned to a long war of raids from the hills, which would bring him back most of Mewar after 1582. In this sense historians speak of a battle won by one side and a war that went the other way.

### How the sources differ

Badauni and Abul Fazl stress the Mughal recovery after the early rout and Pratap's flight. Mewar's chronicles and later Rajasthani writers emphasise the opening success, Pratap's personal duel with Man Singh, and the sacrifices of Jhala Man and Chetak, and some modern writers argue that the result was a draw. Numbers are the clearest example of the gap: Badauni's few hundred dead against the bards' twenty thousand. Even the date is debated by a few days.

### Key points
- **Date and place.** Fought on 18 June 1576 at the Haldighati pass and Khamnor, near Gogunda in the Aravallis.
- **Commanders.** Maharana Pratap, with Hakim Khan Sur, Ram Shah Tanwar, Jhala Man and the Bhil chief Rana Punja, faced Man Singh of Amber and Asaf Khan.
- **The fighting.** Pratap's opening charge routed part of the Mughal army before it rallied; elephants and close combat decided the rest.
- **Legend and record.** Chetak's leap and death and the attack on Man Singh's elephant come mainly from Mewar tradition.
- **Result.** A Mughal battlefield victory that failed to capture Pratap, who continued the war from the hills.
