patan-1790-alliance.story:
Chapter 1: The Last Unity — When Time Made the Rajputs Stand Together

The year 1790 came to Rajputana as a warning. Maratha power was no longer confined to raiding bands; it had become organised, equipped with artillery and politically aggressive. For years Rajasthan had been squeezed in the name of chauth and sardeshmukhi. Forts, towns and fields—all were under Maratha pressure. This time Jaipur and Jodhpur understood that standing apart meant inviting destruction.

This was no ideal unity; it was a unity of necessity. There were old rivalries between the two states, but the Maratha advance brought them onto one platform. Patan was chosen—the frontier region where Maratha supply and movement could be blocked. The Rajput chiefs resolved that if the Marathas were not stopped here, the rest of Rajasthan would slip from their hands as well.

The armies gathered. The combined strength of Jaipur and Jodhpur had veteran cavalry, infantry and a limited number of guns. But they had one more thing—the last line of honour. They knew this war was not only for land, but for the right to the future. The Maratha side was no less prepared. Their armies were disciplined, their artillery capable, and their way of war had evolved with the times.

The earth of Patan felt the weight of both sides—of weapons, of horses, and of the history that was about to take a decisive turn.

Chapter 2: The Clash — When Swords Met Cannon

The battle began with traditional Rajput daring. The combined Rajput cavalry made a furious charge on the forward lines. Clouds of dust rose, war cries rang out, and in the first clash the Maratha vanguard fell back. This was the very moment the Rajputs had hoped for—one decisive push that would break the Maratha lines.

But Maratha warfare did not depend on the charge alone. From behind, the guns spoke. Shot fell across the open field, lines broke, and the horses' momentum was checked. The Maratha commanders wheeled round to press from the flanks, while in the centre the artillery cleared the way. This was a battle of speed and calculation—where coordination was needed as much as courage.

The Rajput alliance counter-attacked. Several times the Maratha detachments fell back, several times Rajput troops were surrounded. Every inch of ground was being bought with blood. Chiefs advanced, fell, and fresh bands came on behind them. This was a battle in which neither side was ready to give up quickly.

But with time a difference became clear. The Maratha supply and artillery stayed constantly active, while the Rajputs had limited resources. The coordination of the combined front—strong on paper—began to falter under pressure on the field. Messages arrived late, attacks came at the wrong moment, and Maratha mobility gained the upper hand.

Chapter 3: The Breaking — When the System, Not Numbers, Decided

As the afternoon wore on, the character of the battle changed. The repeated charges of the Rajput cavalry showed courage, but each time the guns and organised counter-attacks stopped them. Casualties mounted. By estimate thousands of warriors fell on both sides—but Rajput losses were rising fast.

The greatest test of the combined front was coordination. Distance and communication problems emerged between the Jaipur and Jodhpur contingents. The Maratha commanders seized exactly this moment—they increased pressure on the centre and wheeled the flanks to tighten the ring. The Rajput chiefs held their positions bravely, but the battle no longer favoured them.

The order came—close up the lines, get the remaining strength out safely. This was no rout; it was a judicious withdrawal. But the defeat was clear. The Maratha side established control of the field. Patan was now in their hands.

This defeat did not belong to any one king or state. It was the defeat of an age in which traditional warfare had collided with the system of changing times. The Rajputs fought—without doubt—but valour alone was no longer enough to win a war.

Chapter 4: The Meaning of Patan — Warning, Legacy and a Sign of the End

Patan 1790 was not just a battle; it was a sign. A sign that the balance of power in Rajasthan had changed for good. Maratha influence was no longer temporary pressure, but structural dominance. Chauth and political interference grew. The independent policy-making power of the Rajput states was steadily curtailed.

Even so, the story of Patan is not only one of defeat. It is the story of the moment when the Rajputs finally tried to stand together—even if late. It is the story of courage that did not retreat even before modern guns. It is the story of a warning that war changes with time, and those who do not change are left behind by history.

After Patan, Rajputana lost much—but not everything. Honour, memory and lessons survived. For generations to come this battle became a lesson: unity is necessary, but not unity alone—an understanding of strategy, resources and timing is just as essential.

In history some battles bring victory, some defeat—and some set the direction of the future. Patan 1790 was such a battle.

Chapter 1: Marwar After Patan — When War Was Weary, but Not Over

The 1790s were no time of rest for Marwar. After Patan the illusion that Maratha pressure was temporary had been shattered. Now Holkar power wanted a permanent grip towards the north-west—for control of taxes, supplies and military routes. Merta, a strategic town close to Jodhpur's heartbeat, came under attack for exactly this reason. This was not a single battle; it was a series of clashes that went on for years—sometimes on the open field, sometimes in the shadow of forts.

The Rathore power of Marwar was still not lacking in courage, but it had grown weak in resources. Continuous war, the burden of taxes, and the uncertain policies of neighbouring powers—all together were exhausting Marwar. Even so, abandoning Merta was unacceptable. It was not just a town, but a meeting point of routes—the sentinel of the roads leading to Jodhpur.

The Holkar strategy was simple: keep up the pressure, cut the supplies, and win through exhaustion. The Rathore strategy was different: fight for every inch of land, buy time, and counter-attack when the chance came. That is why the war at Merta was not settled at one stroke—it came and went like waves.

Chapter 2: A Series of Clashes — When Every Season Became a War

The first encounters took place on the open field. The Rathore cavalry charged with traditional speed, pushed back the Maratha forward detachments, and gained local advantage. These were the moments when Marwar believed Merta could be saved. But the Holkar army did not rely on its forward troops alone. Behind them were organised forces, artillery and fast-moving bands.

The Maratha counter-attack usually came from the flanks. Night raids, strikes on supply routes and sudden sieges—all became common around Merta. The Rathores in turn relied on forts and high ground. Small detachments sallied out of the forts, fell upon Maratha bands and then returned within the walls. This was a war of speed and patience—where victory was decided not in days, but in months.

The outer areas of Merta changed hands several times. Sometimes the Rathore banner flew, sometimes Maratha dominance showed. With every change the burden on ordinary life grew—fields were laid waste, roads became unsafe, and the tax burden rose. But the war did not stop. Both sides knew that retreating would only invite the next attack.

Chapter 3: Exhaustion and Judgement — When the Meaning of Victory Changed

By the mid-1790s both sides were showing signs of exhaustion. For the Rathores the greatest crisis was resources—horses, weapons, and the men who had been at war for years. The Maratha side had numbers and speed, but they too were paying the price of distant campaigns. Merta was no longer a field of decisive victory, but an arena of attrition.

In some encounters the Rathores gained a clear advantage—Maratha bands fell back, supplies were seized, and local control was restored. On other occasions the Holkars applied pressure—forts were besieged, roads closed, and tax collection enforced. That is why history calls these wars "mixed results". The reality is that there was no quick winner here—only a continuous cost.

In this period Marwar's strategy became more defensive. The primary aim was to avoid losing Merta entirely and to keep Jodhpur secure. The Maratha strategy remained one of constant pressure—they knew time was on their side. The character of the war had changed: it was a test more of patience than of valour.

Chapter 4: The Legacy of Merta — When War Became Memory

By the end of the 1790s the battles of Merta had not ended in any decisive victory, but had arrived at a weary stability. The region leaned sometimes this way, sometimes that—but Marwar did not break completely. That is the real story of Merta: a story of holding on between victory and defeat.

These wars taught Marwar that in a changing age, tradition alone is not enough. Resources, alliances and an understanding of timing are just as necessary. The Maratha power also realised that directly controlling every region is not easy—some places simply cost too much.

Merta today is known not for any single victory, but for the struggle that ground down an entire decade. It was the place where Marwar kept its balance even while falling, and where the Marathas, for all their pressure, found no decisive end.

In history some battles shine, some echo—and some teach slowly. The wars of Merta belong to that third kind: harsh, long and full of lessons.

## Early Conflicts — How the Kachwahas Won a Foothold in Dhundhar

*The founding of Kachwaha power in Dhundhar is known mainly from later Kachwaha genealogies, khyats and James Tod's Annals; contemporary inscriptions record the related Kachchhapaghata rulers of Gwalior and Narwar, but no surviving record describes a sustained war between Kachwahas and Chauhans, and the dates of the founding chiefs are disputed.*

The story of how the Kachwahas came to rule the hill country around **Amber** is often told as a long war between two Rajput houses, the Kachwahas and the Chauhans. The evidence tells a more complicated and more interesting story. The early Kachwahas certainly fought their way into **Dhundhar**, the region of eastern Rajasthan where Jaipur now stands. But according to their own traditions, their main opponents were the **Bargujar** Rajputs and the **Mina** chiefs who held the land before them. The Chauhans mostly appear as relatives by marriage, allies, and later as the overlords of the region.

### Origins: from Gwalior to the Aravallis

The Kachwahas trace their descent to the **Kachchhapaghatas**, a dynasty that ruled around **Gwalior**, **Narwar** and **Dubkund** in central India from the tenth century. Their inscriptions are real and datable. A Gwalior inscription of **977 CE** names **Vajradaman**, who took Gwalior fort, and the great **Sas-Bahu temple inscription of 1093 CE** praises the line of **Mahipala**.

Kachwaha tradition holds that a prince of this house, usually called **Dulha Rai** (or Dhola Rai), son of Sodh Dev, left Narwar after a family dispute and moved west into Dhundhar. The link between the Gwalior Kachchhapaghatas and the Dhundhar Kachwahas is accepted by most historians as likely, but it rests on genealogy, not inscriptions. The date is uncertain: Tod placed Dulha Rai in the **late tenth century (c. 967 CE)**, while several modern historians prefer the **early twelfth century**, around **1128–1137 CE**. The "10th–11th centuries" in the heading should therefore be read as a broad and disputed window.

### The land and its holders

Dhundhar was hill-and-plain country cut by spurs of the **Aravalli** range. Its small forts commanded passes, tanks and fields of millet and barley. When the Kachwahas arrived, the tradition says, the area was divided among **Mina** chiefs (the Susawat Minas at Amber and the Chanda Minas at **Khoh**) and the **Bargujar** Rajputs at **Dausa** and **Deoti**. To the west lay the rising power of the **Chauhans of Shakambhari**, who founded **Ajmer** under **Ajayaraja** in the early twelfth century and, under **Vigraharaja IV**, extended their reach towards Delhi.

### The course of the struggle, as tradition tells it

The khyats describe not a single battle but a run of small campaigns over two or three generations.

- **The marriage alliance.** Dulha Rai is said to have married the daughter of **Ralhan Singh Chauhan** of **Morangarh** (Moran). With his father-in-law's help he took **Dausa** from the Bargujars. This is the clearest Chauhan link in the tradition, and it is an alliance, not a war.
- **Against the Minas.** Dulha Rai then attacked the Mina strongholds. He seized **Khoh** from the Chanda Minas, reportedly by a surprise attack during a festival. Tradition says he later died of wounds received fighting the Minas.
- **Amber.** His son **Kakil Dev** is credited with taking **Amber** from the Susawat Minas and moving the seat of the family there. **Hanu Dev** and **Janad Dev** followed, extending the Kachwaha hold over the surrounding villages.

The methods described are typical of the age: a small band of mounted kinsmen and retainers, fighting from forts at night, seizing cattle and grain, and binding defeated groups by marriage or grants of land. The Minas were not simply driven out. They stayed in Dhundhar, and for centuries Mina families held hereditary roles, including guarding the Kachwaha treasury at **Jaigarh** and **Nahargarh**.

### Where do the Chauhans fit?

The draft this page replaces described decades of open war between Kachwahas and Chauhans over Amber. No inscription or chronicle supports that. Two things are better grounded.

First, the Chauhans of Shakambhari and Ajmer were the leading power of the region by the twelfth century. Small houses like the Kachwahas almost certainly lived in their shadow, paying tribute or serving in their wars, and border clashes over villages and cattle are likely. But they are not documented.

Second, the bardic epic **Prithviraj Raso** makes **Pajjun (Pajawan) Kachwaha** a general of **Prithviraj Chauhan** and husband of his sister. The Raso was much expanded centuries after the events, and historians treat these details with caution. Still, the tradition remembers Kachwahas as Chauhan allies, not enemies.

### Outcome and consequences

By the end of this formative period, however it is dated, the Kachwahas had become masters of a compact territory centred on Amber. They held its forts, had settled kinsmen in its villages, and had made marriage ties with neighbouring Rajput families. There was no sudden victory. Power was built village by village, and the Kachwahas remained a modest regional house for another three hundred years. Only under **Raja Bharmal** in **1562**, when he allied with Akbar, did Amber enter the main stage of Indian politics.

The fall of the Chauhans after **1192**, when Prithviraj was defeated at the second battle of **Tarain**, removed the great power to the west. This helped the small Kachwaha state survive and grow.

### How the sources differ

The main sources are Kachwaha **vanshavalis** and khyats written down from the sixteenth century on; Tod's *Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan* (1829–32), which follows them; and the Kachchhapaghata inscriptions, which say nothing about Dhundhar. Dates for Dulha Rai differ by more than 150 years. The sequence of conquests and the role of individual chiefs come from family tradition and should be read as such. Modern historians agree on the broad outline: a migrant branch of a central Indian dynasty, a struggle with Mina and Bargujar holders, and a slow consolidation at Amber.

### Key points
- **Disputed dates.** Tradition places Dulha Rai's arrival in Dhundhar anywhere from c. 967 to the 1130s CE.
- **Real ancestors.** The Kachchhapaghatas of Gwalior and Narwar are documented in inscriptions from 977 and 1093 CE.
- **Main opponents.** Tradition names the Bargujars of Dausa and the Mina chiefs of Khoh and Amber, not the Chauhans.
- **Chauhan role.** Chauhans appear as in-laws, allies and regional overlords; no recorded war between the two houses survives.
- **Slow growth.** Kachwaha power at Amber grew through small fights, marriages and land grants rather than one decisive battle.

## Living with the Delhi Sultanate — The Quiet Survival of the Kachwahas

*No contemporary Persian chronicle or inscription records a treaty, alliance or regular military service between the Kachwahas of Amber and the Delhi Sultanate in the thirteenth century; what follows sets the thin Kachwaha genealogical tradition against the well-documented history of the Sultanate's wars in eastern Rajasthan, and the "service relationship" is a reasonable inference, not a recorded fact.*

The thirteenth century was the most dangerous period yet for the Rajput houses of northern India. In **1192** Prithviraj Chauhan was defeated at the second battle of **Tarain**. Within a generation a new power, the **Delhi Sultanate**, founded in **1206** under **Qutb-ud-din Aibak**, ruled from the Punjab to Bengal. The small Kachwaha house at **Amber**, in the hills of **Dhundhar**, lay only about 250 kilometres from Delhi. Yet it came through the century intact. How it did so is one of the quieter puzzles of Rajasthan's history.

### What the Kachwaha record says

The Kachwaha genealogies list a series of chiefs for this period: **Pajjun Dev**, **Malesi**, **Bijal Dev**, **Raj Dev**, **Kilhan Dev** and **Kuntal Dev**, the last remembered for building the hill fort of **Kuntalgarh**. Their dates are uncertain, and the genealogies record little beyond names, marriages and local fights. None of these chiefs appears by name in the Persian histories of the Sultanate, such as **Minhaj-us-Siraj's *Tabaqat-i Nasiri*** (completed c. 1260) or **Ziauddin Barani's *Tarikh-i Firuz Shahi*** (1357).

That silence is itself evidence. The Persian chroniclers recorded the great Rajput fortresses that resisted Delhi: **Ranthambhore**, **Chittor**, **Jalor**, **Mandor** and **Gwalior**. Amber does not appear among them. The most likely explanation is that the Kachwahas were too small to be worth a campaign, and that they avoided giving Delhi a reason to send one.

### The wars around them

The Kachwahas did not live in a quiet corner. The Sultanate fought repeatedly in the lands surrounding Dhundhar:

- **Ranthambhore**, held by a branch of the Chauhans, was taken by **Iltutmish** in **1226**. It was lost and retaken several times, and finally fell to **Alauddin Khalji** in **1301** after the famous resistance of **Hammir Dev Chauhan**.
- **Mewat**, the hill country directly north-east of Dhundhar, was the target of harsh campaigns by **Balban** in the **1260s**. Barani describes the clearing of forests and the killing of Mewati raiders who had threatened the roads near Delhi.
- **Chittor** fell to Alauddin in **1303**, and **Jalor** and **Siwana** in western Rajasthan by **1311**.

Sultanate armies marching from Delhi to Ranthambhore and Malwa passed close to Dhundhar. A chief at Amber would have seen what happened to those who resisted openly.

### A strategy of accommodation

Given this, historians generally assume that the Kachwahas, like many smaller chiefs, accepted the Sultanate's overlordship in practice. That would have meant acknowledging the authority of the nearest Sultanate officer (the **iqtadar** or fort commander at Ranthambhore or elsewhere), paying tribute when it was demanded, and keeping the roads through their hills open rather than raiding them. In return they were left alone to rule their villages, settle their kinsmen and fight their own local feuds.

This is not the same as a formal alliance or an "auxiliary contingent" serving Delhi. There is no evidence of Kachwaha troops in Sultanate campaigns during this century. Claims that Amber guarded caravans for Delhi or sent soldiers on its wars are modern guesses, not recorded history. What can be said is that the Kachwahas avoided the fate of Ranthambhore and Chittor, and that avoidance must have involved some degree of submission.

### Forces and leadership

Because no battle is recorded, there are no armies to describe. The Kachwaha chief of this period probably commanded a few hundred mounted kinsmen and retainers, supported by local foot soldiers, including Mina levies. The Sultanate, by contrast, could put tens of thousands of cavalry in the field, with Turkic mounted archers at their core. The gap in strength explains the policy.

### Outcome and consequences

The result of this long, undramatic century was survival. When the Sultanate weakened after **Muhammad bin Tughluq** (died 1351) and broke apart after **Timur's sack of Delhi in 1398**, the Kachwahas were still at Amber. Through the fifteenth century they lived among the regional powers that followed: the Khanzadas of Mewat, the sultans of Malwa and Gujarat, and the rising Sisodias of Mewar. Their first appearance on the wider stage came with **Prithviraj Kachwaha** (r. c. 1503–1527), who is said to have fought for **Rana Sanga** at **Khanwa** in **1527**. Their great political turn came in **1562**, when **Raja Bharmal** allied with Akbar.

Later Kachwaha greatness under the Mughals is sometimes read back into the thirteenth century, as if Amber had already been a trusted partner of Delhi. It was not. The habit of accommodation, though, has a long history: a small house learning to survive beside a much larger power.

### How the sources differ

The **Kachwaha vanshavalis** and later khyats give names and some local events but almost no dates or dealings with Delhi. The **Persian chronicles** describe the Sultanate's Rajasthan campaigns in detail but never mention Amber. **James Tod** fills the gap with bardic material of uncertain age. Modern historians such as **Jadunath Sarkar**, in his *History of Jaipur*, treat the period before the sixteenth century briefly for exactly this reason. Any detailed narrative of Kachwaha–Sultanate relations in this century, including the old draft's account of terms, court debates and patrols, should be treated as reconstruction.

### Key points
- **No treaty on record.** No source documents an alliance or service agreement between Amber and the Delhi Sultanate in the 13th century.
- **Silence as evidence.** Persian chronicles record the sieges of Ranthambhore, Chittor and Jalor, but never mention Amber.
- **Wars nearby.** Iltutmish took Ranthambhore in 1226, Balban ravaged Mewat in the 1260s, and Alauddin took Ranthambhore in 1301 and Chittor in 1303.
- **Likely accommodation.** Historians infer that the Kachwahas accepted Sultanate overlordship in practice and avoided open conflict.
- **Long-term result.** The house survived intact and emerged into wider politics only in the 16th century.

## Haldighati, 1576 — Raja Man Singh Against Maharana Pratap

*The battle is described by an eyewitness on the Mughal side, Abdul Qadir Badauni (Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh), by Abul Fazl's Akbarnama, and on the Mewar side by later works such as the Raj Prashasti inscription (1676), the Amar Kavya and bardic songs; the outline is secure, but numbers, single combats and stories such as Chetak's leap rest partly on tradition.*

On **18 June 1576** (some reckonings give 21 June), two Rajput leaders met in battle at the narrow pass of **Haldighati** in the Aravalli hills, near **Khamnor**, west of **Udaipur**. One was **Maharana Pratap** of Mewar, who refused to accept Mughal overlordship. The other was **Raja Man Singh** of Amber, commanding the army of the emperor **Akbar**. It is the most famous battle in Rajasthan's history and one of the most argued about.

### Background

After Akbar took **Chittor** in **1568**, most Rajput rulers had come to terms with the Mughals. Amber had done so first, under **Raja Bharmal** in **1562**. Pratap, who succeeded his father **Udai Singh II** in **1572**, would not. Between 1572 and 1573 Akbar sent four embassies to him. The second was led by Man Singh himself, followed by **Bhagwant Das** and **Todar Mal**. Pratap received them courteously but would neither attend court in person nor send his heir as a hostage on the terms Akbar wanted.

In **April 1576** Akbar, at Ajmer, gave Man Singh command of an expedition against Mewar. Choosing a Rajput to lead it was a deliberate signal. Man Singh marched to **Mandalgarh**, gathered his forces and moved towards Pratap's base at **Gogunda**.

### The forces and commanders

Numbers are uncertain. Most modern historians estimate the Mughal army at about **5,000–10,000** men and Pratap's at about **3,000**, with a few hundred Bhil archers. Badauni gives 5,000 for the Mughal side; later Mewari accounts give much larger, unreliable figures.

On the **Mughal side**, under Man Singh, rode **Asaf Khan**, the **Sayyids of Barha** under **Sayyid Hashim**, **Jagannath Kachwaha**, **Ghazi Khan Badakhshi**, and Man Singh's kinsman **Madho Singh**. Badauni rode with the army as a volunteer.

On the **Mewar side**, the vanguard was led by the Afghan **Hakim Khan Sur**, an important reminder that the battle was not a religious war. Alongside Pratap fought **Ram Shah Tanwar**, the exiled Raja of Gwalior, and his three sons; **Jhala Man Singh (Bida Jhala)** of Sadri; **Bhama Shah** and his brother **Tarachand**; and **Rana Punja** with his Bhil archers in the hills.

### The course of the battle

Pratap struck first. His charge out of the pass broke the Mughal vanguard and the left wing, made up partly of Rajput allies, and drove it back several miles. Badauni describes the confusion. When he asked Asaf Khan how to tell friendly Rajputs from enemy Rajputs, he was told to shoot anyway, since whichever side lost men, it would be a gain for Islam. The line is often quoted as proof of the battle's bitter Rajput-against-Rajput character.

The Mughal line steadied around the **Sayyids of Barha**, who held their ground on the right, and the centre under Man Singh. The fight then became a close mêlée in the open ground near the pass, later called **Rakt Talai** ("pool of blood"). War elephants clashed: the Mewari elephant **Lona** fought the Mughal **Gajmukta**, and Pratap's elephant **Ram Prasad** was later captured.

At the height of the fighting, tradition says, Pratap rode his horse **Chetak** at Man Singh's elephant and struck at him with his spear. Paintings show Chetak with his forefeet on the elephant's head. The mahout was killed, but Man Singh survived. The turning point came when **Mihtar Khan** of the Mughal reserve rode forward beating drums and shouting that Akbar himself had arrived. This false report revived the Mughal troops.

Pratap was wounded. **Jhala Man Singh** took up the royal parasol and insignia, drew the Mughal attack on himself and was killed. Pratap withdrew into the hills. Mewari tradition says the wounded Chetak carried him over a stream before dying; a memorial stands near the site. Ram Shah Tanwar and his sons died on the field. The fighting lasted about four hours.

### Outcome and consequences

The Mughals held the field, and in that narrow sense they won. But they did not capture or kill Pratap. Exhausted and in rough country, they did not pursue him, and they occupied **Gogunda** only to find themselves hungry and harassed there. Akbar was displeased. Man Singh and Asaf Khan were for a time barred from court, though Man Singh's favour soon returned.

The usual verdict, a tactical advantage for the Mughals but no decisive victory, is fair. Akbar campaigned in Mewar himself later in 1576, and Mughal armies under **Shahbaz Khan** took **Kumbhalgarh** in **1578**. Pratap held out in the hills, recovered much of western and central Mewar after about **1582**, beginning with his success at **Dewair**, and made **Chavand** his capital. He died there in **1597**. Mewar did not accept Mughal terms until **Amar Singh I** made peace with **Jahangir** in **1615**.

For Man Singh, Haldighati was an early command in a long career. He went on to govern Kabul, Bihar and Bengal and became one of the empire's leading men.

### How the sources differ

The **Mughal accounts** present a clear victory and stress Pratap's flight. The **Mewari tradition**, especially from the seventeenth century on, presents a moral victory, sometimes a military one, and adds Chetak's leap and duels between the leaders. In recent years some writers in Rajasthan have argued that Pratap actually won, citing land grants he issued soon after. Most historians still regard the battle as a Mughal tactical success that failed in its strategic aim. Both sides agree on the essentials: Rajputs fought on both sides, an Afghan led Pratap's vanguard, and Pratap escaped to keep fighting.

### Key points
- **Date and place.** 18 June 1576, at Haldighati near Khamnor, west of Udaipur.
- **Commanders.** Raja Man Singh of Amber led Akbar's army; Maharana Pratap led Mewar, with Hakim Khan Sur in his vanguard.
- **Turning point.** The Sayyids of Barha held firm, and a false shout that Akbar had arrived steadied the Mughals.
- **Sacrifice.** Jhala Man Singh took the royal insignia and died covering Pratap's withdrawal.
- **Result.** The Mughals held the field but failed to capture Pratap, who later recovered most of Mewar.

## The Eastern Campaigns — Raja Man Singh in Bihar, Orissa and Bengal

*These campaigns are recorded mainly in Abul Fazl's Akbarnama and in Mughal administrative sources, with later Bengali and Kachwaha traditions (such as the story of the Shila Devi image at Amber); the Mughal chroniclers write from the imperial side and tend to present local resistance simply as "rebellion".*

For most of the 1590s the most important Kachwaha of his age, **Raja Man Singh** of Amber, was fighting and governing more than a thousand kilometres from Rajasthan. His work in the eastern provinces of the Mughal empire was less famous than Haldighati, but it lasted longer and mattered more to the empire. It also cost the Kachwaha house dearly, including the lives of two of Man Singh's sons.

### Background: an unsettled frontier

Akbar's armies had defeated the last Afghan sultan of Bengal, **Daud Khan Karrani**, at **Rajmahal** in **1576**. Conquest, however, was not control. In **1580–81** a great revolt of Mughal officers in Bihar and Bengal shook the province. Afghan chiefs held **Orissa** and the forests of the south-west. In the river delta of east Bengal, the region the Persian sources call **Bhati**, local chiefs known as the **Baro-Bhuyan** (the "twelve landholders") ruled from fortified river towns with fleets of war-boats. The most powerful was **Isa Khan**, who styled himself **Masnad-i-Ala**.

Man Singh came east in **1587** as governor of **Bihar**, succeeding his father **Bhagwant Das**. He was appointed to **Bengal** in **1594**.

### Forces and commanders

Man Singh's armies combined his own Kachwaha contingent, Rajput allies, and imperial mansabdars of every background, Turani, Persian, Afghan and Indian. His sons **Jagat Singh**, **Durjan Singh** and **Himmat Singh** held commands. In the delta the decisive arm was not cavalry but the **nawwara**, the war-fleet, together with river crossings and fortified posts. Here the Mughals were often weaker than their enemies.

The opponents were varied: the Afghan chiefs of Orissa under **Qutlu Khan Lohani** and later **Khwaja Sulaiman** and **Khwaja Usman**; the Baro-Bhuyan of Bhati; and local rajas who shifted allegiance as circumstances changed.

### The course of the campaigns

**Orissa, 1590–1592.** From Bihar, Man Singh marched against the Afghans of Orissa in **1590**. Early in the campaign his son **Jagat Singh**, leading an advance force, was surprised and defeated by the Afghans and narrowly escaped. Qutlu Khan then died, and his successors made terms, recognising Mughal authority and leaving **Puri** under imperial protection. When they broke the agreement, Man Singh returned in **1592**. He defeated the Afghans near **Midnapore**, and Orissa was brought into the empire. Raja **Ramachandra Deva** of **Khurda** submitted and kept his lands.

**Bengal, 1594–1599.** As governor of Bengal, Man Singh founded a new provincial capital at **Rajmahal**, named **Akbarnagar**, in **1595**, a better strategic site than the old capital at Tanda. He then turned against Isa Khan. In **1597** a Mughal force under **Durjan Singh** pressed into the delta near **Vikrampur**. It was trapped by Isa Khan's fleet, and Durjan Singh was killed with many of his men. The same year **Himmat Singh** died of disease. Isa Khan nonetheless judged it wise to make a formal submission, and he died in **1599** still holding most of his territory.

**The Afghan rising and Sherpur Atai, 1600–1601.** In 1599 Man Singh was called west to accompany Prince **Salim** in the war against Mewar. He left Bengal in the hands of Jagat Singh, who died suddenly before he could take up the post, and then of Jagat's young son **Maha Singh**. The Afghans under **Usman** rose again and defeated the Mughals near **Bhadrak**. Man Singh hurried back. In **February 1601** he crushed the Afghans at **Sherpur Atai** in north-west Bengal.

**Against the delta chiefs, 1602–1604.** Man Singh then fought **Kedar Rai** of **Sripur** and the Arakanese (Magh) fleets that raided the coast. Kedar Rai was defeated and died of his wounds in **1603**. Kachwaha tradition holds that the image of the goddess **Shila Devi**, still worshipped in the temple at **Amber Fort**, was brought back from Bengal at this time. Accounts differ on whether it came from Kedar Rai's capital or from **Jessore**.

### Outcome and consequences

Man Singh left Bengal finally around **1605–06**, after Akbar's death. His achievements were real: Orissa was annexed, the Afghan military power was broken at Sherpur Atai, a new capital was founded, and the routes and revenue of west and north Bengal were secured.

The heading's claim that control over Bengal was "consolidated" needs qualifying. The delta was **not** subdued in Man Singh's time. Isa Khan's son **Musa Khan** and the other Bhuyans held out until **Islam Khan**, governor from **1608**, broke them in a series of river campaigns ending around **1611–13**. The Afghan Usman was killed only in **1612**. The eastern frontier was won in stages, and Man Singh's governorship was the first major one.

For the Kachwahas, these years confirmed their place at the heart of the empire. Man Singh rose to a **mansab of 7,000**, the highest rank then held by any noble outside the imperial family. The price was heavy in men and in heirs. The deaths of Jagat Singh, Durjan Singh and Himmat Singh in or around these campaigns shaped the Amber succession for the next generation.

### How the sources differ

**Abul Fazl** gives the fullest narrative but writes as Akbar's official historian, presenting every opponent as a rebel and every success as imperial. **Bengali tradition** remembers the Baro-Bhuyan, especially Isa Khan and Kedar Rai, as defenders of the land, and stories of single combat between Isa Khan and Man Singh are legend rather than record. **Kachwaha sources** stress Man Singh's piety and the Shila Devi image. The *Baharistan-i-Ghaibi*, the key source for the final conquest of the delta, covers only the period after 1608.

### Key points
- **Long service.** Man Singh governed Bihar from 1587 and Bengal from 1594, with interruptions, until about 1605–06.
- **Orissa annexed.** Campaigns of 1590–92 brought Orissa under Mughal rule.
- **Costly delta war.** Durjan Singh was killed fighting Isa Khan's fleet in 1597; the delta held out until after 1608.
- **Sherpur Atai.** In 1601 Man Singh defeated the resurgent Afghans and saved Mughal Bengal.
- **Legacy.** The campaigns raised Man Singh to a mansab of 7,000 and are linked by tradition to the Shila Devi image at Amber.

Chapter 1: From Desert to Snow — The Battlefield Transformed

When the warrior of Rajputana reached the Afghan hills, he understood that this was not Haldighati. There are no battles with colourful banners here. Here the enemy cannot be seen—he hides among the rocks, strikes by night, and is gone by morning. At the start of the 17th century, when Kachwaha chiefs were sent to the Afghan–Kabul frontier, it was not an honour—it was the hardest front of all.

The roads of Kabul, Ghazni and the Khyber were the veins of the Mughal empire. Trade came along these roads, and so did invasion. If these roads loosened, Delhi would become insecure. So the Kachwahas of Amber were posted here—because they were trustworthy, disciplined, and not in the habit of retreating.

This war began with the weather. Icy winds, thin air and unknown mountains. Rajput horses died here. Soldiers' fingers froze. But the order was clear—hold the frontier, whatever the cost.

Chapter 2: The Afghan Mountains — Where War Never Ends

The Afghan tribes were not kingdoms. They went to war because war was their life. They did not build forts—they treated the mountains themselves as forts. The Kachwaha chiefs soon understood that victory here did not mean winning a battle, but keeping up constant pressure.

Mughal policy was simple: make the tribes bow, or break them. And this task was handed to the Kachwaha troops. They built forts in the valleys, set up outposts on the passes, and answered every revolt with twice the severity. This was no heroic saga—it was an exhausting, merciless and endless struggle.

It often happened that a tribe would make terms today and strike from behind tomorrow. The Kachwaha soldiers learned that here mercy was taken for weakness. Villages were laid waste, supplies were cut, and the message made plain—only one power would rule on the frontier.

No count of casualties was kept in this war. Men died not in battle, but from fever, cold and hunger. But every Kachwaha chief knew that if he held on here, his name would be written not only in Rajputana, but in the books of the empire.

Chapter 3: Kabul — The Shield of the Empire

Kabul was not just a city; it was the shield of the empire. Whoever held Kabul kept Hindustan safe. Kachwaha chiefs were appointed here as governors, fort commanders and military commanders. Their job was not only to fight—it was to run the administration.

Here war and governance went hand in hand. Court by day, ambush by night. Sometimes the hill tribes, sometimes foreign raiders. The Kachwaha leadership did here what many could not—they mastered both the sword and the pen.

Living in Kabul meant striking a bargain with death every day. But this was the very place where Kachwaha identity changed. They were no longer just Rajput warriors—they became the frontier guardians of the empire. And this role was not easy. Here defeat meant not only losing one's post, but destabilising the entire north-west.

Chapter 4: Legacy — An Unseen War, a Lasting Impact

There are no folk tales of the Afghan and Kabul campaigns. No Chetak, no jauhar. But those who read history by impact rather than emotion know that this was the hardest chapter of Kachwaha history.

These campaigns decided that Amber would not remain merely a regional power. They proved that Rajputs could be decisive not only in opposition, but in the defence of the empire too. What the Kachwaha chiefs learned here—frontier warfare, long-term suppression, administration—later became the basis of their political power.

Here is a bitter truth: the war that takes the most blood is the one least remembered. The Afghan–Kabul front was just such a war. But had this front fallen, the fire would have reached Delhi.

The Kachwahas put out that fire in the mountains themselves. Without songs, without memorials.
And that is their real legacy.

Chapter 1: The Fire of Succession — When the Empire Burst from Within

When Shah Jahan fell ill in 1657, the Mughal empire split along the line of blood. There were four sons, four armies and one throne. **Dara Shikoh**, the eldest and his father's favourite, held the court at Agra. **Shah Shuja** in Bengal crowned himself and marched west. **Aurangzeb** in the Deccan and **Murad Bakhsh** in Gujarat joined hands.

The greatest Rajput general of the empire was **Mirza Raja Jai Singh I** of Amber. Shah Jahan and Dara gave him the most urgent task: to stop Shuja. Jai Singh was placed beside Dara's young son, **Sulaiman Shikoh**, at the head of the army sent east.

Chapter 2: Bahadurpur — The First Battle of the War

In February 1658 the imperial army found Shuja's camp at **Bahadurpur**, near Benares. Before dawn, the Kachwaha and imperial troops fell on the camp. Shuja's men were not ready; many were still asleep. The camp broke in confusion, and Shuja fled down the Ganga towards Bengal, leaving his guns and baggage behind. It was the first battle of the war of succession, and Jai Singh's men had won it.

Chapter 3: Samugarh — The Battle Jai Singh Did Not Fight

While Jai Singh and Sulaiman were in the east, the war was decided in the west. Aurangzeb and Murad defeated Jaswant Singh of Marwar at Dharmat in April, and on **29 May 1658** they broke Dara's army at **Samugarh**, near Agra. The Rajputs who died for Dara that day were chiefly the **Hadas of Bundi** under **Rao Chhatrasal**, and **Rathore** contingents. The Kachwaha army was hundreds of miles away.

When the news reached the eastern army, Jai Singh made a cold decision. He judged that Dara's cause was lost, left Sulaiman Shikoh, and went over to Aurangzeb with his men. Without the Kachwahas, Sulaiman's army melted away, and the young prince fled to the hills of Garhwal.

Chapter 4: The Price of Judgement

Aurangzeb rewarded Jai Singh with the highest ranks. Before the battle of **Deorai** (1659), it was Jai Singh's letters that persuaded Jaswant Singh not to join Dara. Later, Jai Singh led the campaign against **Shivaji** and made the **Treaty of Purandar** (1665).

History judges Jai Singh in two ways. To some he was a realist who saved Amber by reading the war correctly. To others his change of side was the moment when the last hope of Dara's tolerant vision was lost. Both sides agree on one thing: in 1658 the Kachwahas did not decide the war on the battlefield of Samugarh, but in the camp of the east, with a single decision.

## Battle of Ajmer — Jaipur vs Mughals: The Kachwaha Break with the Throne

*Sources: no contemporary Persian history, Rajasthani khyat or Jaipur court record describes a battle at Ajmer between the Kachwahas and the Mughals in 1702. The documented events are Jai Singh II's service in the Deccan in 1702 and the Rajput rising of 1708 against Bahadur Shah I, recorded in Mughal chronicles and Rajput archives. This account follows that record and treats the "1702 battle" as a later conflation.*

Popular retellings describe a hard fight in the streets of **Ajmer** in **1702**, with Kachwaha horsemen wearing down Mughal garrisons by night raids. The story touches something real, the slow loss of Mughal control over Rajasthan, but no such battle appears in the sources. The real story is more interesting. It is about how a family that had served the Mughals for over a century came to break with them, and why Ajmer mattered so much.

### Ajmer, the key to Rajasthan

Ajmer was the capital of the Mughal province (*subah*) of the same name, which covered most of the Rajput states. **Akbar** had made it a base for his Rajput policy in the 1560s. The shrine of **Khwaja Muin-ud-din Chishti** made it a place of pilgrimage for emperors and commoners alike, and the city sat on the routes between Delhi, Gujarat and Malwa. Whoever held Ajmer could watch Amber, Marwar and Mewar at once. That is why every Mughal crisis in Rajasthan sooner or later became a question about Ajmer.

### The Kachwahas as Mughal partners

The Kachwahas of **Amber** were the oldest Rajput allies of the Mughals. **Raja Bharmal** gave his daughter in marriage to Akbar in **1562**. **Man Singh I** became one of Akbar's greatest generals, and **Mirza Raja Jai Singh I** led Aurangzeb's campaigns against Shivaji in the 1660s. Amber's rulers grew rich and powerful in imperial service, and their state had little reason to rebel.

That partnership came under strain in **Aurangzeb**'s later reign. After the death of Maharaja Jaswant Singh of Marwar in **1678**, Aurangzeb took Marwar under direct control, and the Rathores, led by **Durgadas Rathore** on behalf of the infant **Ajit Singh**, fought a long war of resistance from **1679**. Mewar was drawn in too. The reimposition of the *jizya* in 1679 and the destruction of some temples deepened Rajput distrust. Amber, however, stayed loyal throughout.

### What Jai Singh II was actually doing in 1702

The young **Jai Singh II**, born in **1688**, succeeded his father **Bishan Singh** around **1700**, while still a boy. Like his ancestors he was expected to serve in the field, and the field was the Deccan, where Aurangzeb was spending his last decades fighting the Marathas. In **1702** Jai Singh was with the imperial army at the siege of **Khelna (Vishalgad)**, a Maratha fort that fell to the Mughals that year. Court tradition says that Aurangzeb, impressed by the boy, called him *Sawai*, "one and a quarter", meaning he was worth more than one ordinary man. Historians accept that the title was in use, though the exact story of its granting is a family tradition.

So in 1702 the Kachwaha ruler was not fighting the Mughals at Ajmer. He was fighting for them, a thousand kilometres to the south.

### The real break: 1707–1708

Everything changed when Aurangzeb died at Ahmednagar in **March 1707**. His sons fought for the throne. Jai Singh backed **Azam Shah** at the battle of **Jajau** (June 1707), while his younger brother **Vijay Singh** supported the winner, **Muazzam**, who became emperor as **Bahadur Shah I**. The new emperor punished Jai Singh. Early in **1708** imperial officers occupied Amber, the state was given to Vijay Singh, and a Mughal official took charge of the capital. At the same time Bahadur Shah tried to settle Marwar on his own terms.

This was the moment of open revolt. In **1708** Jai Singh and Ajit Singh of Marwar slipped away from the imperial camp and went to **Udaipur**, where **Maharana Amar Singh II** of Mewar received them. The three houses agreed to act together. The alliance was sealed by the marriage of a Mewar princess to Jai Singh, on the condition that her son would succeed in Amber, a promise that later caused a disputed succession in Jaipur.

The allies moved quickly. The Rathores recovered **Jodhpur**, and Kachwaha forces drove the Mughal officials out of Amber. In late **1708** Rajput troops defeated imperial forces near **Sambhar**, the salt-lake town between Amber and Ajmer. This was the real military clash of the Rajput revolt, and it put Ajmer, the provincial capital, directly under pressure.

### Settlement at the emperor's door

Bahadur Shah could not afford a long war in Rajasthan. In **1709–1710** the Sikh rising under **Banda Singh Bahadur** in the Punjab demanded his attention. In **1710** the emperor came to Ajmer, and terms were reached: Jai Singh and Ajit Singh were confirmed in their states. The revolt had not destroyed Mughal authority, but it had shown that the empire could no longer impose its will on the great Rajput houses.

### Why the episode matters

The "battle of Ajmer" as told in later stories probably compresses this whole period into one dramatic event. The real lesson is the same. Mughal power in Rajasthan rested on partnership, and once that partnership broke, the empire had to bargain. In the following decades Jai Singh II became one of the most influential nobles of the late Mughal court, governed Mughal provinces, founded **Jaipur** in **1727**, and built his famous observatories. Ajit Singh briefly seized Ajmer itself in the early 1720s before being forced out. The Rajput states were no longer junior servants; they were power-brokers in a weakening empire.

### Key points

- **No 1702 battle is recorded.** Contemporary sources describe no Kachwaha–Mughal fight at Ajmer in 1702.
- **Jai Singh II served Aurangzeb.** In 1702 he was at the siege of Khelna in the Deccan, not in revolt.
- **The real break came in 1708.** Bahadur Shah I occupied Amber, prompting the Amber–Marwar–Mewar alliance at Udaipur.
- **Sambhar was the actual clash.** Rajput forces defeated imperial troops near Sambhar in 1708, threatening Ajmer.
- **Ajmer was the strategic key.** As the Mughal provincial capital, it was the centre of imperial control over Rajasthan.
- **The result was a negotiated settlement.** In 1710 Bahadur Shah confirmed the Rajput rulers, a sign of declining Mughal power.

## Battle of Gangwana — Jaipur vs Jodhpur: Rajput Against Rajput

*Sources: the battle of 1741 is recorded in Marwar and Jaipur chronicles (khyats), in Persian accounts of the late Mughal period, and in the work of later historians such as Jadunath Sarkar; James Tod retold the Rathore version. Numbers and heroic details vary between Jaipur and Jodhpur traditions, and bardic poetry (especially in praise of Bakht Singh's charge) should be read as celebration rather than precise record.*

By **1741** the Mughal empire was a shadow. **Nadir Shah** of Persia had sacked Delhi in **1739**, the emperor **Muhammad Shah** ruled in name only, and the **Marathas** were collecting tribute deep into Malwa and Rajasthan. In this vacuum the great Rajput states had more freedom than at any time in two centuries. They did not use it to unite. The battle of **Gangwana**, fought near **Ajmer**, was a clash between the two strongest of them: **Jaipur** under **Sawai Jai Singh II** of the Kachwaha house, and the Rathores of **Marwar**.

### The roots of the quarrel

The rivalry had long roots. Jai Singh II and **Ajit Singh** of Marwar had been allies in **1708** against Bahadur Shah I, but by the 1720s their families were competitors for influence at court and for control of Ajmer. In **1724** Ajit Singh was murdered by his own son **Bakht Singh**; Marwar tradition holds that the deed was urged by his elder son **Abhay Singh**, who became Maharaja of Jodhpur, and some accounts suggest that Jai Singh and Mughal courtiers encouraged it. Bakht Singh received **Nagaur** as his own domain. The murder left a dark stain on the Rathore house and lasting suspicion between Jodhpur and Jaipur.

The immediate cause came from **Bikaner**, ruled by another Rathore line. When Abhay Singh attacked Bikaner around **1739–1740**, its ruler **Zorawar Singh** appealed to Jai Singh. Jai Singh, who saw himself as the arbiter of Rajput affairs, marched into Marwar with a large army and forced Abhay Singh to lift the siege and accept humiliating terms, including a heavy payment. For Jai Singh this confirmed his position as the leading Rajput prince. For the Rathores, and especially for the fiery Bakht Singh, it was an insult that demanded an answer.

### The battle

In **1741** Bakht Singh took the field against Jai Singh's army near **Gangwana**, in the Ajmer region. The accounts agree on the main shape of the fight. Jai Singh commanded a much larger force, supported by artillery and by allied contingents. Bakht Singh came with a far smaller body of Rathore cavalry, chosen men who were willing to stake everything on a charge.

The Rathores attacked head-on in the traditional Rajput manner. Their charge struck the Jaipur army hard and, according to the chronicles, broke into parts of its line and caused serious losses, throwing some divisions into confusion. Jodhpur tradition remembers this as one of the boldest charges in Rathore history. But the numbers were against Bakht Singh. His horsemen could not destroy an army many times their size, and the Jaipur forces, with their guns and reserves, held together. Most of the Rathore force was killed or wounded, and Bakht Singh, himself wounded, was forced to withdraw from the field.

Jai Singh therefore kept the field, and in a formal sense the day belonged to Jaipur. Yet contemporaries saw it as a costly and unconvincing victory. A small Rathore force had shaken the army of the most powerful prince in Rajasthan, and Jai Singh's reputation as an unbeatable arbiter suffered. A peace was soon arranged, and the Rathore claims were not crushed.

### What the battle cost

Exact casualty figures are not reliable; the chronicles give large and conflicting numbers. What is clear is that the dead on both sides were Rajputs, Kachwaha and Rathore, from houses that had fought together at Sambhar a generation earlier. The battle did nothing to defend Rajasthan from outside pressure. It weakened both states at the moment when the Marathas were becoming the real power in the north.

### The door opened to the Marathas

Jai Singh II died in **1743**. His death set off a succession war in Jaipur between his son **Ishwari Singh** and **Madho Singh**, the son of his Mewar queen, whose claim rested on the marriage pact of 1708. Mewar backed Madho Singh, and both sides turned to the Marathas for help. Maratha armies were drawn into Rajasthan as paid allies and soon as arbiters. Ishwari Singh won the field at **Rajmahal** in **1747**, but in **1748** at **Bagru** the coalition supporting Madho Singh forced him to accept terms, and in **1750**, under heavy Maratha pressure, he took his own life. Marwar too fell into succession disputes in which the Marathas intervened.

Gangwana was not the cause of all this, but it is a clear marker of the turn. The Rajput states had escaped Mughal control only to spend their strength on one another, and the Marathas, and later the British, were the ones who gained.

### Key points

- **A Rajput civil war.** Gangwana (1741) was fought between Jaipur under Sawai Jai Singh II and the Rathores of Marwar led by Bakht Singh.
- **Rooted in old rivalries.** The quarrel grew from competition over Ajmer, the murder of Ajit Singh in 1724, and Jai Singh's intervention to save Bikaner.
- **A famous Rathore charge.** Bakht Singh's much smaller cavalry force struck the Jaipur army hard but was overwhelmed and forced to withdraw.
- **A costly Jaipur victory.** Jai Singh held the field, but the battle damaged his prestige and settled little.
- **The Marathas gained.** After Jai Singh's death in 1743, Jaipur's succession war drew Maratha armies deep into Rajasthan.

## Battle of Patan — Jaipur–Jodhpur vs Marathas: When the Old Charge Met the New Army

*Sources: the battle of 20 June 1790 is well documented in Maratha correspondence, in British and European accounts of Mahadji Scindia's army (including the papers and early biographies of Benoît de Boigne), and in Rajasthani chronicles; modern historians such as Jadunath Sarkar describe it in detail. Figures for troops and losses differ between sources and should be treated as approximate.*

The battle of **Patan** was fought on **20 June 1790** near Patan in the **Torawati** tract of north-eastern Rajasthan, in today's **Sikar** district, between the Shekhawati hills and the road to Delhi. It is sometimes placed on the Gujarat border, but that is a confusion with the better-known town of Patan in Gujarat. Here the forces of **Jaipur**, aided by **Jodhpur**'s Rathore cavalry and by the rebel Mughal noble **Ismail Beg**, met the army of **Mahadji Scindia**, the most powerful Maratha chief in the north. The result was a clear Maratha victory and a turning point in the history of Rajasthan.

### Rajasthan between Mughals and Marathas

By the 1780s the Mughal emperor **Shah Alam II** lived in Delhi under Mahadji Scindia's protection, and Mahadji used the imperial name to demand tribute from the Rajput states. Jaipur, under **Maharaja Pratap Singh**, and Jodhpur, under **Maharaja Vijay Singh**, both owed large arrears and resented the demands. Their own rivalry had often given the Marathas an opening, but now they had a shared interest in resisting.

They had reason for confidence. In **1787** at **Lalsot** (also called the battle of Tunga), the combined Rajput armies, with the Rathore cavalry prominent, had fought Mahadji to a standstill and forced him to withdraw from Rajasthan. Some of his troops deserted, and for a time his position in the north seemed shaken. Ismail Beg, a Mughal commander who had turned against him, joined the Rajputs. It looked as if Rajput valour could still decide the fate of the region.

### Mahadji's new army

Mahadji drew a different lesson from Lalsot. He expanded the infantry brigades raised and trained by the Savoyard officer **Benoît de Boigne**. These were disciplined battalions of musketeers drilled in the European manner, with a strong force of field artillery, paid regularly and organised in permanent units. Alongside them Mahadji kept the traditional Maratha light cavalry for scouting, raiding and pursuit. By 1790 this combination of infantry, guns and horse was the most modern army in north India.

### The battle

In 1790 Mahadji sent his army, with de Boigne's brigades and Maratha cavalry under his commanders, against Ismail Beg and the Rajput forces gathered near Patan. The allied army took up a position in the hilly country there, and for some days the two sides watched each other.

When the battle was joined on 20 June, the allies attacked in the familiar way. Ismail Beg's troops and the Rajput horsemen, the Rathores among them, made determined charges. Accounts agree that they fought bravely and pressed the Maratha line in places. But de Boigne's infantry stood firm in close formation, and their artillery and steady musket fire broke the momentum of each charge before it could break their ranks. The Maratha cavalry then threatened the flanks.

The allied command was divided. Ismail Beg's Mughal troops, the Jaipur contingent and the Rathore cavalry did not act as one army, and several sources suggest that not all the Rajput forces committed themselves fully. As charges failed and losses mounted, the allied army broke. Ismail Beg fled the field. The victors captured a large number of guns and much of the allied baggage. Losses on the allied side were severe, though the exact figures given in different sources do not agree.

### Merta and the end of resistance

Patan was followed within months by a second blow. In **September 1790**, at **Merta** in Marwar, de Boigne's brigades again defeated the Rathore army. The Rathore cavalry made a famous and costly charge that broke into the Maratha position, but they could not hold it, and the infantry and guns destroyed the attack. After Merta, Vijay Singh of Jodhpur had to accept Maratha terms, including heavy payments and the surrender of Ajmer, which had been in Rathore hands. Jaipur too was forced to pay.

### The meaning of Patan

Patan did not end the Rajput states. Jaipur and Jodhpur survived, with their rulers and their courts. But it showed that the old way of war, built on heavy cavalry, personal leadership and the honour of the charge, could no longer defeat a trained army supported by artillery. It also confirmed that the Rajput states, divided among themselves, could not keep their independence against the Marathas. For the next quarter century Maratha commanders and freebooting armies drew tribute from Rajasthan, until the states signed treaties with the **British East India Company** in **1817–1818**.

### Key points

- **Date and place.** The battle was fought on 20 June 1790 near Patan in the Torawati region (Sikar district), not on the Gujarat border.
- **The sides.** Jaipur and Jodhpur forces, with the Mughal noble Ismail Beg, faced Mahadji Scindia's army under Benoît de Boigne.
- **Revenge for Lalsot.** Mahadji rebuilt his army with trained infantry and artillery after the Rajput success at Lalsot in 1787.
- **Discipline beat the charge.** De Boigne's infantry and guns broke repeated cavalry charges, and the divided allied army collapsed.
- **Merta completed it.** A second defeat at Merta in September 1790 forced Jodhpur and Jaipur to accept Maratha terms.
- **A lasting shift.** Maratha dominance over Rajasthan continued until the British treaties of 1817–1818.

rani-padmini.story:
## Rani Padmini (Padmavati) — The Queen Between History and Poem

*The siege and fall of Chittor in 1303 are recorded by Amir Khusrau and later Persian historians; Rani Padmini herself first appears in Malik Muhammad Jayasi's poem Padmavat (1540), and her story was retold by Rajasthani poets, Muhnot Nainsi, Ferishta and James Tod, so most of what follows is literary tradition rather than documented record.*

Few names in Rajasthan carry as much feeling as **Rani Padmini**, the queen of **Chittor** whose story has been told for nearly five centuries in verse, song, painting and, more recently, film. Yet she is also one of the hardest figures to pin down. To understand her properly, one has to keep two stories side by side: the historical siege of Chittor by **Alauddin Khalji** in **1303**, and the poem that turned that siege into an epic of love, beauty, loyalty and sacrifice.

### The historical frame

At the end of the thirteenth century, Chittor was the stronghold of the **Guhila** rulers of Mewar. An inscription of 1302 from Dariba names the reigning king as **Ratnasimha**, the **Rawal Ratan Singh** of later tradition, who had only recently succeeded his father Samarasimha. Alauddin Khalji, Sultan of Delhi since 1296, was then pushing his armies into Gujarat, Ranthambore and Malwa, and Chittor, commanding the routes between the Gangetic plain and Gujarat, was an obvious target.

The Sultan marched on Chittor in late January 1303 and besieged it for about seven months. His court poet **Amir Khusrau**, who accompanied the campaign, describes the siege in his *Khaza'in ul-Futuh* and records that the fort fell on **26 August 1303**. He says the Rai surrendered and was spared, while thousands of others were put to death on the Sultan's order; Chittor was handed to Alauddin's young son Khizr Khan and renamed Khizrabad. Khusrau says nothing about a queen named Padmini, a rescue, or a jauhar, although some historians read hints of a desperate last resistance in his account.

### The poem

The figure we know as Padmini comes from the Sufi poet **Malik Muhammad Jayasi**, who completed the Awadhi epic **Padmavat** in **1540**, more than two centuries after the siege. In Jayasi's telling, Padmavati is the princess of **Singhal-dweep** (usually understood as Sri Lanka), whose beauty is described by a talking parrot, Hiraman. Ratan Sen of Chittor, enchanted by the parrot's words, sets out as a wandering yogi, crosses the seas, endures trials and wins her hand. The court Brahmin Raghav Chetan, banished from Chittor, later goes to Delhi and praises Padmavati's beauty to Alauddin, who demands her.

The poem's famous episodes follow: Alauddin, received as a guest, glimpses Padmavati's reflection in a mirror; he treacherously seizes Ratan Sen; the warriors **Gora and Badal** rescue their king by smuggling soldiers into the Sultan's camp in covered palanquins disguised as the queen and her attendants. Ratan Sen later dies fighting Devpal of Kumbhalner, and Padmavati and his other queen, Nagmati, mount his funeral pyre. When Alauddin finally takes Chittor, he finds only ashes. Jayasi closes with an allegory (Chittor as body, Ratan Sen as soul, Padmavati as wisdom), showing he meant the poem partly as spiritual parable.

### How the legend grew

After Jayasi, the story spread and changed. The Jain poet **Hemratan** wrote *Gora Badal Padmini Chaupai* in 1589, a Rajasthani version that gives Gora and Badal a much larger role. Persian historians such as **Ferishta** (early seventeenth century) folded the tale into their histories. The Marwari chronicler **Muhnot Nainsi** recorded Mewari traditions, and in the nineteenth century **James Tod**, in his *Annals and Antiquities of Rajast'han*, presented Padmini as a Chauhan princess of Ceylon and described a great **jauhar** in which she led the women of Chittor into the fire before the men rode out to die. Tod's version, with the mirror and the jauhar at its heart, shaped most modern retellings.

Several claims in popular versions have no basis even in the poem's own tradition: that she was "the most beautiful woman in the world", that she ran schools or governed directly, or that she "performed the first great jauhar". Earlier jauhars are recorded, for example at Ranthambore in 1301, described by Khusrau himself.

### What historians say

Historians remain divided. Some, such as K. S. Lal, argued that a real queen may lie behind the legend, since a jauhar at Chittor in 1303 would fit the pattern of sieges in that age. Others, including Kalika Ranjan Qanungo and many later scholars, conclude that Padmini is essentially a literary creation, built by Jayasi on the memory of the siege. There is no contemporary inscription or chronicle that names her. What can be said with confidence is that Chittor was besieged and taken by Alauddin in 1303, that Ratnasimha was its ruler, and that by the sixteenth century the memory of that disaster had become a powerful poem.

Jauhar itself, the self-immolation of women to avoid capture and enslavement when a fort was about to fall, is part of the documented history of medieval Rajasthan. It should be understood as a response to the brutal realities of conquest in that age, not as something to admire uncritically.

### Memory and legacy

Chittorgarh today shows visitors a **Padmini Mahal**, a palace beside a pool where tradition places the mirror episode, though the present building is much later. Folk singers, painted scrolls and school readers across Rajasthan keep the story alive, and it has inspired plays, novels, films from the 1960s onward and the controversial 2018 film *Padmaavat*, whose release provoked large protests and showed how deeply people still feel about her.

Padmini's lasting importance lies in what her story has meant: for Rajput communities, a symbol of dignity and resistance; for Jayasi, a parable of the soul; for historians, a case study in how memory turns events into legend. Holding these meanings together, without confusing poem with record, is the best way to honour her.

### Key points
- **Historical anchor.** Alauddin Khalji besieged Chittor from January 1303 and took it on 26 August 1303; the ruler was Ratnasimha (Ratan Singh).
- **Literary origin.** Padmini first appears in Jayasi's *Padmavat* (1540), written more than two centuries after the siege.
- **Later tradition.** Hemratan, Ferishta, Muhnot Nainsi and James Tod expanded the tale, adding Gora and Badal's role and the great jauhar.
- **No contemporary record.** Amir Khusrau, an eyewitness to the siege, does not mention her.
- **Enduring symbol.** She remains a central figure in Rajasthani memory, debated by historians and celebrated in folk culture.

maharana-pratap.story:
## Maharana Pratap — the king who would not bow

*Maharana Pratap's life is unusually well recorded, in the Persian chronicles of Akbar's court, in the memoirs of men who fought against him, and in the bardic traditions of Mewar. Where the chronicles end and the legends begin, this story says so.*

Pratap was born, by the traditional reckoning of Mewar, on **9 May 1540**, in the fortress of **Kumbhalgarh**, high on the ridges of the Aravallis. The fort had been built a century earlier by his great ancestor Rana Kumbha, and in 1540 it was a refuge as much as a palace. His father, **Udai Singh II**, was then fighting to win back the throne of Mewar from the usurper Banbir, who had murdered Udai Singh's brother. The boy's mother was **Jaiwanta Bai**, a Songara Chauhan princess of Pali. Pratap was the eldest son, and the bards say that his birth came in the very year his father's fortunes turned, when Udai Singh retook Chittor and was seated firmly on the throne of his forefathers.

He grew up in a Mewar that remembered its glory and feared for its future. His grandfather, **Rana Sanga**, had been the strongest Hindu king of north India until his defeat by Babur at Khanwa in 1527. Chittor had been sacked by Bahadur Shah of Gujarat in 1535. The boy learned to ride and fight in the hills, and tradition says that he spent much of his youth among the **Bhils** of the forest, learning their paths and earning a trust that would one day save his kingdom. The Bhils called him *Kika*, a word for a little one, and the name stayed with him in the songs of the hills.

In 1567 the new Mughal emperor, **Akbar**, marched on Chittor. Udai Singh, on the advice of his council, withdrew into the hills, leaving the fortress in the care of **Jaimal Rathore** and **Patta Chundawat**. The siege lasted from October 1567 to **February 1568**. When the walls were breached, the women of the fort performed jauhar, the garrison went out to die, and Akbar ordered a massacre of the defenders and the people who had sheltered in the fort. Pratap, then a young man of twenty-seven, was not in Chittor; but the fall of the ancestral capital shaped everything he did afterwards. Udai Singh built a new seat in the valley he had already chosen, beside the lake that bears his name, and there the city of **Udaipur** began to grow.

Udai Singh died at **Gogunda** in **February 1572**. In his last years he had favoured **Jagmal**, his son by a younger queen, and named him heir. But the great nobles of Mewar would not accept him. Led by **Krishnadas Chundawat** and other chiefs, tradition says they took Jagmal by the arm as he sat on the throne and led him to a lower seat, and then placed Pratap on the gaddi at Gogunda on **28 February 1572**. Jagmal left in anger for Akbar's court, and later received the town of Jahazpur from the emperor. The quarrel showed the danger Pratap faced: a divided family, a lost capital, and an empire that was growing stronger every year.

By 1572 almost every great Rajput house had made terms with Akbar. The Kachhwahas of Amber had become his kinsmen by marriage, and Bikaner, Jaisalmer and Bundi had accepted his overlordship. Akbar wanted Mewar too, and he tried first with diplomacy. Over the next two years he sent four embassies to the new Rana: **Jalal Khan Qorchi**, then **Raja Man Singh** of Amber, then Man Singh's father **Bhagwant Das**, and finally **Raja Todar Mal**. Each was received with courtesy. Pratap even sent his son **Amar Singh** to Bhagwant Das as a mark of goodwill. But he would not go to court himself and bow before the emperor, and that was the one thing Akbar required. Later legend made the meeting with Man Singh a scene of insult at a feast; the chronicles only say that the talks failed.

War came in 1576. Akbar sent Man Singh, with **Asaf Khan** and a strong army, from Ajmer towards Gogunda. Pratap chose to meet them in the narrow country of the Aravallis, at the pass of **Haldighati**, named for the yellow, turmeric-coloured earth of its hills. On **18 June 1576** the armies met near **Khamnor**. Pratap's force was smaller, perhaps three thousand horse against Man Singh's five thousand or more, but it held men of every kind: the Sisodia chiefs, the old Tomar king **Ram Shah Tanwar** of Gwalior and his sons, the Afghan commander **Hakim Khan Sur** leading the vanguard, and the Bhils under **Rana Punja**, who guarded the hills on the flanks.

The first charge of the Mewar army drove the Mughal front back in confusion, and for a time it seemed that the day would be Pratap's. The historian **Badayuni**, who rode with the Mughal army, left a vivid account of the fighting and admitted the force of that charge. But the Mughal reserves held, and the imperial war elephants and the steadier Mughal line slowly turned the battle. Pratap himself fought in the thick of it. Tradition says he rode his horse **Chetak** straight at Man Singh's elephant and struck at the Raja with his lance, and that Chetak's leg was cut by the sword on the elephant's trunk.

As the Mughals closed around the wounded Rana, **Jhala Man**, the chief of Bari Sadri, took the royal umbrella and insignia upon himself, drew the enemy towards him, and died in Pratap's place. Ram Shah Tanwar and three of his sons fell in the same fight. Pratap escaped from the field. The legend that Chetak carried him across a stream on three legs and then died is told all over Rajasthan, and a memorial to the horse stands near Haldighati today. The chronicles agree that Pratap withdrew with much of his army intact, and that the Mughals, exhausted and wary of an ambush in the hills, did not pursue.

Haldighati was a defeat, but it was not the end. Man Singh occupied Gogunda, yet his army could find little food in a country whose people had fled to the hills, and Akbar was displeased with the result. In the autumn of 1576 the emperor himself came to Mewar and took Gogunda, Udaipur and the surrounding country. Over the next years he sent his commander **Shahbaz Khan** on three campaigns. In **1578** Shahbaz Khan captured Kumbhalgarh, Pratap's birthplace, after a hard siege. Pratap was driven from one stronghold to the next, and his family lived through years of hardship in the forests.

The bards remember this time with stories of hunger: of the Rana's children eating bread made from wild grass, of a wild cat snatching that bread from a child's hand, and of Pratap's resolve almost breaking. They also tell of letters exchanged with **Prithviraj Rathore** of Bikaner, a poet at Akbar's court, who reminded him in verse of his duty. These are beloved legends, not documented history, but they hold a real truth: the war was long, and the cost was paid by the whole family and the whole land.

What saved Mewar was the method Pratap now chose. He would not risk his men in open battle again. Instead, with the Bhils as his scouts and the hills as his fortress, he struck Mughal convoys and outposts and vanished. He forbade his people to cultivate the plains, so that the Mughal garrisons would find nothing to feed on. His minister **Bhamashah**, tradition says, brought him a great treasure at the darkest hour, enough to raise and pay an army again. In **1580** the Khan-i-Khanan **Abdul Rahim** was sent against him; a story told in Mewar says that Amar Singh captured the women of Rahim's household, and that Pratap ordered them returned with honour.

The turning point came at **Dewair** in **1582**. In a pass in the north of Mewar, Pratap and Amar Singh attacked the Mughal post commanded by **Sultan Khan**. Tradition says that Amar Singh drove his lance through Sultan Khan and his horse together. After Dewair, the Mughal outposts across Mewar fell one after another, and some thirty-six of them, the chronicles of Mewar say, were abandoned or taken. Kumbhalgarh was won back. In **1584** Akbar sent **Jagannath Kachhwaha** on one last major campaign, but after 1585 the emperor moved to Lahore to face the dangers of the north-west, and Mewar was largely left alone.

In those last twelve years Pratap rebuilt. He made **Chavand**, in the southern hills, his capital, and built there a palace and a temple to the goddess **Chamunda**. He recovered nearly all of Mewar, except **Chittor**, **Mandalgarh** and the country around them. Scholars and poets came to his court, among them **Chakrapani Mishra**, who wrote works on statecraft and ritual under his patronage, and the beginnings of the Chavand school of painting date from these years. The land that had been laid waste was resettled and farmed again.

Pratap never saw Chittor again. The bards say that he took a vow not to sleep on a bed, eat from gold or silver plates, or live in a palace of comfort until the old capital was free, and that for centuries afterwards the rulers of Mewar placed a leaf beneath their dishes and straw beneath their beds in memory of it. He died at Chavand on **19 January 1597**, aged fifty-six. Tradition says that his death followed an injury suffered while drawing a hard bow during a hunt. His *chhatri*, his memorial, stands at **Bandoli**, near Chavand, beside a small stream.

He was succeeded by his son **Amar Singh I**, who carried on the war for eighteen more years before making an honourable peace with Akbar's son Jahangir in 1615, on the condition that no Maharana would ever have to attend the Mughal court in person. Pratap's refusal had become the law of his house. In the centuries since, his name has stood across India for the right of a people to remain free, and the hills of Haldighati still remember the man the Bhils called Kika.

## Highlights of his life

- **Birth at Kumbhalgarh (1540).** Born to Udai Singh II and Jaiwanta Bai in the fortress built by Rana Kumbha.
- **Accession at Gogunda (1572).** The nobles of Mewar set aside Jagmal and crowned Pratap as Maharana.
- **Refusal of Akbar's embassies (1572–1573).** He received four Mughal envoys but would not attend the imperial court.
- **Haldighati (18 June 1576).** He led a smaller army against Man Singh; Jhala Man died in his place, and Pratap escaped to fight on.
- **The long hill war.** With the Bhils under Rana Punja and the support of Bhamashah, he wore down the Mughal garrisons from the forests.
- **Victory at Dewair (1582).** Pratap and Amar Singh broke the Mughal outposts, and he went on to recover most of Mewar.
- **Capital at Chavand.** He rebuilt the kingdom from Chavand, patronising scholars and building the temple of Chamunda.
- **Death at Chavand (1597).** He died undefeated in spirit, and his son Amar Singh I continued the struggle.

chapters.title: The Legend of Haldighati
chapters.story:
Maharana Pratap Singh — a symbol of valour, self-respect and unbroken struggle. This heroic warrior was not merely a king but the guardian of Mewar's identity, who devoted every moment of his life to defending freedom and the pride of Rajputana. He was born on 9 May 1540 in Kumbhalgarh Fort. His father was Maharana Udai Singh and his mother Rani Jaivanta Bai. From childhood he showed remarkable courage, a gift for leadership, and deep piety.

Maharana Pratap's greatest contribution was his flat refusal to accept the overlordship of the Mughal emperor Akbar. While other Rajput kings had accepted Akbar's friendship or suzerainty, Pratap alone kept his independence. He paid a heavy price for it — he had to give up his capital, Chittor, and live for years in the forests.

The Battle of Haldighati (18 June 1576) was the most important event of Maharana Pratap's life. With only 22,000 soldiers he faced Akbar's vast army of 80,000. Pratap fought with astonishing courage. Riding his horse Chetak, he charged into the midst of the Mughal army, and his spear brought down Man Singh's elephant. Chetak too showed matchless courage — even after one of his legs was cut in the battle, he carried Pratap to safety.

After the battle, Maharana Pratap had to live for years in the forests, and his family endured great hardship. There came a time when he could not even find food for his children. But Pratap did not give up. With the help of the Bhil people he rebuilt his strength, and little by little he freed most of Mewar.

Maharana Pratap's life teaches that a true Rajput never compromises his principles. He proved that one can struggle to any length for freedom and honour. He died on 19 January 1597, but the saga of his valour still lives in the heart of every Indian.

Many inspiring stories are told of his life — such as his bond with the Bhils, whom he treated as his equals. The Bhils in turn showed him unshakeable loyalty, and Bhil warriors did not hesitate to give their lives for him.

Maharana Pratap not only raised the pride of Rajputana but gave all of India the message that there is no need to kneel before foreign rule. His life remains a source of inspiration for every Indian.
