chapters.story:
Maharana Pratap — the greatest Rajput warrior-king of India, who never surrendered to the Mughals and fought at the Battle of Haldighati. This heroic warrior lived in the 16th century.

Maharana Pratap was born in 1572 CE. He belonged to the Sisodia dynasty and became ruler of Mewar. His reign fell in an age when Mughal invasions of India were under way.

He never surrendered to Akbar. He fought at the Battle of Haldighati and resisted the Mughals. Inspired by his courage, many Rajput clans joined him.

Maharana Pratap strengthened the army of Mewar. He adopted new methods of war and modernised his forces. His army was so powerful that no enemy could stand against it.

He lived in the forests for many years. He fought bravely and stood firm against Akbar. He chose death over surrender.

Maharana Pratap's life teaches that a great warrior must go to any length for his principles. He proved that Indian warriors could stand up to the Mughals.

rana-sanga.story:
## Rana Sanga — the scarred king who challenged Babur

*Rana Sanga's life is known from the chronicles of Mewar and the bards of Rajasthan, from the Persian histories of the sultanates he fought, and from the memoirs of his last great enemy, Babur. Where the bardic tales go beyond the record, this story says so.*

**Sangram Singh**, remembered by everyone as **Rana Sanga**, was born in **1482**, a son of **Rana Raimal** of Mewar and a grandson of the great builder-king **Rana Kumbha**. His father had taken the throne after driving out Kumbha's murderer, his own brother Uda, and Mewar under Raimal was a strong kingdom, guarded by the forts that Kumbha had built. But the court was full of ambitious princes, and Sanga was not the eldest. His brothers **Prithviraj** and **Jaimal** were bold, quarrelsome young men, and each of the three believed he deserved the throne.

The bards tell how the rivalry broke into open violence. The three brothers, they say, went to a Charan priestess of the goddess to ask which of them would rule, and when she declared for Sanga, Prithviraj drew his sword in fury. In the fight that followed Sanga lost the sight of one eye. Wounded and in danger of his life, he fled from Mewar. For a time, tradition says, he lived in disguise, and took service with **Karmachand Panwar**, a chief of the Ajmer country, as an ordinary soldier, until his bearing and courage gave away his birth.

Fate removed his rivals one by one. Jaimal was killed in a quarrel far from home, and Prithviraj, a famous and reckless warrior, died of poison given to him, tradition says, by his own brother-in-law of Sirohi. Sanga was recalled as heir, and when Raimal died in **1508**, he became Rana of Mewar. He was about twenty-six years old, already marked by war, and determined to make Mewar the first power of north India.

The moment was favourable. The sultanate of Delhi under the Lodis was weakening, Malwa was torn by quarrels among its nobles, and Gujarat was busy with its own wars. Sanga brought the Rajput chiefs of the region together under his leadership, through marriage, friendship and the force of his reputation. The houses of Marwar, Amber, Gwalior, Ajmer, Chanderi and many others came to follow him in war. His Persian enemies recognised him as the greatest of the Rajput rulers of his time.

His first great contest was with Malwa. When the nobles of Malwa rose against **Sultan Mahmud Khalji II**, the Rajput minister **Medini Rai** gained great power at Mandu, and when the Sultan turned against him, Medini Rai turned to Sanga. Medini Rai held **Chanderi** and the country around it under Mewar's protection. In **1519** Mahmud marched against him, and at **Gagron** Sanga met the Sultan's army and defeated it. Mahmud himself was wounded and taken prisoner. Sanga treated him with honour, had his wounds cared for, and later released him, keeping a pledge of loyalty and territory in return, an echo of what Mewar remembered of Kumbha's victory at Sarangpur.

To the west, Sanga fought **Gujarat** over the small kingdom of **Idar**. Two Rathore princes claimed its throne, Gujarat backed one and Sanga the other, a prince who had found refuge at Chittor and was betrothed to Sanga's daughter. The quarrel grew into a war. Around **1517** Sanga marched into Gujarat, placed his candidate on the throne of Idar, and raided as far as Ahmednagar in Gujarat, carrying off rich plunder. Gujarat answered with a great expedition against Mewar in the following years, but Sanga's forts and his alliance held.

To the north stood the Lodi sultans of Delhi. **Ibrahim Lodi**, who came to the throne in 1517, tried to check Sanga's rise. At **Khatoli**, near the border of the Delhi sultanate, around **1517**, the armies met, and the Rajputs won. In that battle, tradition says, Sanga lost an arm to a sword stroke and was lamed in one leg by an arrow. Another clash came near **Dholpur** soon after, and again Sanga prevailed and extended his power towards the Chambal and Bayana. The bards say that he won eighteen pitched battles against the sultans of Delhi and Malwa, and that his body carried the scars of eighty wounds. The numbers are poetic, but the picture is true. With one eye, one arm and a crippled leg, the Rana still led his armies from the front.

Then, in **1526**, everything changed. **Babur**, the Timurid prince of Kabul, invaded India and destroyed the army of Ibrahim Lodi at **Panipat** on 21 April, killing the Sultan. Delhi and Agra fell to him. Babur later wrote in his memoirs that Sanga had sent him word promising to attack Ibrahim from the other side, and accused him of failing to keep his word; Rajput tradition remembers the matter differently, and the truth of those early messages cannot now be known. What is clear is that after Panipat, Sanga saw a foreign conqueror in the place where the weakened Lodis had been, and he decided to drive him out before he could take root.

Sanga gathered the greatest Rajput army of the age. With him came the Rajput chiefs of Marwar, Amber, Vagad, Chanderi and Merta, and with him too came Afghans who had lost everything at Panipat: **Hasan Khan Mewati** of Alwar and **Mahmud Lodi**, a brother of Ibrahim, who hoped to recover his family's throne. Early in **1527** Sanga's advance guard defeated a Mughal force near **Bayana**, and fear spread through Babur's camp. Babur wrote that his men were disheartened. He answered by breaking his wine cups, renouncing drink, and calling his army to holy war.

On **16 March 1527** the two armies met at **Khanwa**, near Fatehpur Sikri. Babur fought as he had at Panipat: a line of carts chained together protected his matchlockmen and his cannon, with cavalry on the flanks ready to wheel around the enemy. Sanga's horsemen charged again and again into the guns. For hours the battle hung in the balance, and the Rajput attacks pressed hard on Babur's right. But the cannon and the turning cavalry wore them down. In the midst of the fighting Sanga was struck by an arrow and fell unconscious. His companions carried him from the field, and **Ajja Jhala** took the royal insignia so that the army would not know its leader had fallen. Without him, the Rajput army broke. Among the dead were **Rawal Udai Singh** of Vagad, **Hasan Khan Mewati** and many chiefs of Mewar and Marwar.

Babur's victory was complete. He took the title of **Ghazi**, and, as he himself recorded, raised a tower of the heads of the slain on a hill near the field, as the Timurid conquerors before him had done. Rajput tradition remembers the defeat with bitterness, and tells that **Silhadi**, the chief of Raisen, deserted to Babur in the course of the battle and weakened Sanga's line; the story is widely told, but historians are divided on whether it is true. What is certain is that Babur's guns and his disciplined tactics, still new to the warfare of north India, had broken an army of horsemen that would have swept any other foe from the field. The victory secured the Mughal hold on Delhi and Agra far more firmly than Panipat had done.

Sanga woke far from the battlefield and was told that the day was lost. Tradition says he swore that he would not return to Chittor until he had defeated Babur. Within months he was raising a new army. In January 1528 Babur marched against Chanderi, still held by Medini Rai, and Sanga moved to help his old ally. He never reached him. At **Kalpi**, on **30 January 1528**, Rana Sanga died. Tradition says that he was poisoned by his own nobles, who feared another war that they believed could not be won. He was about forty-six years old.

He left a powerful widow, **Rani Karnavati**, a Hada princess of Bundi, and several sons. His son **Ratan Singh II** succeeded him, followed by **Vikramaditya**, and then by **Udai Singh II**, the father of Maharana Pratap. Through his son **Bhoj Raj**, who died before him, Sanga was also the father-in-law of the saint-poet **Mirabai**, whose devotion to Krishna made the court of Chittor famous in another way.

Khanwa ended the hope that a Rajput king would rule from Delhi, and opened the way for the Mughal empire. Yet even Babur, in his memoirs, wrote of Sanga with respect, saying that he had risen to his greatness by his own valour and sword. In Rajasthan he is remembered as **Hindupat**, the champion of the Hindu kings of his age, a warrior who gave an eye, an arm and finally his life to a cause he would not abandon.

## Highlights of his life

- **Exile and return.** Wounded and driven out by his brothers' rivalry, he lived in disguise before returning as heir and becoming Rana in 1508.
- **Leader of the Rajput chiefs.** He gathered the Rajput houses of north and central India under his leadership, making Mewar the strongest power in the region.
- **Victory at Gagron (1519).** He defeated and captured Sultan Mahmud Khalji II of Malwa, and released him with honour.
- **War with Gujarat over Idar (c. 1517).** He placed his candidate on the throne of Idar and raided deep into Gujarat.
- **Victories over Ibrahim Lodi.** At Khatoli and Dholpur he defeated the Sultan of Delhi, losing an arm and the use of a leg in the fighting.
- **Khanwa (16 March 1527).** He led a great Rajput and Afghan alliance against Babur, and was carried wounded from the field when the battle was lost.
- **Death at Kalpi (1528).** He died while marching to fight Babur again, poisoned, tradition says, by his own nobles.

prithviraj-chauhan.name: Prithviraj Chauhan III
prithviraj-chauhan.significance: Last Hindu emperor of North India
legends: Defeated Muhammad Ghori in First Battle of Tarain
Master archer who could shoot blindfolded
prithviraj-chauhan.story:
## Prithviraj Chauhan III — The Last Chahamana King of Ajmer

*His reign is documented by inscriptions, coins, the contemporary Sanskrit poem Prithviraja Vijaya, and Persian histories such as the Taj-ul-Ma'asir and Tabaqat-i Nasiri; the Prithviraj Raso attributed to Chand Bardai, the source of the Sanyogita romance and the blind-archer revenge, is a much later bardic epic and is treated by historians as legend.*

**Prithviraj III**, remembered across North India as **Prithviraj Chauhan** or Rai Pithora, ruled the **Chahamana** (Chauhan) kingdom of **Sapadalaksha**, centred on **Ajmer**, in the late twelfth century. His defeat at **Tarain** in **1192** opened North India to the **Ghurid** conquest and the later Delhi Sultanate, and that turning point made him the most celebrated and most mythologised Rajput king of his age.

### Birth and accession

Prithviraj was born around **1166**, probably in Gujarat, to the Chahamana king **Someshvara** and Queen **Karpuradevi**, a princess of the Kalachuri house. Someshvara had grown up at the Chaulukya court of Gujarat before returning to claim the Ajmer throne. When he died in about **1177**, Prithviraj was still a boy of around eleven, and Karpuradevi governed as regent with the help of ministers, notably **Kadambavasa**. By about 1180 the young king had taken power into his own hands.

The kingdom he inherited covered much of present-day eastern and central Rajasthan, with influence reaching into Haryana. **Delhi**, held by the **Tomara** family, had come under Chahamana overlordship in the time of his uncle Vigraharaja IV, and later tradition remembers a Tomara relative, **Govindaraja**, as Prithviraj's governor there.

### Wars with his neighbours

The early years of the reign were busy with campaigns. Prithviraj put down the revolt of a cousin, **Nagarjuna**, and campaigned against the **Bhadanakas**, a people of the region near present-day Rewari and Bharatpur. His best-recorded war was against the **Chandela** king **Paramardi** of Jejakabhukti (Bundelkhand). Inscriptions found at **Madanpur**, dated **1182–83**, record that Prithviraj ravaged the Chandela territory. The bardic Alha-Khand later turned this war into an epic of the heroes **Alha and Udal**, but the inscriptions confirm only the raid and do not suggest any lasting conquest.

He also fought the **Chaulukyas** of Gujarat under Bhima II, a long rivalry that ended in a treaty. Relations with the **Gahadavala** king **Jayachandra** of Kannauj were hostile, though the details are known mainly from later literature.

### The battles of Tarain

The **Ghurid** ruler **Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad of Ghor**, known in India as **Muhammad Ghori**, had taken Ghazni, Multan and Lahore and was pressing towards the Ganga plain. In **1191** he seized the fortress of **Tabarhindah** (probably Bathinda). Prithviraj marched against him and the two armies met at **Tarain** (Taraori, near Karnal). In this **First Battle of Tarain** the Chahamana army routed the Ghurids; Govindaraja of Delhi is said to have wounded Muhammad himself, who was carried from the field. Prithviraj then besieged Tabarhindah, which surrendered after a long siege.

Muhammad returned in **1192** with a larger, well-organised army of mounted archers. At the **Second Battle of Tarain**, according to the Persian accounts, he used feigned retreats and repeated harassing attacks to wear down the larger Rajput host before a final charge broke it. Govindaraja was killed, and Prithviraj fled the field but was captured near Sarasvati (probably Sirsa).

### Death

What happened next is reported differently. Persian sources such as **Hasan Nizami** say Prithviraj was taken to Ajmer, allowed to rule briefly as a vassal, and then executed after being accused of plotting rebellion. Coins bearing his name together with Muhammad's support the idea of a short vassal period. His son **Govindaraja IV** was placed on the throne of Ajmer as a Ghurid tributary and later moved to **Ranthambore**, where a Chahamana branch survived for another century.

The **Prithviraj Raso** tells a different, legendary story: Prithviraj is blinded and taken to Ghazni, where, guided by Chand Bardai's couplet, he kills Muhammad with an arrow by sound alone. This did not happen. Muhammad of Ghor lived until **1206**, when he was assassinated on the bank of the Jhelum, fourteen years after Tarain.

### Legend and poetry

The romance of **Sanyogita** (Samyogita), daughter of Jaichand, who chooses Prithviraj at her swayamvara and is carried off by him, is found only in the Raso and later works. The Raso itself grew over centuries; its surviving versions use language much later than the twelfth century, and historians do not regard it as a contemporary record. The claim that Prithviraj could shoot blindfolded belongs to the same bardic tradition.

By contrast, the **Prithviraja Vijaya**, written by the Kashmiri poet **Jayanaka** at Prithviraj's own court, survives only in incomplete form but gives a contemporary picture of his genealogy and early life. It does not contain the Sanyogita story.

### Legacy

Modern writers often call Prithviraj "the last Hindu emperor" of North India. This is a later label; in his own day he was one of several powerful regional kings, alongside the Gahadavalas, Chaulukyas and Chandelas. His defeat mattered because it removed the strongest power on the Ghurid route into the Ganga plain, and within a few years Delhi, Ajmer and Kannauj had all fallen.

He remains a towering figure in memory. The ruins at Ajmer's **Taragarh**, the remains of "Qila Rai Pithora" in Delhi, statues, schoolbooks, TV serials and films keep his name alive. The bards turned a defeated king into a hero who triumphed in death, and that story, though legend, says much about how communities remember loss.

### Key points
- **Dynasty.** Chahamana (Chauhan) king of Sapadalaksha with capital at Ajmer, born c. 1166, son of Someshvara.
- **Minor ruler.** Became king around 1177 as a boy, with his mother Karpuradevi as regent.
- **Campaigns.** Raided the Chandela kingdom (Madanpur inscriptions, 1182–83) and fought the Chaulukyas of Gujarat.
- **Tarain.** Defeated Muhammad Ghori in 1191 but was defeated and captured in 1192, and later executed.
- **Legend vs record.** The Sanyogita romance and the killing of Ghori come from the later Prithviraj Raso; Ghori actually died in 1206.

hamir-dev.name: Rao Hamir Dev
hamir-dev.significance: Defender of Ranthambore against Alauddin Khilji
legends: Fought against Alauddin Khilji for 12 years
hamir-dev.story:
## Rao Hamir Dev — The Unyielding Lord of Ranthambore

*The siege of Ranthambore (1299–1301) is described by Amir Khusrau, who was present, and by Ziauddin Barani and Isami; Hammir's life is told at length in Nayachandra Suri's Sanskrit Hammira Mahakavya (15th century) and in later bardic works such as the Hammir Raso, which add heroic detail that cannot always be verified.*

**Hammiradeva**, remembered in Rajasthan as **Rao Hamir Dev** or simply **Hammir**, was the last king of the **Chahamana** (Chauhan) branch of **Ranthambore**. His refusal to give up refugees who had sought his protection brought the full weight of **Alauddin Khalji**'s army against his fort, and his death in **1301** became one of the great stories of Rajput steadfastness. In Rajasthani speech his name is still a byword for an unbreakable resolve.

### Origins

The Ranthambore Chahamanas descended from **Govindaraja**, son of **Prithviraj Chauhan III**, who moved to the fort after the Ghurid conquest of Ajmer in 1192. For a century the family held this formidable hill fort in eastern Rajasthan, sometimes as tributaries of Delhi and sometimes independent. Hammir was the son of **Jaitrasimha**, and he came to the throne around **1283**.

The *Hammira Mahakavya* describes an energetic early reign in which Hammir led a **digvijaya**, a "conquest of the quarters", raiding neighbouring powers including the Paramaras of Malwa and the rulers of Mewar, and then performed a great sacrifice. Its account of these victories is poetic and probably exaggerated, but it suggests that Ranthambore under Hammir was a confident regional power.

### Facing the Khaljis

Delhi was then ruled by the **Khalji** dynasty. In **1290–91**, Sultan **Jalaluddin Khalji** marched against Ranthambore, sacked the nearby town of **Jhain**, looked at the fortress and withdrew. Barani reports him saying that he did not value such a fort above the life of a single Muslim soldier. Hammir had survived the first test.

The crisis came under Jalaluddin's nephew and successor, **Alauddin Khalji**. In **1299**, after a Delhi army returned from the conquest of Gujarat, a group of **Mongol** soldiers who had converted and served the Sultan rebelled over the division of plunder near Jalor. Their leaders, **Muhammad Shah** (the "Mahimasahi" of the Sanskrit poem) and his brother **Kehbru**, fled to Ranthambore, and Hammir gave them refuge. When Alauddin demanded their surrender, Hammir refused. For Rajput tradition this became the heart of the story: a king who would not betray those who had sought his protection.

### The siege

Alauddin sent his brother **Ulugh Khan** and the general **Nusrat Khan** against Ranthambore. They took Jhain, but when they began the siege Nusrat Khan was struck by a stone from a mangonel and died a few days later. The Chauhan garrison then sallied out and drove the Delhi army back.

Alauddin came in person, probably in **1300**. The siege dragged on for months, and the Sultan faced trouble elsewhere: an attempt on his life by his nephew **Akat Khan**, revolts in Awadh, and an uprising in Delhi itself. He held on. His troops built a great ramp of earth and sacks against the walls, and blockade gradually starved the fort.

According to the *Hammira Mahakavya*, the end was hastened by betrayal. Two of Hammir's officers, **Ratipala** and **Ranamalla**, went over to Alauddin, and the defenders were left short of food. Faced with certain defeat, Hammir's queen **Ranga Devi** and the women of the fort performed **jauhar**, entering the fire rather than face capture. Amir Khusrau also alludes to women perishing in fire. Hammir and his remaining warriors, together with Muhammad Shah, then went out to fight to the end. The fort fell in **July 1301**.

Popular retellings claim the siege lasted twelve years, that Hammir "performed jauhar with 12,000 women", or that Alauddin honoured him afterwards. None of this is supported. The full Khalji campaign took about two years, and no reliable source gives the number who died in the jauhar. Barani and Khusrau report that the wounded Muhammad Shah, when asked what he would do if spared, answered that he would kill the Sultan and place Hammir's son on the throne; Alauddin had him executed. Even the Sultan's chroniclers could not hide the loyalty that bound the Mongol fugitive to his Rajput protector.

### Death and legacy

Hammir died in the final fighting, or, as the *Hammira Mahakavya* says, took his own life to avoid capture. With him the Chahamana kingdom of Ranthambore ended, and the fort passed to Delhi.

His memory, however, grew. The *Hammira Mahakavya* of the Jain poet **Nayachandra Suri**, written in the fifteenth century at Gwalior, presents him as an ideal king. The Hindi **Hammir Raso** of Jodharaj and many bardic songs followed. A popular saying sums up how he is remembered:

> *Singh suvan, satpurush vachan, kadali phalai ik baar;*
> *Tiriya tel, Hammir hath, chadhai na dooji baar.*

"A lion mates once, a good man gives his word once, the plantain fruits once; a bride is anointed with oil once, and Hammir's resolve, once taken, is never taken twice." The proverb captures what the bards valued in him: a promise kept whatever the cost.

Inside **Ranthambore Fort**, now part of a UNESCO World Heritage serial site, visitors are shown Hammir's palace, the **Hammir Mahal**, and other structures associated with him by tradition. The national park around it, famous for its tigers, draws visitors who often hear his story first from guides.

Hammir's story, like many from this age, should be read with care. Its central facts are secure: a Chauhan king of Ranthambore sheltered fugitives, refused to give them up, resisted a powerful Sultan for months and died when the fort fell. The rest belongs to poetry, which turned that refusal into a model of honour.

### Key points
- **Dynasty.** Last Chahamana ruler of Ranthambore (c. 1283–1301), descended from Prithviraj Chauhan III.
- **Cause of war.** Gave shelter to Mongol rebels from Alauddin Khalji's army and refused to surrender them.
- **The siege.** Nusrat Khan was killed early; Alauddin came in person, and the fort fell in July 1301.
- **Jauhar.** Queen Ranga Devi and the women of the fort performed jauhar, as recorded in the Hammira Mahakavya.
- **Memory.** Celebrated in the Hammira Mahakavya, the Hammir Raso and the proverb "Hammir hath".

kesar-dev.name: Kesar Dev Sisodia
kesar-dev.significance: Brave warrior who sacrificed his life for Mewar
kesar-dev.story:
## Kesar Dev Sisodia — The Loyal Sword of Hammir's Mewar

*No warrior named Kesar Dev appears in the inscriptions, khyats or chronicles of Mewar, nor in James Tod's Annals; his story is best read as a traditional tale of loyalty set in the real age of Rana Hammir Singh (c. 1326–1364), whose recovery of Chittor is recorded in Mewar's later inscriptions and chronicles.*

The bards of Mewar have always told stories about two kinds of heroes: the kings who led, and the companions who gave their lives so that the king might live. **Kesar Dev Sisodia** belongs to the second kind. In the tale told of him, he was a warrior of the house of **Sisoda** who stood beside **Rana Hammir Singh** when Mewar was being reborn after the catastrophe of 1303, and who died shielding his lord in battle. No historical record confirms that he lived. But the world in which his story is set is real, and it helps explain why such tales were told and treasured.

### Mewar after 1303

When **Alauddin Khalji** took **Chittor** in **1303**, the main line of the **Guhila** rulers of Mewar was broken. Chittor was given to the Sultan's son Khizr Khan, and later placed in the hands of **Maldeo**, a Sonigara Chauhan chief of Jalor who held it on behalf of Delhi. Mewar tradition says that the Guhila collateral branch of **Sisoda**, a village in the hills, lost its head **Lakshman Singh** and several of his sons in the defence of Chittor, and that one grandson, **Hammir**, survived.

Over the following decades Hammir rebuilt the family's power from the hills, harassing the lowland garrisons and gathering allies. Around the **1320s or 1330s** he regained Chittor. Tradition says he was offered Maldeo's daughter in marriage, perhaps as a trap, and that she helped him take the fort. Whatever the truth of that story, Hammir became the founder of the **Sisodia** line that ruled Mewar for the next six centuries, and he took the title of **Rana**. The Kumbhalgarh inscription of 1460 and later chronicles praise him as a great warrior.

Mewar tradition also credits Hammir with defeating an army of **Muhammad bin Tughluq** at **Singoli** and capturing its commander. This victory is told in later chronicles and by Tod, but it does not appear in the Persian histories of the time, and historians treat its details with caution. What is clear is that Hammir's reign was a time of constant fighting, as the restored Sisodias reasserted control over the old Guhila lands.

### The tale of Kesar Dev

It is into this setting that the bards place Kesar Dev. In the tale, he was not a prince but a kinsman and trusted companion of the Rana, raised among the fighting men of the Sisoda clan and known for his skill with the lance. When an enemy force crossed into Mewar, Hammir rode out to meet it. In the confusion of battle, word came that the Rana had been cut off and surrounded. Kesar Dev, the story says, gathered a few riders and forced his way through the enemy ranks to the Rana's side, holding off the attackers long enough for Hammir to break free. He himself was overwhelmed and died of his wounds, and the Rana, safe, is said to have honoured his family.

Popular versions add numbers and speeches: that he fought "a thousand enemies single-handed", that he killed an enemy commander in single combat, and that his last words were that the king was safe. Such details are the stuff of bardic poetry, and they cannot be taken as record. Even the identity of the enemy is left vague: some tellings imply a Sultanate army, others a neighbouring chief.

### Why such stories were told

Tales like this one served a purpose. In Rajput society, the bond between a ruler and his kinsmen and retainers was the backbone of the state. The ideal of **swami-bhakti**, devotion to one's lord, was celebrated in songs and memorial stones. Across Rajasthan, the **devli** or hero stone records men who fell in battle, and many villages honour such stones with offerings to this day.

Mewar's real history is full of documented examples of this ideal. At **Haldighati** in **1576**, **Jhala Man Singh** of Bari Sadri is said to have taken up the royal parasol and insignia of **Maharana Pratap**, drawing the Mughal attack upon himself while Pratap withdrew; he was killed. During the siege of Chittor in **1567–68**, **Jaimal Rathore** of Merta and **Patta** of Kelwa commanded the defence after Maharana Udai Singh had left the fort. The story of Kesar Dev reflects the same values, transferred to an earlier and less documented age.

It is also worth remembering that the fourteenth century in Mewar is thinly recorded. Most of what we know about Hammir's companions comes from genealogies compiled much later, and many names have been lost. It is possible that the tale preserves the memory of a real retainer under a name that cannot now be traced. It is equally possible that it is a composite, drawing on many such stories.

### Legacy

Whatever its origin, the story of Kesar Dev Sisodia carries a message that runs deep in Mewar's sense of itself: that the survival of the kingdom after 1303 depended not only on Hammir, but on the men who followed him into exile and back. Mewar's later rulers traced their descent to Hammir, and the Sisodia clans and sub-clans honoured the many unnamed warriors who stood with him.

For readers today, the honest way to approach Kesar Dev is as a figure of tradition. His tale is set against real events: the fall of Chittor in 1303, Hammir's recovery of it, and the long struggle to rebuild Mewar. It speaks for the ordinary fighting men whose loyalty made that recovery possible, and whose names history did not keep.

### Key points
- **Not in the record.** No inscription, chronicle or khyat names Kesar Dev; his story is traditional.
- **Real setting.** Rana Hammir Singh (c. 1326–1364) recovered Chittor and founded the Sisodia line of Mewar.
- **The tale.** Kesar Dev is said to have rescued the surrounded Rana in battle and died of his wounds.
- **Disputed victory.** Hammir's reputed win over Tughluq forces at Singoli comes from Mewar tradition, not Persian sources.
- **Ideal of loyalty.** The story reflects swami-bhakti, seen in documented figures such as Jhala Man Singh at Haldighati.

jaimal-mertia.name: Jaimal Mertia
legends: Fought alongside Patta in Chittorgarh siege
jaimal-mertia.story:
Jaimal Mertia – the heroic ruler of Merta, who gave his life defending Chittor against Akbar's vast army. This heroic warrior was the pride of the state of Merta, and the stories of his valour still thrill the people of Rajasthan.

Jaimal Mertia lived in the 16th century, when the Mughal emperor Akbar had taken control of most of India. He was a ruler of the Rathore line of Merta and was famous for his valour and leadership. All of Marwar was impressed by his resolve and courage.

When Akbar attacked Chittor in 1567, Jaimal Mertia was present there. At that time Chittor was ruled by Maharana Udai Singh. Akbar began the siege of Chittor and offered the king terms of surrender. But the heroes of Chittor rejected the offer.

Jaimal Mertia dedicated himself to the defence of Chittor. He asked Maharana Udai Singh to hand him command of Chittor. With him was Patta Chundawat of Kelwa, a young Sisodia chief. Together the two of them planned the defence of Chittor.

Akbar's army surrounded Chittor. The Mughal army far outnumbered the defenders, while Chittor had only a few thousand men. But Jaimal and Patta did not give up. They made every possible effort to defend the fort.

One night Jaimal Mertia went out to raid the Mughal camp. He displayed astonishing valour. His spear struck down hundreds of Mughal soldiers. Jaimal was gravely wounded in this fight. One of his arms was broken, but he kept on fighting.

When Chittor's position became critical, Jaimal and Patta decided to fight the final battle. They sent Maharana Udai Singh out of the fort and readied themselves to defend Chittor.

In the final battle Jaimal Mertia displayed astonishing valour. He drove alone into the midst of the Mughal army. His spear struck down hundreds of enemies. In the end he was martyred, having given his life in the defence of Chittor.

Moved by Jaimal Mertia's sacrifice, even Akbar praised him. He said that if he had such heroes in his kingdom, he would fear no enemy.

Jaimal Mertia's life carries the message that a true warrior can go to any lengths for his duty. He proved that for a Rajput, protecting his friend and keeping his word are paramount. His valour still inspires the people of Rajasthan today.

A memorial to him stands in Merta. Every year special ceremonies are held on the anniversary of his sacrifice. His life is a symbol of the glory of the Rathore dynasty.

gora-badal.name: Gora & Badal
gora-badal.significance: Legendary warriors who saved Rani Padmini
legends: Saved Rani Padmini from Alauddin Khilji
Symbol of Rajput bravery and loyalty
gora-badal.story:
Gora and Badal – the heroic warriors of Chittor who, through their valour and loyalty, saved Rani Padmini from the clutches of Alauddin Khilji. These two brothers are considered among the most illustrious soldiers of Chittor, and the story of their valour still inspires the people of Rajasthan.

Gora and Badal lived at the end of the 13th century, when Chittor was ruled by Rawal Ratan Singh. The two brothers were trusted soldiers of Chittor and were famous for their valour and loyalty. All of Chittor was impressed by their resolve and courage.

When Alauddin Khilji attacked Chittor in 1303, his desire was to obtain Rani Padmini. Khilji offered Rawal Ratan Singh a proposal: if he sent Rani Padmini to him, he would not touch Chittor. But Rawal Ratan Singh rejected the proposal.

After this Khilji began the siege of Chittor. Over the months this siege lasted, Chittor's position became very precarious. At this point Rani Padmini devised a plan. She sent Khilji a message that she was ready to meet him, but needed a guarantee of her safety for it.

Khilji accepted the proposal. Rani Padmini proposed keeping Gora and Badal with her. She said that the two were her brothers and would protect her. Khilji accepted this, but he had no idea how formidable these two heroic warriors were.

When Rani Padmini went to Khilji's camp, Gora and Badal displayed astonishing valour. They forced their way into the midst of Khilji's army and brought Rani Padmini safely back to Chittor. In this episode they struck down hundreds of Khilji's soldiers.

After this Khilji attacked Chittor again. This time he attacked with full force. Chittor's position became very precarious. Rani Padmini decided to perform jauhar. Gora and Badal supported this decision and stood ready to protect the queen.

At the time of the jauhar Gora and Badal guarded Rani Padmini. They struck down many enemies and escorted the queen safely to the jauhar pyre. After this both of them joined the battle and displayed astonishing valour.

In the final battle Gora and Badal displayed astonishing valour. The two of them drove alone into the midst of the Khilji army. Their spears struck down hundreds of enemies. In the end both were martyred, but they had protected Rani Padmini.

Moved by the sacrifice of Gora and Badal, even Khilji praised them. He said that if he had such heroes in his kingdom, he would fear no enemy.

The lives of Gora and Badal carry the message that true warriors can go to any lengths for their duty. They proved that for a Rajput, protecting his friend and keeping his word are paramount. Their valour still inspires the people of Rajasthan today.

A memorial to them stands in Chittor. Every year special ceremonies are held on the anniversary of their sacrifice. Their lives are a symbol of the glory of Chittor.

rana-kumbha.name: Rana Kumbha
rana-kumbha.significance: Greatest Mewar king, builder of 32 forts, patron of arts
legends: Defeated all enemies including Gujarat and Malwa
Defeated combined armies of Gujarat and Malwa
rana-kumbha.story:
## Rana Kumbha — the scholar-king who built in stone and song

*Rana Kumbha is known from his own inscriptions, above all the great praise-poem carved at Chittor in 1460, from the Sanskrit works written under his name, and from the Persian histories of his enemies in Malwa and Gujarat. Each side claimed victories the other denied; where the record is uncertain, this story says so.*

Kumbhakarna, whom history remembers as **Rana Kumbha**, was born in the early fifteenth century into the Sisodia house that had ruled Mewar from Chittor since Rana Hammir won the fortress back in the previous century. His father was **Rana Mokal**, and his grandfather was **Rana Lakha**, in whose reign silver had been found at Jawar and the treasury of Mewar had grown rich. His grandmother, **Hansa Bai**, was a Rathore princess of Mandore, and through her the Rathores had come to hold great influence at the court of Chittor.

The boy grew up in a court of learning. Mewar's princes were taught to ride and fight, but Kumbha was also taught Sanskrit, grammar, music and the sacred texts, and he loved them all his life. He was still young when disaster struck. In **1433**, while on campaign, Rana Mokal was murdered by **Chacha** and **Mera**, his own kinsmen, sons of an earlier Rana by a lesser wife. The killers fled into the hills, and the young Kumbha was placed on the throne of a kingdom suddenly in danger.

The man who restored order was **Rao Ranmal Rathore**, Hansa Bai's brother and Mokal's uncle. He hunted down the murderers and destroyed them. But Ranmal then made himself master of the court, filling the great offices with Rathores and pushing aside the Sisodia nobles. He brought about the death of **Raghavdev**, the respected brother of **Chunda**, the prince who had long ago given up his right to the throne and gone into exile in Malwa. The Sisodia chiefs began to fear that Mewar would become a Rathore possession.

In **1438** the matter was settled with violence. Ranmal was killed at Chittor by a plot of the Sisodia nobles, and his son **Jodha** fled for his life towards Marwar. Chunda, who had returned to Mewar, pursued him and occupied **Mandore** itself. For years Mandore was held by Mewar, until Jodha recovered it in 1453. In the end Kumbha made peace with him and fixed a boundary between their lands, and Jodha went on to found the city of **Jodhpur** in 1459. With the Rathore danger at court ended, Kumbha could rule in his own right.

His great enemy was the sultanate of **Malwa**, ruled from Mandu by the ambitious **Mahmud Khalji**. Malwa had given shelter to enemies of Mewar, and in **1437** Kumbha marched against it. Near **Sarangpur** he defeated the Sultan's army. The Chittor inscriptions say that Mahmud was taken prisoner and held at Chittor for some months before Kumbha released him without ransom, a gesture of royal generosity that the Rajput tradition loved to remember. The Malwa histories tell the story differently, and historians still argue about the details, but there is no doubt that Sarangpur was a great victory for Mewar.

Mahmud Khalji did not forget. In the 1440s he invaded Mewar again and again. He attacked Kumbhalgarh, marched on Chittor, and tried more than once to take the strong fort of **Mandalgarh**. Some of these campaigns did real damage, and both sides claimed success: Mahmud even built a tower of victory of his own at Mandu. But Mewar held its ground, and none of the Sultan's invasions broke the kingdom.

To the west lay the sultanate of **Gujarat**. When the ruler of **Nagaur**, **Firuz Khan**, died in the early 1450s, a struggle over the succession gave Kumbha a chance to intervene. He backed one claimant, then turned on him when the promised terms were broken, and around **1456** he took Nagaur by force. Gujarat answered with war. Sultan **Qutbuddin Ahmad Shah II** marched against Sirohi and Kumbhalgarh, and in **1456** he and Mahmud Khalji agreed, by the treaty of Champaner, to attack Mewar together and divide it between them. It was the gravest danger of Kumbha's reign. Yet the allied attacks of the following years failed to take the great forts, and Mewar survived the combined assault of its two neighbours.

Kumbha was also a ruler of the hills and frontiers. He brought the Hada chiefs of the Bundi country, the rulers of **Abu** and the princes of the south under his power, and he strengthened Mewar's border with a chain of fortresses. Tradition says that of the eighty-four forts that defended Mewar, thirty-two were built or rebuilt by him. He rebuilt the fort of **Achalgarh** on Mount Abu, strengthened Chittor, and raised new strongholds wherever an enemy might enter.

The greatest of them was **Kumbhalgarh**. Begun around **1443** and completed in **1458** under the architect **Mandan**, it rises more than a thousand metres above sea level on a ridge of the Aravallis. Its wall runs for about thirty-six kilometres over hill and valley, wide enough, it is said, for several horsemen to ride side by side. Inside it stood palaces, gardens, water tanks and dozens of temples. It was almost never taken by force. A popular legend says that the walls kept collapsing until a man offered himself as a sacrifice, and that a shrine marks the place where his head fell; this is a tale told by local people, not recorded history.

At Chittor he raised his most famous monument, the **Vijay Stambha**, the Tower of Victory. Built in the 1440s to celebrate his triumph over Mahmud Khalji, it rises nine storeys, about thirty-seven metres, and its walls are covered inside and out with sculptures of the gods of the Hindu world, each labelled with its name. Its architect was **Jaita**, working with his sons. The tower is often confused with the older **Kirti Stambha** nearby, a Jain tower of the twelfth century that Kumbha did not build.

Kumbha's reign also saw the building of the great Jain temple of **Ranakpur**, begun in **1437** by the merchant **Dharna Shah** under the king's patronage, with its forest of more than a thousand carved pillars. It is a sign of the confidence and wealth of Mewar in his time that such a temple could be built while its armies were at war.

Kumbha himself was a devotee of Vishnu as well as of Ekalinga, the lord whom every king of his house served as *dewan*. At Chittor he built up the temple now called **Kumbhashyam**, dedicated to Vishnu, and within Kumbhalgarh rose shrines to many gods. Yet he gave his patronage freely to the Jain merchants and monks of his kingdom, whose wealth and learning were part of Mewar's strength. Picture the Rana in the cool of an evening at Chittor: the drums of the temples sounding across the rock, the masons' scaffolding still standing around his tower, a court poet reading verses to him while the messengers of the frontier wait outside with news of the Sultan's armies. That was the double life of his reign, war on the borders and building at the centre, and he seems to have carried both with the same restless energy.

Above all, Kumbha was a scholar. Works on music under his name include the vast *Sangitaraja*, a treatise covering song, instrument and dance. He wrote the *Rasikapriya*, a commentary on Jayadeva's *Gita Govinda*, and works on the theory of music and drama are attributed to him. He patronised the architect Mandan, whose books on building are still studied, and his court was full of poets, scholars and craftsmen. The **Chittor prashasti of 1460**, the great Sanskrit inscription set up in his tower of victory and composed by the poets **Atri** and his son **Mahesha**, records his deeds and the genealogy of his house. A popular belief makes the saint-poet Mirabai his queen; she was in fact the wife of a grandson of Rana Sanga and lived in the following century.

The end of this great reign was dark. In his last years, tradition says, Kumbha suffered from a disturbance of the mind and withdrew from the business of the state. In **1468**, at Kumbhalgarh, he was murdered by his own son **Udaysimha**, known as **Uda**, who wanted the throne. Tradition says he was killed while at prayer at a shrine within the fort. Uda was shunned by the nobles of Mewar as a parricide, and within about five years his brother **Raimal** drove him out and took the throne. Raimal's son would be **Rana Sanga**.

Kumbha ruled for thirty-five years. He found Mewar shaken by murder and the ambitions of its neighbours, and left it the strongest kingdom of Rajasthan, ringed by forts and adorned with towers, temples and books. His grandsons would fight the Lodis and the Mughals from the fortresses he raised, and the walls of Kumbhalgarh, the birthplace of Maharana Pratap, still climb over the hills he chose.

## Highlights of his life

- **Accession in crisis (1433).** He came to the throne after the murder of his father, Rana Mokal, and freed the court from Rathore domination in 1438.
- **Victory at Sarangpur (1437).** He defeated Mahmud Khalji of Malwa; Mewar's inscriptions say the Sultan was captured and later released.
- **Survival against Malwa and Gujarat.** He held off repeated invasions, including the combined attack planned by the two sultans in 1456.
- **Capture of Nagaur (c. 1456).** He took Nagaur during its succession struggle, extending Mewar's power to the north-west.
- **Builder of Kumbhalgarh (c. 1443–1458).** He raised the great hill fortress with its thirty-six-kilometre wall, and many other forts of Mewar.
- **The Vijay Stambha.** He built the Tower of Victory at Chittor to celebrate his triumph over Malwa.
- **Scholar-king.** He wrote or sponsored the *Sangitaraja* and a commentary on the *Gita Govinda*, and patronised Mandan and the builders of Ranakpur.
- **Death at Kumbhalgarh (1468).** He was murdered by his son Uda, whose brother Raimal soon took the throne.

bappa-rawal.name: Bappa Rawal
bappa-rawal.significance: Founder of Guhila dynasty in Mewar
bappa-rawal.story:
## Bappa Rawal — the cowherd who became the regent of Shiva

*Much of Bappa Rawal's life comes to us through the traditions of Mewar: the bardic chronicles, the Ekalinga Mahatmya and the memory kept at the temple of Eklingji. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

In the early years of the eighth century, the Guhila clan held small territories in the hills of what is now southern Rajasthan and northern Gujarat. They traced their line to **Guhadatta**, and further back to the solar race of Rama. Their power was modest: a few hill towns, a few forts, and the loyalty of the forest tribes.

Tradition says that Bappa was born into this house as the son of a Guhila chief, and that his father was killed while the boy was still an infant. The bards tell of a night of fire and swords, of a palace that fell, and of a mother who fled into the hills with her child held against her chest. Whether the enemy was a rival chief or a rebellious hill clan, the story agrees on one thing: the heir of the Guhilas survived because someone carried him out of the flames and hid him.

He was taken to **Nagda**, a quiet settlement in a green valley north of where Udaipur stands today. There he was raised not as a prince, but as an ordinary boy in a Brahmin household. Nobody spoke his lineage aloud. His name, *Bappa*, was not even a name at first. It was an affectionate word, something like "little father", the kind of name a village gives a child it loves.

As a boy, Bappa's work was to take the village cows out to graze in the forests around Nagda. He knew every path in those hills, every stream and every cave. The forest tribes, the Bhils, knew him too, and in later years they would stand beside him in war.

Among the cows in his care was one that came home every evening with no milk. The Brahmin who owned her suspected the boy of drinking it on the way. Bappa, hurt by the accusation, followed the cow one day. Deep in a thicket he saw her stop above a stone and let her milk flow onto it of her own accord.

When Bappa cleared away the leaves, he found a **Shiva linga**, and beside it an old ascetic deep in meditation. This was **Harit Rishi**, a sage of the Pashupata tradition. When the sage opened his eyes, tradition says, he looked at the cowherd boy for a long time and told him who he really was.

For years after that day, Bappa served the sage and the hidden shrine. He brought water, gathered flowers, and guarded the place from wild animals. In return, Harit Rishi taught him. The lessons were not only prayers. They were lessons about duty, about the purpose of power, and about the difference between a king and a robber with an army.

The most important lesson became the foundation of a dynasty. The land, the sage said, belongs to **Ekalinga**, the lord Shiva of that shrine. The king is only his servant, his *dewan*, who governs in his name. For more than twelve centuries afterwards, the rulers of Mewar called themselves the **Dewan of Eklingji**, and every Maharana bowed before the shrine as a servant, not a master.

When the time came for the sage to leave the world, the legends say he wished to bless Bappa with immortality, and that Bappa, reaching up too slowly, received the blessing on his body but not his life. Whatever the meaning of the story, he left the forest of Nagda with a sense of purpose that never left him.

As the years passed, the boy grew into a young man. The young man who came down from the hills had little: a sword, a small band of companions, the friendship of the Bhils, and a name the forest people already trusted. He took service, tradition says, with the ruler of **Chittor**, **Man Mori**, of the Maurya (Mori) line that then held that great rock fortress. Some chronicles make Man Mori his maternal uncle.

In Chittor, Bappa rose quickly. He was bold in war and generous in victory, and soldiers followed him gladly. The older nobles of the court resented the newcomer. When an enemy army threatened Chittor, the story goes, those nobles refused to march, and Bappa led the defence with his own men and won.

The victory made him the most powerful man in Chittor. Around **734 CE**, according to Mewar's traditional date, Bappa took the fortress for himself. The bards say the nobles who had abandoned Man Mori opened the way to him. Chittor would remain the heart of Mewar for more than eight hundred years, until Akbar's siege of 1568.

These were dangerous years for all of western India. In the decades after the Arab conquest of Sindh in 712, the governors of the Umayyad Caliphate sent raiding armies east, into Rajasthan, Gujarat and Malwa. Under **Junaid**, the governor of Sindh, these raids reached deep into the region in the 720s and 730s. Old kingdoms fell, and cities were plundered.

The tide was turned by the Indian kings of the region. **Nagabhata I** of the Pratiharas drove the invaders back from Malwa, and in **739 CE** the Chalukya general **Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin** defeated them decisively at **Navsari** in Gujarat. After these defeats, the Arab raids into the interior of India ended for centuries.

Mewar's tradition places Bappa Rawal among the defenders of this age, fighting the invaders and driving them back towards Sindh. The bards go further, telling of a march to the west as far as **Ghazni** and Khorasan. Historians cannot confirm Bappa's exact part in these wars, and the far western campaign is legend. But the memory is important: Mewar has always remembered its founder as a ruler who stood against invasion when the whole region was under threat.

Bappa was not only a warrior. Holding Chittor and Nagda, he had to make the hill country into a state. He bound the Bhil chiefs to the Guhila house with gifts and honour, a bond that lasted for centuries: at the coronation of a Maharana, a Bhil chief traditionally marked the new ruler's forehead with blood from his own thumb.

He also kept faith with the shrine where his life had changed. Tradition credits Bappa with founding the temple of **Eklingji**, near Nagda, around 734 CE, as the seat of the kingdom's true lord. The present temple was rebuilt many times, most of all by **Rana Raimal** in the fifteenth century, but the lineage of worship goes back to him.

A gold coin found at Ajmer, bearing the name **"Shri Voppa"** together with Shaiva symbols, has been linked by many scholars to Bappa. If the attribution is right, it is one of the very few objects that may come from his own reign.

Historians have long asked which Guhila ruler of the inscriptions "Bappa" really was. *Bappa* and *Rawal* are titles of affection and rank rather than a personal name, and the later inscriptions of the dynasty, such as the **Atpur inscription of 977 CE**, list the Guhila kings without using it. Many scholars identify him with **Kalabhoja**, a Guhila ruler of the eighth century. Others suggest different names. What is certain is that the later rulers of Mewar, from the Guhilas to the Sisodias, all looked back to Bappa Rawal as the founder of their kingdom.

Every tradition of Bappa ends in the same way: not on a battlefield, but in renunciation. Having established his kingdom, Bappa is said to have handed power to his son and turned back towards the life of the forest that had formed him. He took up the life of an ascetic in the service of Ekalinga, as his teacher had once lived.

He died around **753 CE**. His *samadhi*, the memorial over his last resting place, is shown near **Nagda**, close to the valley where a cow once gave her milk to a hidden stone, and where a cowherd boy learned that a king is only a servant of something greater.

## Highlights of his life

- **Survival and upbringing at Nagda.** Saved as an infant after his father's death, he was raised in secret as a cowherd in the hills.
- **Disciple of Harit Rishi.** From the sage he received the idea that the ruler is the *dewan* (servant) of Ekalinga. This principle defined Mewar's kingship for over twelve hundred years.
- **Founder of the Eklingji tradition.** Tradition credits him with founding the temple of Eklingji around 734 CE.
- **Conquest of Chittor (c. 734 CE).** He took the fort from the Mori ruler Man Mori, making it the capital of Mewar for over eight centuries.
- **Defender in the age of the Arab raids.** He is remembered as one of the rulers who resisted the Umayyad raids of the 720s and 730s. The decisive victories of 739 CE were won by Nagabhata I and Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin.
- **Alliance with the Bhils.** He bound the forest tribes to the Guhila house, a bond later honoured at every coronation.
- **Renunciation.** He gave up the throne for the life of an ascetic and died around 753 CE near Nagda.

rana-sangram-singh.name: Rana Sangram Singh
rana-sangram-singh.significance: Defender of Rajput honor against Bahmani Sultanate
legends: Fought against combined armies of Bahmani and Gujarat
rana-sangram-singh.story:
*Historical note: This profile is about the same ruler as Rana Sanga (Sangram Singh I, r. 1508–1528). Several details here are dramatised; see the Rana Sanga profile for the historical outline.*

When the sun sank crimson over the ranges of the Aravallis, the ramparts of Chittor looked like a wall of fire. Amid that fire, in the 15th century, the land of Mewar saw the birth of a ruler in whose eyes there gleamed not only the crown but the blaze of the battlefield—he was Rana Sangram Singh.

Born into the tradition of the Sisodia dynasty, Sangram Singh had heard the approach of war since childhood. Within the high ramparts of Chittor he learned that a kingdom is kept safe not by the sword alone, but by unity. The victory tales engraved on palace walls, the veteran chiefs sitting in council, and the dust rising on the borders—all were part of his childhood.

Unlike other princes, he did not lose himself only in hunting and festivities. With the first light of morning he would reach the stables. Balance on horseback, a firm grip on the bowstring, complete control of the sword's edge—his training was rigorous. But more than that, he was learning the lessons of diplomacy. Sitting in the court, he listened to the disputes of the nobles, understood the discussions of trade routes, and recognised the moves of neighbouring sultanates.

At that time the Malwa Sultanate to the south-east and the Gujarat Sultanate in the west were at the height of their power. Both had their eyes on Mewar—the fort of Chittor was not just stone, it was prestige. And when the two planned a combined attack, the smell of a storm filled the air of Rajputana.

The council was grave. Some chiefs said—"Two powers together… this will be hard."
Sangram Singh replied calmly—"Hard, but not impossible. If the Rajputs are one, even mountains bow."

He sent envoys. Marwar, Bundi, Dungarpur—messages reached wherever help could be found. "This is not only Mewar's war; it is the honour of Rajputana."

The first attack came on the southern border. The Malwa army tried to cross the hills and advance. Sangram Singh set up outposts in the mountain passes. He divided his army into three—infantry in the centre forming a wall of shields, cavalry on both sides.

As soon as the enemy entered the narrow pass, arrows rained from above. Horsemen crashed in from below. The clang of swords made the Aravallis tremble. The Malwa lines scattered. But this was only the beginning.

The second and fiercer battle was fought against the army of Gujarat. This time the enemy came armed with gunpowder and heavy cavalry. The two armies faced each other on open ground. The kettledrums thundered. A vast cloud of dust rose.

The first roar of the guns shook the Mewari lines. Many soldiers fell. Smoke spread everywhere. Sangram Singh ordered—"Do not break ranks! Hold steady!"

After the next volley of the guns he gave the signal—"Now!"

The horsemen burst forward like lightning. The cry of "Victory to Eklingji!" made the air tremble. Swords met. Spears struck home. Blood flowed over the earth. A Gujarat commander challenged him—"Surrender!"

Flames blazed in Sangram Singh's eyes—"Sisodias do not bow!"

The two faced each other. Blow after blow. Strikes on the shield. At last Sangram Singh's blow landed true. The commander fell. The enemy fell back.

But the third attempt of the combined army was the most terrible. Detachments of both sultanates advanced together on Chittor. The siege of the fort began. Catapults rained stones on the ramparts. The walls shook, but morale within stood firm.

Sangram Singh himself stood on the bastion. He said to his soldiers—"This is not stone, it is our oath. Do not let it break."

By night he adopted guerrilla tactics. Small detachments were sent out, which cut the enemy's supply routes. One night he went out himself with twenty horsemen. In the darkness they fell upon the camp. Swords flashed. Fire flared up. Chaos broke out. And they vanished back into the darkness.

At last the siege began to break. The combined army was exhausted. Supplies were running low. Sangram Singh ordered the final blow.

The gates opened. The Mewari army poured out like a storm. The flash of swords, the boom of kettledrums, and the cry of "Jai Eklinga!"—the lines of the combined army wavered. Within a few hours they were forced to withdraw.

Chittor was saved.

But Sangram Singh's victory was not of the sword alone—it was of diplomacy too. He had understood that unity is strength. He kept the Rajput states together. He secured the trade routes. He had the forts repaired. Temples were built. Scholars and poets came to his court. Mewar became not only a battlefield, but a centre of culture too.

In his final years, when he stood on the ramparts, he would gaze at the land stretching far into the distance—peaceful, but watchful. He told his successors—"Strength lies not only in the arm, but in the mind too."

When his final moment came, the sun was setting. A red glow had spread over the walls of Chittor. He looked one last time at the fort—the fortress he had saved from the combined storm.

His breath stopped, but his saga came to live in the ramparts.

Rana Sangram Singh was not just a warrior. He was the resolve that showed that when the Rajputs are one, no combined power can make them bow. He proved that valour and diplomacy can go hand in hand.

Even today, when the winds of Chittor strike the ramparts, a voice echoes in them—
"Mewar stands unshaken… the Sisodias are immortal."

rawal-kumar-singh.name: Rawal Kumar Singh
rawal-kumar-singh.significance: Defender of Jaisalmer against Muhammad Ghori
legends: Led final charge against Ghori's army
rawal-kumar-singh.story:
*Historical note: No Bhati ruler of this name is found in the historical record. The fort of Jaisalmer was founded by Rawal Jaisal in 1156. Read this story as legend, not history.*

That fortress standing on a golden hill rising in the heart of the Thar… whose walls blazed like fire at sunset. It was Jaisalmer—the golden crown of the desert. And to defend that crown, in the 12th century, a ruler was born in the lap of the Bhati dynasty who accepted death but would not bow—he was Rawal Kumar Singh.

He was born between sand and valour. Raised in the tradition of the Bhati dynasty, the boy knew from childhood that the land of the desert is kept safe by the sword. Jaisalmer at that time was a centre of trade routes—camel caravans, carts laden with spices and silk, and havelis that gleamed like gold. There was prosperity, but with it, envy too.

The boy Kumar Singh would reach the stables with the first light of morning. Both camels and horses were his mounts. His arm did not tremble as he drew the bowstring. His balance with the sword was remarkable. But more than that, he understood the structure of the fort—where an enemy could climb, where stones could be dropped, from which bastion one could keep watch far into the distance.

As he came of age he took the throne. In his time a storm had already risen across northern India. After 1192, when Muhammad Ghori's army challenged many Rajput kingdoms, its gaze turned west as well—to that golden fortress, the sentinel of the desert.

A sea of dust rose on the horizon. A vast army—horsemen, foot soldiers, archers. The scene was watched from the ramparts of Jaisalmer. The council was anxious. Some chiefs said—"Their numbers are beyond counting."

Rawal Kumar Singh replied calmly—
"Victory comes not from numbers, but from resolve."

The siege began. Camps all around the fortress. Watch kept on the water sources. Supply routes cut. For months arrows rained on the ramparts. Catapults hurled stones from below. The walls shook, but did not fall.

The first great assault came at the main gate. The enemy tried to advance behind a line of heavy shields. Kumar Singh posted archers on the heights.
"Let them come close first," he said.

As soon as they reached the foot of the wall, arrows rained from above. Boiling oil and stones began to pour down. Screams rang out. The gate opened for a moment, and the Bhati warriors burst out. Swords clashed. The sand turned red. The enemy fell back.

But the siege went on and on. The grain began to run out. Water was limited. Hunger began to weaken soldiers and citizens alike. Children cried, the elderly sat in silence. But inside the fort only one thing echoed—"No surrender."

One night a council was called. Some chiefs said—"Raja, the people are dying of hunger."

Rawal Kumar Singh's eyes grew hard.
"Dying of hunger is better than living in disgrace. Rajputs do not become slaves."

The second assault came on the western bastion. The darkness of night. Ladders struck the wall. The enemy began to climb. A fierce fight broke out on the narrow rampart. Swords clashed so close that sparks flew. Kumar Singh himself was in the front line. He parried an officer's blow and with his counter-stroke struck off his head. But the enemy's numbers were beyond counting.

After months of siege, the time of decision came. The supplies were gone. Hunger and exhaustion had weakened the bodies, but the spirit remained unshaken.

In the final council Rawal Kumar Singh said—
"The fort will not hold much longer. Tomorrow at dawn we will open the gates. There will be a final battle. Whoever survives, let him return with glory. Whoever falls, will be immortal."

Dawn came. The sun was crimson. The gates opened. The Bhati army poured out like a desert storm.
The cry of "Jai Bhati!" made the air tremble.

The enemy was taken by surprise. Starving, but ferocious. Swords flashed like lightning. Kumar Singh was on horseback in the front line. He brought down one enemy after another. His sword was already red with blood.

A spear drove into his side. He pulled it out and flung it away. A second blow landed on his shoulder. He staggered, but did not stop.
"Surrender!" the enemy called.

He replied—
"Bhatis die, they do not bow!"

And he charged again.

At last, from many blows, his body gave out. He sank to his knees. His gaze turned back towards the fort—the golden ramparts gleaming in the sun. A faint smile came to his lips.

He fell to the ground—but his sword still pointed forward.

That day Jaisalmer was stained with blood, but its self-respect lived on. Rawal Kumar Singh's sacrifice sank into the sands of the desert—and from there the roots of immortality sprang.

He was not just a ruler. He was the flame that proved that for a Rajput, the kingdom and honour come above all. He chose death, but not slavery.

Even today, when the winds of Jaisalmer strike the ramparts of the golden fort, the clang of swords can be heard in them.

And in every echo a voice rings out—
"Jaisalmer stands unshaken… the Bhatis are immortal."

raja-bhairav-singh.name: Raja Bhairav Singh
raja-bhairav-singh.significance: Brave ruler of Bundi who fought against Mughals
raja-bhairav-singh.story:
*Historical note: No 15th-century Hada ruler named Bhairav Singh is found in the historical record. Taragarh at Bundi was built around 1354 by Rao Bar Singh, and the Mughals did not reach Rajasthan until the 16th century. Read this story as legend, not history.*

Bundi, nestled in the southern arms of the Aravallis… a town hidden among the hills, where the sound of waterfalls and the roar of war drums could be heard side by side. In the 15th century, when empires were spreading across northern India and borders were being drawn on the edge of the sword, a ruler was born in the lap of the Hada dynasty who turned a small kingdom into an unshakeable fortress—he was Raja Bhairav Singh.

He was born amid challenge more than splendour. Bundi was then a small kingdom standing in the shadow of vast empires. There were hills, narrow passes and a few scattered settlements—but within them was a stubborn will. From childhood the boy Bhairav Singh saw that if the kingdom was to survive, it would have to rise above fear.

With the first light of morning he would reach the stables. Balance on horseback, the straight edge of the sword, the precise thrust of the spear—his training was rigorous. But more than that, he read the hills. Which pass opened in which direction, from where an army could come, where an ambush could be laid—all of it was engraved in his memory.

As he came of age he resolved—Bundi would not remain merely a refuge; it would become a power.

As soon as he took the throne he pointed to the highest peak in the hills.
"A fort will rise here," he said.

And cutting through the rocks, joining stone to stone, Taragarh rose on the heights—Taragarh Fort. Its ramparts were such that an enemy's heart would quake from afar. Narrow paths, hidden gates, high bastions—this was not just construction, it was strategy.

But a fort being built does not stop enemies. The first challenge came from the frontier. A Mughal general took Bundi for an easy target. A vast army, lines of horsemen, the roar of kettledrums.

Bhairav Singh divided his army among the mountain passes. The front line offered light resistance and began to fall back. The enemy took this for weakness and entered the narrow way. Just then arrows and stones rained from above. Hada horsemen crashed in from below.
The cry of "Hada!" made the valley tremble. Swords met. A cloud of dust and blood rose. Within a few hours the enemy fell back.

This was not just a victory—it was a message that Bundi was no longer prey.

The second and fiercer battle was fought on the open plain. This time the enemy came with gunpowder and heavy cavalry. The first roar of the guns shook the earth. Many soldiers fell. Smoke spread everywhere.

Bhairav Singh ordered—"After the guns fire, spread out, then charge together."

The guns were fired. The smoke cleared. He raised his sword—
"Bundi!"

The horsemen burst forward like lightning. The field rang with the clang of swords. A Mughal officer challenged him—
"Surrender!"

Flames blazed in Bhairav Singh's eyes—
"Hadas do not bow!"

The two faced each other. Blow after blow. Strikes on the shield. At last Bhairav Singh's blow landed true. The officer fell. The enemy lines wavered.

But the hardest struggle came when Taragarh was besieged. For months the enemy stayed camped below the fort. Stones were hurled from catapults. The ramparts shook, but did not fall.

By night Bhairav Singh adopted guerrilla tactics. Small detachments went out. Supply routes were cut. One night he himself fell upon the camp with twenty horsemen. Flames leapt up. Chaos broke out. And they returned into the darkness.

The siege broke.

But he was not only a warrior. He made Bundi prosperous too. Reservoirs were built among the hills. Temple spires rose. Art and painting received patronage. Poets and scholars came to his court. Trade routes were secured. Bundi became not just a fortress, but a centre of culture.

Once someone in the court asked—
"Maharaj, why make so small a kingdom so strong?"

Bhairav Singh replied—
"It is not the size of a kingdom that should be great, but its self-respect."

Time went by. Bundi's borders expanded. The name of the Hada dynasty began to echo far and wide. The ramparts of Taragarh gleamed in the sun—as if ready each day for a new challenge.

In his final years, when he stood on the heights of the fort, he would look at the town spread out below—the sound of waterfalls, the bells of temples, and safe settlements. All of this was the fruit of his resolve.

When his final moment came, the sun was setting. A red glow had spread over the walls of Taragarh. He looked one last time at the fortress he had made unconquerable through sheer will.

His breath stopped, but Bundi lived on.

Raja Bhairav Singh was not just a ruler. He was the resolve that turned a small kingdom into an unshakeable power. He proved that Rajputs are standard-bearers not only on the battlefield, but in building and administration too.

Even today, when the winds of Bundi strike the ramparts of Taragarh, a voice echoes in them—
"Bundi stands unshaken… the Hadas are immortal."

rani-durgavati.name: Rani Durgavati
rani-durgavati.significance: Brave queen who fought against Mughal invasion
legends: Fought against Akbar's general Asaf Khan
rani-durgavati.story:
Between the hills of the Vindhyas and the Satpuras, near the calm waters of the Narmada, lay Gondwana—a land of dense forests, high forts and indomitable pride. In 1524 that land saw a daughter born in the lap of the Chandela dynasty, in whose eyes there was more courage than beauty. She was Rani Durgavati.

As a girl Durgavati had learned to draw the bowstring with ease. Riding on horseback she would race through the forests, hunt, and strike every target with unerring aim. Her education was not limited to the scriptures—weapons were part of her life too. The tradition of the Chandela royal house had taught her that a daughter of the royal line could also step onto the battlefield.

Time turned. She was married to Raja Dalpat Shah of Gondwana. She was no longer just a princess, but a queen. The hills, rivers and forts of Gondwana embraced her. But married happiness did not last long. Dalpat Shah's untimely death left the kingdom as good as orphaned. Her son was still a child. The court was in confusion.

Durgavati stepped forward. She took the throne.
"A kingdom is not widowed," she said in the assembly, "as long as its queen lives."

She organised the administration. The guard forts on the borders were strengthened. The trade routes were secured. Prosperity grew from the timber and minerals of the forests and from agriculture. Gondwana became not just a kingdom of forests, but an organised power. Justice in her court was strict, but fair.

But in the north a vast empire was spreading its power—Akbar. On his behalf the general Asaf Khan cast his eye on Gondwana's prosperity. The year 1564—a vast cloud of dust rose on the horizon. The Mughal army was advancing.

In the council some chiefs said—"Maharani, their army is vast."

Durgavati replied—
"Courage is greater than numbers."

She organised the army. She planned to take advantage of the hills and narrow passes. She decided to lead the battle herself.

The first clash took place near the pass of Narrai. Dense forest, high rocks, and the stream of the Narmada flowing between. Durgavati rode her elephant "Sarman". A bow in her hand, a sword at her waist.

The Mughal army wanted open ground, but the pass narrowed their lines. Arrows rained from above. Gond warriors burst out from behind the trees. The forest rang with the cry of "Jai Maa Durga!" Swords met. Spears struck home. Dust and smoke mingled in the air.

The first blow succeeded. The Mughal army fell back. But they reorganised and returned.

The second and fiercer battle took place on the plain of Damanpur. This time the guns were fired. The earth shook. Many Gond soldiers fell. Smoke spread everywhere.

Durgavati drove her elephant forward—
"Do not fall back!"

Her arrows were bringing down enemies one by one. The flash of her sword cleared the ground around her. A Mughal officer challenged her—
"Surrender! Your life will be spared!"

Flames blazed in her eyes—
"Freedom is greater than life!"

The battle went on for hours. Suddenly an arrow struck and lodged near her eye. Blood flowed. Her elephant was wounded too. But she did not stop. She pulled out the arrow, flung it away, and raised her sword again.

But the situation had become critical. The army began to scatter. The elephant staggered. Her trusted soldiers came close—
"Maharani, fall back!"

She said calmly—
"To go back is subjection."

Even wounded, she struck her final blows. But when enemies closed in on every side and escape became impossible, she made her decision.

She looked at her trusted attendant—
"Do not let me be taken alive."

A moment's silence. When he hesitated, she drew her own dagger and drove it into her breast.

Rani Durgavati fell to the ground—but her gaze was turned to the sky. On her lips was a faint smile—of freedom.

That day Gondwana was stained with blood. The kingdom eventually passed under the Mughals. But its queen did not accept servitude.

She was not just a ruler. She was the flame that proved a woman could stand as unshaken on the battlefield as any warrior. She chose death, but not dishonour.

Even today, when the Narmada flows through the winds of central India, the clang of swords can be heard in its waves.

And in every echo a voice rings out—
"Durgavati is immortal… freedom is immortal."

nagabhata-i.name: Nagabhata I
nagabhata-i.significance: Founder of Pratihara dynasty, repelled Arab invasions
legends: Protected northern India from Islamic invasion
nagabhata-i.story:
## Nagabhata I — The Sentinel of Avanti

*Nagabhata I is known chiefly from the Gwalior prashasti of his descendant Mihira Bhoja, from Rashtrakuta and Chahamana copper plates, and from Arab historians such as al-Baladhuri; dates for his reign are approximate, and later bardic claims about him are best read as tradition.*

In the first half of the eighth century, the political map of western India was being redrawn from two directions at once. In the south the **Chalukyas** of Badami were giving way to the rising **Rashtrakutas**, and from the west the armies of the **Umayyad caliphate**, which had conquered **Sindh** in **712 CE**, were pressing towards the rich lands of Gujarat, Rajasthan and Malwa. Out of this turmoil emerged a ruler who would found one of the great imperial houses of early medieval India: **Nagabhata I**, founder of the imperial line of the **Gurjara-Pratiharas**.

### Origins

Almost nothing is known of Nagabhata's birth or early life. The family's own account, preserved in the **Gwalior prashasti** composed in the reign of Mihira Bhoja a century later, traces the line to **Lakshmana**, brother of Rama, who served as Rama's *pratihara* or door-keeper, and explains the dynastic name through that image. Historians read this as a learned genealogy rather than a record of descent. Whether the Pratiharas were Gurjaras by ethnicity, rulers of a land called **Gurjaratra**, or a lineage whose name came from an office, remains one of the long-running debates of Indian historiography. Later bardic tradition counted them among the four **Agnikula** clans born from a sacrificial fire on **Mount Abu**, but that story appears centuries later and is not found in the Pratiharas' own records.

Nagabhata's base appears to have been **Avanti**, the region around **Ujjain** in western Malwa, though some scholars place the family's early seat at **Bhinmal** (Shrimala) in south-western Rajasthan. His reign is usually dated to roughly **730–760 CE**.

### The Arab incursions

The deed for which Nagabhata is remembered is his resistance to the Arab raids. The governor of Sindh, **Junaid ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Murri**, led campaigns in the 720s and 730s that, according to al-Baladhuri, struck at places identified with Marwar, Bharuch, Ujjain, Bhinmal and the land of the Gurjaras. These were raids for plunder and tribute, and in the short term several succeeded.

Within a few years, however, the tide turned. Arab writers themselves record that under Junaid's successor **Tamim** the Muslims lost ground in India and fell back, and that a new fortified town, **al-Mahfuza** ("the guarded"), had to be built in Sindh as a refuge. Indian inscriptions explain why. The **Gwalior prashasti** praises Nagabhata as one who appeared like Narayana to protect the people and crushed the large armies of a powerful *mlechchha* king — a phrase almost universally understood as a reference to the Arabs. The **Navsari plates** of the Chalukya prince **Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin**, dated to about **739 CE**, describe how he too repulsed the Tajikas (Arabs) after they had overrun Sindh, Saurashtra and the Gurjara country.

The honest conclusion is that the Arab advance was checked by several Indian powers, of whom Nagabhata was one of the most important. Modern writing sometimes credits him alone with "saving India", and some accounts pair him with **Bappa Rawal** of Mewar in a grand alliance; the latter rests on later tradition, not on contemporary evidence. There is no reliable record of a personal duel with Junaid, or of the specific battle sequences found in popular retellings.

### Between the Arabs and the Rashtrakutas

Nagabhata's other great rival lay to the south. The Rashtrakuta king **Dantidurga** expanded into Malwa in the mid-eighth century, and later Rashtrakuta records claim that at a great ceremony held at Ujjain the "Gurjara lord" served as door-keeper — a boastful pun on the Pratihara name, probably reflecting a temporary submission. The **Hansot plates** of a Chahamana feudatory, dated **756 CE**, name an overlord called **Nagavaloka**, often identified with Nagabhata, which suggests his influence reached as far as Bharuch in Gujarat.

It is important to correct one common error: **Kannauj was not Nagabhata I's capital**. The city on the Ganga was won by his descendant **Nagabhata II** in the early ninth century. Nagabhata I's power was centred in Malwa and western Rajasthan.

### Death and succession

Nagabhata I died around **760 CE**. He was succeeded not by a son but by his nephews, **Kakkustha** (Kakuka) and then **Devaraja**.
