Devaraja's son **Vatsaraja** carried the dynasty into the great three-way struggle for Kannauj with the **Palas** of Bengal and the Rashtrakutas — the so-called "tripartite struggle" that shaped northern Indian politics for a century.

### Legacy

Nagabhata I founded a dynasty that, under **Nagabhata II**, **Mihira Bhoja** and **Mahendrapala I**, would rule an empire stretching from the Sutlej to Bengal's borders and from the Himalayas to the Narmada. Arab travellers of the ninth century described the Pratihara king as the most hostile of Indian rulers to their faith, with excellent cavalry and a land safe from robbers — a reputation rooted in the frontier defence begun by Nagabhata.

In modern Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh, Nagabhata has become a symbol of resistance, and several communities claim descent from the Pratiharas. Historians caution that the evidence for his reign is thin and largely retrospective, but even read conservatively, the record shows a ruler who built a durable state on a dangerous frontier and helped to end the period of Arab expansion beyond Sindh.

### Key points
- **Founder.** Nagabhata I (c. 730–760 CE) founded the imperial line of the Gurjara-Pratiharas, based in Avanti (Ujjain) or possibly Bhinmal.
- **Arab frontier.** The Gwalior prashasti credits him with crushing the armies of a mlechchha king, understood as the Arabs of Sindh.
- **Shared resistance.** The Chalukyas of Lata and other powers also repelled the Arabs around 739 CE; the victory was not his alone.
- **Rashtrakuta rivalry.** He faced Dantidurga's expansion into Malwa, and may have submitted for a time.
- **Not Kannauj.** Kannauj became the Pratihara capital only under Nagabhata II, in the ninth century.
- **Succession.** His nephews Kakkustha and Devaraja followed him, then Vatsaraja.

mihir-bhoja.name: Mihir Bhoja
mihir-bhoja.significance: Greatest Pratihara emperor, expanded empire across North India
mihir-bhoja.story:
## Mihira Bhoja — The Adivaraha of Kannauj

*Mihira Bhoja's reign is well documented by his own inscriptions — the Barah and Daulatpura copper plates, the Gwalior prashasti and the Pehowa inscription — by his "Adivaraha" coins, and by the Arab merchant Sulaiman's account of 851 CE; the battle scenes and speeches of popular retellings are not found in these sources.*

By the ninth century, northern India's politics revolved around a single prize: **Kannauj**, the old imperial city on the Ganga that had been Harsha's capital. Three powers contested it — the **Palas** of Bengal, the **Rashtrakutas** of the Deccan, and the **Gurjara-Pratiharas** of Malwa and Rajasthan. The Pratiharas finally made it their own, and under **Mihira Bhoja** (also known as **Bhoja I**) they reached the height of their power.

### Origins and accession

Mihira Bhoja was the son of **Ramabhadra** and the grandson of **Nagabhata II**, the king who had captured Kannauj around **815 CE**. Kannauj was therefore not conquered by Bhoja; he inherited it. But Ramabhadra's short reign had been troubled, and the Pratiharas appear to have lost ground, possibly to the Pala king **Devapala**. Bhoja came to the throne around **836 CE**, and his earliest record, the **Barah copper plate** of that year, shows him restoring a land grant in the Kannauj region that had lapsed under his predecessors — a small but telling sign of a king re-establishing his authority.

His titles were **Mihira** (the sun) and, most famously, **Adivaraha**, identifying him with Vishnu's boar incarnation who raised the earth from the waters. Silver coins bearing the legend *Shrimad Adivaraha* and the figure of the boar circulated widely in northern India for generations after him.

### The long wars

Bhoja's reign lasted nearly half a century, and much of it was spent at war. The record is mixed rather than a string of victories.

In the east, he contended with the Palas. Devapala's inscriptions claim to have humbled the "Gurjara lord", suggesting early reverses for Bhoja; later in his reign, against Devapala's weaker successors, the Pratiharas pressed eastwards, and the frontier moved towards Bihar.

In the south and west, he clashed repeatedly with the Rashtrakutas. Rashtrakuta records claim victories over him, while Pratihara records claim the opposite; the fighting around **Ujjain** and the **Narmada** seems to have swung both ways. Bhoja also fought the Rashtrakuta branch of Gujarat. Through these wars he relied on loyal feudatories and allies: the Guhila **Harsharaja** of Chatsu, who is said to have presented him with fine horses, and the Kalachuri **Kokalla I** of Tripuri, whose descendants' inscriptions claim he gave Bhoja protection.

By the end of his reign, Bhoja's authority extended over most of the territory between the Sutlej and the Ganga basin. The **Pehowa inscription** (882 CE) shows his rule in Haryana, while grants and inscriptions from Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and central India confirm a wide domain. The **Daulatpura plate** (843 CE) documents his grants in Rajasthan.

### Against the Arabs

The Arabs of Sindh remained a frontier concern, though by Bhoja's time their power had shrunk to the principalities of Mansura and Multan. The Arab merchant **Sulaiman**, writing in **851 CE**, described the king of "Juzr" (the Gurjaras) as maintaining numerous forces, with the finest cavalry in India, as the greatest enemy of the Muslims among Indian kings, and as ruling a land where people were safe from robbers. There is no record of a specific desert battle with an Arab army in his reign; Sulaiman's testimony is better evidence of a strong, well-ordered state that the Arabs regarded as their most dangerous neighbour.

### The ruler

Bhoja was a devotee of Vishnu, as his Adivaraha title shows, and his inscriptions also honour the goddess Bhagavati. His **Gwalior prashasti** is itself a literary work, giving the Pratihara genealogy from Lakshmana and praising each of his ancestors. Kannauj under him was again a great capital, and the Pratihara period saw a wave of temple-building across central India and Rajasthan. Specific monuments are difficult to tie to Bhoja personally, however, and claims that he "built magnificent temples" should be read as a description of the age rather than a list of his commissions.

### Death and succession

Bhoja died around **885 CE** and was succeeded by his son **Mahendrapala I**, whose court was graced by the poet and dramatist **Rajashekhara**. Under Mahendrapala the empire reached Bengal and Saurashtra. Decline came in the tenth century: the Rashtrakuta **Indra III** sacked Kannauj around **916 CE**, feudatories such as the Chandelas and Paramaras gained independence, and in **1018** Mahmud of Ghazni took the city.

### Legacy

Historians generally regard Mihira Bhoja as the greatest Pratihara emperor and one of the most powerful rulers of early medieval India. His coins, his inscriptions and Sulaiman's testimony describe an empire that held the north together through a long age of rivalries. In modern times he has become a contested figure of identity: both Gurjar and Rajput organisations claim him, and statues and memorials to him have sometimes become the subject of disputes. The historical Bhoja, as far as the sources allow us to see him, belongs to the wider history of India — a king who restored a faltering inheritance and ruled for forty-nine years from Kannauj.

### Key points
- **Inherited Kannauj.** Nagabhata II captured Kannauj; Bhoja (r. c. 836–885) restored Pratihara authority there after Ramabhadra's troubled reign.
- **Adivaraha.** His coins bear the boar of Vishnu and the legend Shrimad Adivaraha.
- **Mixed wars.** He fought the Palas and Rashtrakutas for decades, with victories and setbacks on both sides.
- **Arab testimony.** The merchant Sulaiman (851 CE) praised the Gurjara king's cavalry and the safety of his land.
- **Wide empire.** Inscriptions from Pehowa to Gwalior show rule over much of northern India.
- **Succession.** His son Mahendrapala I extended the empire further.

anangpal-tomar.name: Anangpal Tomar
anangpal-tomar.significance: Founder of Delhi, built Lal Kot fort
legends: Built Lal Kot fort in Delhi
anangpal-tomar.story:
## Anangpal Tomar — The King Who Peopled Delhi

*Anangpal II Tomar is attested by a short inscription on the Iron Pillar at Mehrauli and by Tomar coins, but most of his story — the founding of Lal Kot, the "loose nail" legend and his link to Prithviraj Chauhan — comes from later bardic chronicles such as the Prithviraj Raso and local tradition; archaeology at Lal Kot supports a Tomar-period settlement without confirming every detail.*

Delhi is a city of many founders, but the one remembered as its first Rajput king is **Anangpal Tomar** — more precisely **Anangpal II** of the **Tomara** dynasty, who ruled in the mid-eleventh century and is traditionally credited with building the fortified citadel of **Lal Kot**, the oldest of the "seven cities" of Delhi.

### The Tomaras

The Tomaras appear in the historical record as a clan of the north-west, first as feudatories of the **Gurjara-Pratiharas**. The ninth-century **Pehowa inscription** mentions a Tomara family serving the Pratihara emperor Mahendrapala. As Pratihara power faded in the tenth century, the Tomaras established an independent principality around **Dhillika**, the old name of Delhi, and the land between the **Yamuna** and the **Aravalli** ridge, a region the sources sometimes call **Hariyanaka**.

Bardic genealogies give the dynasty a long list of kings and place an earlier founder, **Anangpal I**, in the eighth century. These lists are inconsistent and cannot be confirmed. What is better established is that the Tomaras held Delhi and parts of Haryana in the eleventh and twelfth centuries, and that they faced repeated pressure from the **Ghaznavids** in the Punjab.

### The inscription on the Iron Pillar

The strongest piece of evidence for Anangpal II is a short, roughly inscribed line on the famous **Iron Pillar**, now standing in the Qutb complex at Mehrauli. It records, in the year **Samvat 1109** (about **1052 CE**), that "Anangpal peopled" — or settled — Delhi. The pillar itself is far older, an inscribed Gupta-era monument of the fourth or fifth century, and tradition holds that Anangpal brought it to its present site as the centrepiece of his new capital.

From this inscription comes the conventional date for the re-founding of Delhi, and the traditional reign of **c. 1051–1081**. Coins of the Tomara kings of Delhi, of the horseman-and-bull type common in the region, also circulated, and the later term *dehliwal* for a coin points to Delhi's growing importance as a mint town.

### Lal Kot and Anangpur

Tradition credits Anangpal with **Lal Kot**, a rubble-walled fortification on the rocky ridge of south Delhi. Excavations by the Archaeological Survey of India — notably in the 1990s at the site of the **Anang Tal** reservoir and Lal Kot's walls, and further work in recent years — have found evidence of an eleventh-century settlement and fortification consistent with a Tomara date. The reservoir **Anang Tal** near Mehrauli and the old dam at **Anangpur** near Faridabad both carry his name, and **Surajkund**, the stepped amphitheatre-tank nearby, is traditionally linked with a Tomara king named Surajpal.

Lal Kot was later enlarged by the Chauhans into **Qila Rai Pithora**, and after 1192 it became the first seat of the Delhi Sultanate. The Qutb Minar and the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque stand within the Tomara-Chauhan citadel.

### Defence and the Ghaznavids

Anangpal's reign coincided with a period of Ghaznavid raids out of Lahore. A Ghaznavid army under Mas'ud had taken **Hansi** in 1037, and the Tomaras and their allies fought to recover it; the later Persian historian Firishta describes a confederacy led by the "Raja of Delhi" that drove the Ghaznavids back from Hansi, Thanesar and Nagarkot around 1043. Which Tomara king led those efforts is not certain. Popular accounts of Anangpal personally defeating invaders in pitched battles beneath Lal Kot's walls are later elaborations; what can be said is that his dynasty held the eastern frontier of the Punjab against the Ghaznavids for over a century.

### The legend of the loose nail

The best-known story about Anangpal comes from the **Prithviraj Raso**. In it, a Brahmin tells the king that the iron pillar is driven so deep that it rests on the head of the serpent Vasuki, and that so long as it stands his dynasty will endure. Doubting this, Anangpal has the pillar pulled up, and finds its base wet with blood. When it is reset it will not stand firm — it remains *dhili*, loose — and so, the bards say, the city came to be called **Dilli**, and the Tomara line was doomed. The tale is a folk etymology, not history, but it has been retold for centuries.

The Raso also makes Anangpal the maternal grandfather of **Prithviraj Chauhan**, who inherits Delhi from him. Historians reject this: inscriptions show that Delhi was taken by the Chauhan king **Vigraharaja IV** around the 1150s, after which the Tomaras ruled as Chauhan feudatories.

### Death and legacy

Nothing reliable is known of Anangpal II's death. He is remembered not for a final battle but as a builder and founder — the king who turned a ridge-top settlement into a capital. In recent years organisations in Delhi and Haryana have campaigned for greater recognition of him, and he is commemorated as the founder of Delhi in public events and proposals for memorials. The Iron Pillar inscription remains the one line in which he speaks to us directly, across nearly a thousand years.

### Key points
- **Delhi's Rajput founder.** Anangpal II Tomar (traditional reign c. 1051–1081) is credited with re-founding Delhi as his capital.
- **Inscription.** A line on the Iron Pillar dated Samvat 1109 (c. 1052 CE) records that Anangpal peopled Delhi.
- **Lal Kot.** The citadel traditionally attributed to him has been confirmed archaeologically as an eleventh-century fortification.
- **Ghaznavid frontier.** The Tomaras held Delhi and Haryana against Ghaznavid pressure from the Punjab.
- **Legend.** The Raso's "dhili" pillar story is a folk etymology for the name Delhi.
- **Chauhan succession.** Vigraharaja IV took Delhi in the twelfth century; the Raso's grandfather story is not historical.

arnoraja-chauhan.name: Arnoraja Chauhan
arnoraja-chauhan.significance: Chauhan king who expanded kingdom and built temples
arnoraja-chauhan.story:
## Arnoraja Chauhan — The King of Anasagar

*Arnoraja's reign is known from Chahamana inscriptions such as the Bijolia rock inscription (1170 CE), from fragments of an Ajmer prashasti, from the Sanskrit poem Prithviraja Vijaya, and from Jain chronicles of Gujarat; claims that he built temples at Pushkar are not supported by the record, and battle details in popular retellings are later invention.*

In the first half of the twelfth century, the **Chahamanas** (Chauhans) of **Shakambhari** were transforming themselves from a regional lineage of the Sambhar salt-lake country into the leading power of Rajasthan. The city of **Ajmer** — **Ajayameru** — had just been founded by **Ajayaraja**, and it fell to his son **Arnoraja**, also called **Anaji** or **Analadeva**, to defend and extend the new capital. He ruled from about **1135 to 1150 CE**.

### Origins

Arnoraja was born into a dynasty that traced itself to a legendary ancestor named **Chahamana** and, in later bardic accounts, to the **Agnikula** fire-born clans of Mount Abu. The family's own inscriptions describe a solar descent instead; the fire-origin story belongs to the later **Prithviraj Raso**. By Arnoraja's day the Chahamanas had been feudatories of the Pratiharas, then independent kings, and had absorbed much of central and eastern Rajasthan. His father Ajayaraja had fought the Paramaras of Malwa and the Ghaznavid raiders from the Punjab, and had moved the royal seat from Shakambhari to the more defensible site of Ajmer in the Aravalli hills.

### Victory over the Turushkas and Anasagar

The deed most closely associated with Arnoraja is a victory over a raiding army of **Turushkas** — Turkic troops of the **Ghaznavid** rulers of Lahore — who advanced towards Ajmer, probably across the desert of Nagaur. A fragmentary inscription from Ajmer and the **Prithviraja Vijaya** of the poet **Jayanaka** describe a great slaughter of the invaders near the city. According to the Prithviraja Vijaya, the ground was so soaked with blood that Arnoraja had it purified by filling it with water, creating the lake that bears his name: **Anasagar**, "the ocean of Ana". Whether or not that poetic explanation is literally true, the lake, fed by the Chandra river and still one of Ajmer's landmarks, is his most lasting monument. The marble pavilions on its embankment were added much later by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan.

This victory is the basis for the old story's claim that he "defeated Muslim invaders". It was a single significant engagement against a Ghaznavid raid, not a series of set-piece battles; there is no record of the speeches or duels found in modern retellings.

### Wars with Gujarat and Malwa

Arnoraja's longer struggles were with his Hindu neighbours. Like many Rajput kings of his age, he fought both with and against the **Chaulukyas** (Solankis) of Gujarat, the most powerful kingdom of western India. Early in his reign he was defeated by **Jayasimha Siddharaja**, and the peace was sealed by marriage: Arnoraja married Jayasimha's daughter **Kanchanadevi**, who became the mother of **Someshvara** — and so the grandmother of **Prithviraj Chauhan**.

After Jayasimha's death in 1143, Arnoraja backed a rival claimant against the new king **Kumarapala**. The resulting war went badly for him: Jain chronicles of Gujarat, such as those of **Hemachandra** and later Merutunga, describe Kumarapala's victory over the "king of Sapadalaksha" around **1150**, and Arnoraja was obliged to make peace on terms that acknowledged Gujarat's strength. The chronicles add colourful anecdotes about insults exchanged at the Chahamana court, but these are literary embellishment. These Gujarati sources naturally favour Kumarapala, but Chahamana sources do not contradict the defeat.

Arnoraja also campaigned against the **Paramaras** of Malwa and raided towards the lands of the **Tomaras** of Delhi; the Bijolia inscription claims his armies watered their horses in the Yamuna region. The real conquest of Delhi would come under his son.

### Patronage

Arnoraja was a devotee of Shiva and is known to have patronised Brahmins and religious institutions; local tradition credits him with the original **Varaha temple** at **Pushkar**, a town that was already a major Brahmanical pilgrimage centre. That temple has been destroyed and rebuilt several times, and the present structure dates from the eighteenth century, so no surviving building at Pushkar can be securely attributed to him, and the claim in some modern accounts that he "built the Pushkar temples" should be treated as tradition at best. He was tolerant of Jainism, and Jain merchants of Ajmer flourished in his time.

### Death

Arnoraja's end was violent and domestic, not heroic. Around **1150** he was killed by his own son **Jagaddeva**, an act the Prithviraja Vijaya condemns. Jagaddeva's rule was brief; he was soon displaced by his brother **Vigraharaja IV**, who became the greatest Chahamana king before Prithviraj.

### Legacy

Arnoraja stands at a turning point in the history of Ajmer. He defended the new capital against the Ghaznavids, gave it its great lake, and bound his dynasty by marriage to the Chaulukyas of Gujarat — a tie that shaped Prithviraj's own childhood, much of which was spent at the Gujarat court with his mother. His sons Vigraharaja IV and Someshvara would build on his foundations. In Ajmer today, Anasagar is his memorial, visited daily by people who may know little of the king whose name it carries.

### Key points
- **Ruler of Ajmer.** Arnoraja (Anaji), son of Ajayaraja, ruled the Chahamana kingdom from about 1135 to 1150 CE.
- **Turushka defeat.** He destroyed a Ghaznavid raiding army near Ajmer, as recorded in the Prithviraja Vijaya.
- **Anasagar.** The poem says he created Anasagar lake to cleanse the battlefield; the lake remains his main monument.
- **Gujarat ties.** He married Jayasimha Siddharaja's daughter but was later defeated by Kumarapala around 1150.
- **Pushkar caution.** No Pushkar temple can be securely attributed to him.
- **Death.** He was killed by his son Jagaddeva, who was soon replaced by Vigraharaja IV.

vigraharaja-iv-chauhan.name: Vigraharaja IV Chauhan
vigraharaja-iv-chauhan.significance: Greatest Chauhan king before Prithviraj, expanded empire
vigraharaja-iv-chauhan.story:
## Vigraharaja IV — The Poet-King Who Took Delhi

*Vigraharaja IV (Visaladeva) is unusually well documented: his own inscription on the Delhi-Topra Ashokan pillar (1164 CE), the plays carved in stone at Ajmer, the Bijolia rock inscription (1170 CE) and the Prithviraja Vijaya; the dramatic storming of Lal Kot in popular retellings has no basis in these sources.*

Among the Chahamana (Chauhan) kings of Ajmer, **Prithviraj III** is the best known, but historians often regard his uncle **Vigraharaja IV**, also called **Visaladeva** or **Bisaldev**, as the dynasty's greatest ruler. In a reign of about fourteen years, from roughly **1150 to 1164 CE**, he made the Chahamanas the dominant power of north-western India, took **Delhi** from the **Tomaras**, and left behind some of the most remarkable literary inscriptions of medieval India.

### A violent accession

Vigraharaja was a son of **Arnoraja**, the king of Ajmer who had defeated a Ghaznavid army and built the Anasagar lake. Around **1150**, Arnoraja was murdered by another son, **Jagaddeva**. Vigraharaja soon displaced his parricide brother and took the throne. His half-brother **Someshvara**, Arnoraja's son by a Chaulukya princess, was then being raised at the Gujarat court; Someshvara's son would later be Prithviraj.

### Conquests

Vigraharaja's first wars were against the **Chaulukyas** of Gujarat, who had humiliated his father. The **Bijolia inscription** claims that he punished the Chaulukya king **Kumarapala**, and that he destroyed or ravaged towns such as **Pali**, **Nadol** and **Jalore**, whose rulers were Chaulukya feudatories. Gujarat sources tell a different story, and the wars probably did not change the frontier decisively, but they ended the period of Chahamana subordination.

His greatest achievement lay to the north-east. The Bijolia inscription states that he took **Dhillika** (Delhi) and **Ashika** (Hansi), weary as they were from earlier fighting. The Tomara kings of Delhi were not exterminated; they became **feudatories** of the Chahamanas and continued to rule Delhi under Ajmer's overlordship. The process seems to have been one of campaigns and submission rather than a single assault, and no source describes the siege scenes, gate-breaking or street fighting found in popular versions.

Possession of Delhi and Hansi brought the Chahamanas face to face with the **Ghaznavids** of Lahore, and Vigraharaja seems to have fought them successfully. His own words survive. In **1164 CE** (Samvat 1220) he had an inscription carved on the **Ashokan pillar** that Firoz Shah Tughlaq later moved from **Topra** to Delhi, where it still stands at **Firoz Shah Kotla**. In it he claims to have conquered the land between the **Vindhyas** and the **Himalayas**, and to have made Aryavarta once again worthy of its name by repeatedly exterminating the *mlechchhas*. The inscription also urges his successors not to let their minds be idle in subduing the rest. Historians read this as royal rhetoric, but it shows that the Chahamanas now saw themselves as defenders of the whole northern frontier.

### The poet-king

Vigraharaja's title was **Kavi-bandhava**, "friend of poets", and he earned it. At Ajmer he built a Sanskrit college and temple of learning. Its walls carried literature engraved on stone slabs, among them his own play, **Harakeli Nataka**, modelled on Bharavi's Kiratarjuniya and dealing with the encounter between Shiva and Arjuna, and **Lalita-Vigraharaja Nataka** by his court poet **Somadeva**, which celebrates the king himself. After the Ghurid conquest, the building was converted into a mosque, now known as the **Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra**; the inscribed slabs were found there in the nineteenth century and are now in the Ajmer museum. They are among the very few medieval Sanskrit plays preserved in stone.

He is also credited with founding the town and reservoir of **Visalpur** (Bisalpur) on the Banas river, today the site of one of Rajasthan's largest dams, and with other public works. The old claim that he built "massive fortifications" is not specifically supported; his building record is mainly of temples, a college and waterworks.

### In bardic memory

Rajasthani literature remembers him in a very different register. The **Bisaldev Raso**, an early Rajasthani poem attributed to **Narpati Nalha**, tells of Bisaldev's marriage to the Paramara princess **Rajmati** and his long absence in Orissa, leaving his queen to pine for him. Its date is disputed and it has little historical content, but it is valued as one of the earliest works of Rajasthani and Hindi literature.

### Death and succession

Vigraharaja died around **1164**, shortly after his Delhi-Topra inscription. He was succeeded by his son **Amaragangeya**, who was soon overthrown by a cousin, **Prithviraja II**. After Prithviraja II, the throne passed to Someshvara, and then, in **1177**, to the young **Prithviraj III**, who inherited a kingdom stretching from Ajmer to Delhi and Hansi — largely Vigraharaja's creation.

### Legacy

Vigraharaja IV combined military success with real cultural achievement. He freed the Chahamanas from Gujarat's shadow, brought Delhi into their orbit, faced the Ghaznavids on the frontier, and wrote poetry good enough to be carved in stone. Prithviraj's struggle with Muhammad of Ghor a generation later was fought on the frontier that Vigraharaja had drawn.

### Key points
- **Reign.** Vigraharaja IV (Visaladeva) ruled Ajmer from about 1150 to 1164 CE, after displacing his parricide brother Jagaddeva.
- **Delhi.** He took Delhi and Hansi; the Tomaras continued as Chahamana feudatories.
- **Pillar inscription.** His 1164 inscription on the Delhi-Topra pillar claims rule from the Vindhyas to the Himalayas.
- **Poet-king.** His play Harakeli Nataka survives on stone slabs from his Ajmer college, later the Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra.
- **Visalpur.** He is credited with founding Visalpur on the Banas.
- **Succession.** His achievements laid the foundation for Prithviraj III's kingdom.

jaichand-gahadavala.name: Jaichand Gahadavala
jaichand-gahadavala.significance: Last great Gahadavala king, fought against Ghurids
jaichand-gahadavala.story:
Kannauj, on the banks of the Ganga… where the water turned golden at sunrise and the bells of the temples rang up to the sky at dusk. That was the 12th century—when the politics of northern India trembled with swords and ambitions—and in that age a ruler was born in the lap of the Gahadavala dynasty whose destiny was bound up with both splendour and ruin. He was Jaichand Gahadavala.

The 12th century. Born in the royal palace, this boy grew up amid prosperity. Kannauj was then the heart of northern India—a centre of trade, culture and power. But storms of power struggle were rising all around it. There was the sound of new invasions from the west, and within, rivalry among the Rajput dynasties.

From childhood Jaichand learned both the scriptures and the weapons. Balance on horseback, a precise grip on the bowstring, unshakeable faith in the sword's edge. But he also understood the complexities of administration. The tax system, the trade routes, the security of the forts—all were within his sight.

As soon as he took the throne he resolved to strengthen Kannauj. The forts were repaired. Sentries were posted on the banks of the Ganga. Temple spires rose. Scholars and poets came to the court. Kannauj was at the height of its prosperity.

But at the same time Chauhan power was rising in Rajputana. His political dispute with Prithviraj Chauhan has echoed through history. Tales of the Rajasuya sacrifice and the swayamvar became the talk of the courts. But this was not only personal; it was a question of the balance of power. Both rulers were standard-bearers of their own glory.

But the storm rising from the west changed every equation. Muhammad Ghori's army was advancing on northern India again. After Tarain his target was the Gangetic plain—and Kannauj was in his sights.

The council was anxious.
"Maharaj, the enemy's army is vast," said a chief.

Jaichand replied—
"Kannauj is not just a city; it is our prestige. Defending it is our dharma."

He organised his army. Lines of elephants, bands of horsemen, the shields of the infantry. Outposts were set up along the Ganga. The place of battle was chosen—Chandawar.

The field of Chandawar… the stream of the Ganga flowing close by. A vast cloud of dust rose. Ghori's army advanced—disciplined, swift and organised.

The kettledrums thundered. Jaichand rode on an elephant. There was resolve in his eyes.
The cry of "Har Har Mahadev!" made the field tremble.

The Gahadavala elephants struck first. They advanced to break the enemy line. For a while Ghori's army wavered. Arrows rained down. Swords met.

But the enemy's strategy was sharp. He ordered his horsemen to encircle from the flanks. The Gahadavala army began to be trapped in the middle. The sky was covered in dust and smoke.

An officer of Ghori's challenged Jaichand—
"Surrender!"

Flames blazed in Jaichand's eyes—
"Kannauj does not bow!"

He came down from his elephant and, sword in hand, entered the front line. Blow after blow. Strikes on the shield. Streams of blood flowed towards the Ganga.

But the scales of battle slowly began to tilt towards Ghori. The Gahadavala army began to tire. Jaichand's elephant was surrounded. An arrow struck and lodged in his body. He staggered, but did not stop.

At last, amid many blows, he fell to the ground. His gaze was turned towards the Ganga—the river that had given Kannauj life.

The battle of Chandawar ended in defeat. Kannauj eventually passed under the enemy. But Jaichand did not leave the battlefield—he fought until the last moment.

His life was not only a story of controversy. It was a meeting of prosperity and valour. He gave Kannauj its splendour, gave culture its patronage, and in the end raised his sword to defend it.

When his final moment came, the sun was setting. The water of the Ganga turned crimson. He looked one last time towards the sky—and grew still.

Jaichand Gahadavala was not just a ruler. He was the warrior who proved that the Gahadavala dynasty was unshaken not only in prosperity but on the battlefield too.

Even today, in the waves of the Ganga, in the memories of Kannauj and in the soil of the field of Chandawar, a voice echoes—
"Kannauj stands unshaken… the Gahadavalas are immortal."

govindachandra-gahadavala.name: Govindachandra Gahadavala
govindachandra-gahadavala.significance: Greatest Gahadavala king, patron of learning
govindachandra-gahadavala.story:
When the stream of the Ganga kissed the shore of Kannauj, the echo of empire could be heard in its waves. That was the 12th century—when the politics of northern India was taking shape amid the flash of swords and the shadow of banners—and in that age an emperor was born into the Gahadavala dynasty who made war and learning the two arms of his kingdom. He was Govindachandra Gahadavala.

The late 11th century. Born in the royal palace of Kannauj, this boy grew up between splendour and responsibility. The prosperity of this city on the banks of the Ganga was famous far and wide. But that very prosperity also drew the eyes of invaders. Detachments coming from the west, dust rising on the borders, and deliberation in the court—this was his early world.

From childhood Govindachandra learned two streams—the sword and the scriptures. With the first light of morning he would reach the stables. His confidence grew to the rhythm of hoofbeats. His grip on the bowstring was firm. His faith in the sword's edge was unshakeable. But as evening fell he would sit among scholars, listen to learned debates and grasp the principles of statecraft.

As soon as he took the throne he proclaimed—
"Kannauj will be not only a centre of prosperity, but a pillar of power."

At that time raiding detachments from the west were advancing on the Gangetic plain. They tested the borders and challenged the outposts. Govindachandra reorganised his army. He strengthened the cavalry bands. He prepared lines of elephants. He raised guard forts on the borders.

The first great clash took place near the Ganga. The enemy attacked at speed. Rather than stopping them on open ground, Govindachandra drew them into a narrow way. Arrows rained from above. A wall of shields stopped the blows. Then he gave the signal—
"Now!"

The Gahadavala horsemen crashed in like lightning. The sky rang with the clang of swords. Streams of blood flowed over the earth. The enemy fell back.

But the second attack was fiercer. This time the enemy was organised and greater in number. The two armies faced each other on the field. The kettledrums thundered. A vast cloud of dust rose.

Govindachandra rode an elephant in the front line.
The cry of "Har Har Mahadev!" lifted the soldiers' spirits.

The elephants tried to break the line. The enemy tried to encircle from the flanks. Govindachandra immediately changed his strategy—hold the centre steady, and spread the cavalry out on both sides.

A crescent was formed. The enemy was trapped in the middle. Swords clashed. Shields cracked. An enemy commander challenged him—
"Surrender!"

Flames blazed in his eyes—
"Kannauj does not bow!"

The two faced each other. Blow after blow. At last Govindachandra's blow landed true. The commander fell. The enemy lines broke.

Kannauj remained safe.

But his greatness lay not only on the battlefield. He made his court a centre of learning. Scholars received patronage. The echo of learned debates could be heard in the palace. Temple spires rose. Centres of learning were established. Kannauj became a meeting place of both knowledge and power.

He secured the trade routes. He founded new towns. He strengthened the tax system. Ghats were built on the banks of the Ganga. Prosperity came to the markets.

One day a scholar in the court asked—
"Maharaj, why do you show equal zeal for both war and learning?"

Govindachandra replied—
"The sword protects the kingdom, and learning keeps its soul alive."

His reign lasted 41 years. In every battle he stayed in the front line. His resolve shone through in every building. The power of the Gahadavala dynasty reached its height.

In his final years, when he stood on the banks of the Ganga, he would see his reflection in the water—that of a warrior and a patron. There was contentment in his eyes that he had not only saved Kannauj, but made it prosperous too.

When his final moment came, the sun was setting. The water of the Ganga turned crimson. He looked one last time towards Kannauj—the capital he had strengthened with both power and knowledge.

His breath stopped, but his saga kept flowing in the waves of the Ganga.

Govindachandra Gahadavala was not just a ruler. He was the balance that proved greatness lies in the harmony of both war and culture.

Even today, in the winds of Kannauj, in the waves of the Ganga and in the bells of the temples, a voice echoes—
"Kannauj stands unshaken… the Gahadavalas are immortal."

chand-bardai.name: Chand Bardai
chand-bardai.significance: Warrior-poet who died with Prithviraj Chauhan
chand-bardai.story:
When the sands of Rajputana turned crimson at sunset, it seemed as if the story of some hero were written in every grain. In that age of the 12th century—when swords were the very ink of history—a man was born whose voice was a weapon and whose weapon was a voice. He was Chand Bardai.

He was not born into an ordinary home, but into a tradition of valour and words. From childhood there was a different light in his eyes. While other boys learned only arms, Chand was mastering the power of words alongside weapons. His teacher would say—
"Words strike farther than the sword."

But he did not want to be only a poet—he wanted to witness the battlefield where valour is born.

As soon as he came of age, his path led him to Ajmer—to the court where the roar of the Chauhan dynasty echoed. There on the throne sat Prithviraj Chauhan—a symbol of prowess while still young.

When Chand first saw Prithviraj, the words came out of him on their own—
"This is not just a king; this is fire."

He became the court poet, but he also took part in the wars. When the kettledrums sounded, Chand did not only compose poetry—he put on armour, raised his sword, and rode onto the battlefield with his lord.

The first great clash took place on the field of Tarain. An army advancing from the west—led by Muhammad Ghori. His army was disciplined, swift and ambitious.

The field of Tarain filled with dust. The boom of kettledrums. The roar of "Har Har Mahadev!" Prithviraj in the front line. Chand behind him—but not merely as a spectator.

When the enemy struck head-on with cavalry, the Chauhan army wavered. Chand drew his sword.
"My king, today it is not words but weapons that will speak!"

Swords clashed. Arrows rained down. A cloud of dust and blood rose. Prithviraj challenged the enemy commander. Chand watched—the two face to face. Blow after blow. At last the Chauhan blow landed true. The first battle of Tarain ended in victory.

Returning to the court, Chand took up his pen. He shaped valour into words. So was born the poem that would echo for ages—the Prithviraj Raso. But it was not just a poem—it was a living picture of the battlefield.

But the current of history does not stand still. Ghori returned—and the second battle of Tarain was fought. This time fortune did not favour them. On the battlefield the Chauhan army broke. Prithviraj was taken prisoner.

Chand's heart burned. He saw his lord being bound in chains. But he did not turn back. He went too—not as a prisoner, but as a friend and poet.

*From here the story follows the legend of the Prithviraj Raso; history records that Prithviraj was put to death after Tarain, and that Ghori was assassinated in 1206.*

The court of Ghazni. Humiliation and challenge. Prithviraj had been blinded. But Chand's voice was still alive.

One day Ghori mocked—
"What can your king do now?"

Chand stepped forward.
"He can strike a target by sound alone."

Silence fell over the court. Slowly Chand recited a verse—
"Chaar baans chaubees gaj, angul asht pramaan…" (four bamboos, twenty-four yards, and eight finger-breadths…)

It was not just a poem—it was a signal. Prithviraj raised his bow. The string was drawn. The arrow flew.

A moment. Then a scream.

The arrow struck its target squarely. Ghori fell to the ground.

Chaos in the court. Soldiers running. Swords flashing.

Chand looked at Prithviraj.
"My king, the final moment has come."

The two looked into each other's eyes—years of friendship, memories of the battlefield, and the flame of honour.

Swords were raised. Enemies fell upon them from every side. Chand struck one last blow. Streams of blood flowed.

At last both fell to the ground—not in slavery, but with vengeance done.

Chand Bardai was not just a poet. He was the flame that proved words and weapons can go together. Through his poetry he made valour immortal, and through his blood he made it true.

Even today, when the wind blows across the sands of Rajputana, a voice echoes in it—
"Words are immortal… the Chauhans are immortal… Chand is immortal."

rawal-ratan-singh.name: Rawal Ratan Singh
rawal-ratan-singh.significance: Defender of Chittor against Alauddin Khilji
rawal-ratan-singh.story:
Chittor, standing firm in the harsh ranges of the Aravallis… the fortress where even stones took oaths, where the blood flowing on the ramparts wrote history. In that turbulent age of the 13th century—when the ambition of the Delhi Sultanate was advancing towards Rajputana—a ruler was born into the Guhila dynasty whose destiny would pass through fire and blood. He was Rawal Ratan Singh.

He was born within the high ramparts of Chittor. From childhood he saw it all—talk of war in the council halls, sentries posted on the bastions, and the echo of pride in the court. His teacher would tell him—
"A king's sword does not only protect the land; it protects honour."

The young Ratan Singh learned balance on horseback, a firm grip on the bowstring, fearlessness with the sword's edge. He was not just a warrior, but the guardian of the fortress. Every gate of Chittor, every secret passage, every bastion was known to him.

1303 CE. A vast cloud of dust rose on the horizon. The army of Alauddin Khilji, Sultan of Delhi, was advancing on Chittor. The roar of kettledrums, lines of countless soldiers, and a storm of ambition.

The council was grave. Some spoke of a treaty. Ratan Singh rose and said—
"Chittor was not made to bow."

The siege began. A vast camp outside the fortress. Catapults began to rain stones on the ramparts. The sky was covered in dust and smoke.

The first assault came at the eastern gate. The enemy advanced behind a line of heavy shields. Ratan Singh posted archers on the heights.
"Patience," he said, "let them come close."

As soon as they neared the gate, arrows rained from above. Boiling oil and stones fell. From below, Rajput warriors threw open the gate and charged out.
The cry of "Victory to Eklingji!" made the earth tremble. Swords met. Streams of blood flowed over the stones. The enemy fell back.

But the siege went on long. Supplies dwindled. Water was limited. Still Ratan Singh went to every bastion. He sat with the wounded soldiers.
"As long as we are here, Chittor lives," he would say.

The second assault came on the western rampart. This time the enemy chose the dark of night. Shadows danced in the torchlight. Ladders struck the wall. The enemy began to climb.

Ratan Singh himself reached the front line, sword in hand.
"Do not let the wall break!"

A fierce struggle broke out on the narrow rampart. Swords clashed so close that sparks flew. An enemy officer challenged him—
"Surrender, and your life will be spared!"

Flames blazed in his eyes—
"Chittor is greater than life!"

The two faced each other. Blow after blow. At last Ratan Singh's blow landed true. The officer fell. But the enemy's numbers were beyond counting.

The third and decisive moment came when a section of the rampart broke. A cloud of dust. The roar of kettledrums. The enemy poured inside.

Battle broke out in the streets within the fort. Ratan Singh organised the remaining army.
"Block the central passage!"

A wall of shields rose in the narrow lanes. There was no room for horsemen—this was a fight on foot. Swords clashed. Spears struck home. Blood flowed over the stones.

A spear drove into Ratan Singh's shoulder. He pulled it out and flung it away. His sword rose again. A second blow landed on his chest. He staggered, but did not fall back.

"Surrender!" the enemy called.

He replied—
"Guhilas do not bow!"

At last, amid many blows, he sank to his knees. His gaze went to the fortress's banner—still flying in the wind.

He fell to the ground—but his sword pointed forward.

That day Chittor was stained with blood, but its self-respect lived on. Ratan Singh's heroic death made the ramparts even more unshakeable.

He was not just a king. He was the flame that proved that even death is acceptable for the sake of honour.

Even today, when the winds of Chittor strike the ramparts, the clang of swords can be heard in them.

And in every echo a voice rings out—
"Chittor stands unshaken… the Guhilas are immortal."

jaitra-singh.name: Jaitra Singh
jaitra-singh.significance: Guhila king who resisted Delhi Sultanate
jaitra-singh.story:
When clouds thundered over the high ranges of the Aravallis, the ramparts of Chittor too seemed to roar in reply. In that age of the 13th century—when the Delhi Sultanate was pushing its power towards Rajputana—a boy was born in the lap of the Guhila dynasty who did not merely save Mewar, but expanded it too. He was Jaitra Singh.

1213 CE. Born in the royal palace of Chittor, this boy grew up not amid peace, but amid the sounds of struggle. Scattered wars on the borders, talk of strategy in the court, and news of the growing ambition coming from Delhi—this was his childhood.

From childhood Jaitra Singh understood the sword not merely as a weapon, but as a responsibility. With the first light of morning he would reach the stables. Balance on horseback, a firm grip on the bowstring, the straight thrust of the spear—his training was rigorous. But more than that, he was learning politics and strategy. He knew—if Mewar was to survive, defence alone was not enough; expansion was necessary too.

As soon as he took the throne he proclaimed in the court—
"Mewar will not remain a kingdom confined within its borders. Whoever comes against us will feel the strength of the Aravallis."

At that time the Delhi Sultanate was extending its influence over Rajputana. Its armies were equipped with heavy cavalry and mounted archers. But Jaitra Singh made the land his ally.

The first great clash came on the northern border. The Sultanate's army tried to fight on open ground. Instead of facing them head-on, Jaitra Singh drew them into the mountain passes. In the narrow way their vast army scattered. Arrows rained from above. Mewari horsemen crashed in from below.
The cry of "Victory to Eklingji!" made the valley tremble. Swords met. A cloud of dust and blood rose. In a short while the enemy fell back.

This victory was one not only of courage, but of strategy.

But Jaitra Singh did not stop there. He turned his gaze westward—to Nadol and Jalore, where the Chauhan dynasty held sway. He knew that if Mewar was to be strengthened, the surrounding powers would have to be balanced.

An army advancing on Nadol. On the open field the two armies faced each other. The kettledrums thundered. A vast cloud of dust rose.

The Chauhan horsemen struck first. They charged like lightning. The Mewari line wavered, but did not break. Jaitra Singh gave the signal—form a wall of shields in the centre, and spread the cavalry out on both sides.

The horsemen formed a crescent. The Chauhan army was trapped in the middle. Swords met. Spears struck home. A Chauhan commander challenged him—
"Turn back!"

Flames blazed in Jaitra Singh's eyes—
"Mewar does not retreat!"

The two faced each other. Blow after blow. At last his blow landed true. The commander fell. The Chauhan army began to fall back. Nadol's power weakened. Mewar's influence grew.

But the hardest struggle came when Delhi attacked again. This time the army was better organised. The roar of cannon and lines of heavy cavalry—the field trembled.

Jaitra Singh divided his army into three. Infantry in the centre, cavalry on both sides. After the first volley of the guns he gave the signal—
"Now!"

The horsemen crashed in like lightning. The sky rang with the clang of swords. The rain of arrows broke the enemy's lines. The battle went on for hours. In the end the Sultanate's army was forced to fall back.

Chittor remained safe. Mewar expanded.

But Jaitra Singh was not only a warrior of the battlefield. He had strategic forts built. Guard forts rose on the borders. Temple spires began to touch the sky. Learning and culture received patronage. Poets and scholars came to his court. The prestige of the Guhila dynasty spread far and wide.

One day someone in the court asked—
"Maharaj, why do you show equal zeal for both war and building?"

Jaitra Singh replied—
"Only when a kingdom's soul is strong do its borders hold."

For years he strengthened Mewar. Rajput lineages kept joining him. His valour and leadership made him not just a ruler, but a standard-bearer.

In his final years, when he stood on the ramparts of Chittor, he would gaze at the land stretching far away—expanded, secure and glorious. Within him was contentment that he had expanded Mewar not only in its borders, but in its influence too.

When his final moment came, the sun was setting. A red glow had spread over the walls of Chittor. He looked one last time at the fortress he had made unshakeable and expansive.

His breath stopped, but his saga came to live in the ramparts.

Jaitra Singh was not just a ruler. He was the resolve that proved the Guhila dynasty was not only a defender, but an expander too. He showed that when courage and strategy go together, no power can confine Mewar.

Even today, when the winds of the Aravallis strike the ramparts of Chittor, a voice echoes in them—
"Mewar stands unshaken… the Guhilas are immortal."

hammir-singh.name: Hammir Singh
hammir-singh.significance: Restored Mewar independence from Delhi Sultanate
hammir-singh.story:
## Hammir Singh — the lion of the hard passes who brought Chittor home

*Hammir's life comes to us through the inscriptions of his descendants, above all those of Rana Kumbha, through Kumbha's commentary Rasikapriya, and through the bardic chronicles of Mewar gathered centuries later. The inscriptions remember him as a victorious king; the bards fill in the story of his youth and his return. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

In the first years of the fourteenth century, the house of Bappa Rawal came close to vanishing from the earth. In **1303 CE** the Delhi Sultan **Alauddin Khalji** laid siege to **Chittor**, the great rock fortress that had been the heart of Mewar for centuries. The siege lasted for months. When it ended, the ruler **Rawal Ratan Singh** was dead or lost, the women of the fort had chosen the fire of *jauhar*, and the fortress belonged to Delhi. Alauddin renamed it **Khizrabad** after his son **Khizr Khan** and left it in his hands.

Among those who fell in those years were the men of a junior branch of the Guhila house, the lords of **Sisoda**, a village in the hills to the north-west of Chittor. Mewar's tradition says that **Lakshman Singh** of Sisoda died defending the fort together with many of his sons. One of those sons was **Ari Singh**. And Ari Singh, the bards say, had left behind a small boy named **Hammir**.

The bards tell a gentle story about the boy's mother. Ari Singh, they say, was out hunting one day near a village in the hills when a wild boar broke through a field of millet. A young woman of the Chandana Rajputs, working on a raised platform in the field, struck the beast down with a single stone from her sling before the prince could reach it. Ari Singh asked her father for her hand, and from that marriage Hammir was born. The tale cannot be checked, but it says something the bards wanted remembered: that the restorer of Mewar grew up not in a palace but among the farming people of the hills.

So the boy grew up in the years when Chittor was a Sultanate garrison. He learned to ride and to use the bow in the rough country of the Aravallis, the region of narrow passes, thorn forest and hidden valleys that would always be Mewar's refuge in bad times. The surviving Sisodia and Guhila retainers gathered around him. Tradition remembers that his uncle **Ajay Singh**, who now led the Sisoda family, recognised the boy's courage and chose him as the heir of the branch over his own sons.

Meanwhile Delhi's grip on Chittor loosened. Holding a distant hill fortress surrounded by hostile country was expensive and dangerous. Within a few years Alauddin gave Chittor to a Rajput ally, **Maldeo**, a **Songara Chauhan** chief related to the house of **Jalore**, who held it as a vassal of the Sultan. Alauddin himself died in **1316**, and Delhi entered a time of murder and confusion until the **Tughluq** dynasty took power in **1320**. In all these years the Sisodias kept up a quiet war from the hills, raiding the lands around the fort and waiting.

The bards tell how Chittor was finally won back, and their story is one of the most famous in Mewar. Maldeo, they say, wished to make peace with the troublesome young chief of the hills, and offered Hammir his daughter in marriage. Hammir's companions warned him that it was a trap, but he went. At the wedding, the bride told her new husband the truth: she had already been married as a child and widowed, and her father had given her away to shame the Sisodia prince. Instead of anger, the story says, the two found trust. She told Hammir she would help him win back the fort of his ancestors. When their son was born, she took the child to Chittor to visit her family, and through her the gates were opened to Hammir's men.

Historians treat the details of this tale with caution. What is certain is that around **1326 CE**, after the death of Maldeo, Hammir took Chittor from his successors and made it the seat of his family once again. More than two decades after the great siege, the fort was back in the hands of Bappa Rawal's descendants.

This return changed the dynasty itself. The old main line of the Guhilas, who had ruled as **Rawals**, had been broken in 1303. Hammir belonged to the Sisoda branch, whose chiefs bore the title **Rana**. From his time onward, the rulers of Mewar were the **Sisodias**, and they kept the title Rana, later Maharana, until the end of princely rule in the twentieth century. Every later Maharana, from Kumbha and Sanga to Pratap, descended from Hammir.

Winning Chittor was one thing; keeping it was another. The new Tughluq Sultan, **Muhammad bin Tughluq**, who came to the throne in **1325**, ruled the largest empire Delhi had ever held, and he could not be expected to accept the loss of the fortress quietly. Mewar's tradition tells of a great battle at **Singoli**, in which Hammir defeated an army sent from Delhi, captured the Sultan himself, and held him prisoner for three months until he paid a heavy ransom, including lands such as **Ajmer**, **Ranthambhor** and **Nagaur**.

This is the most famous claim about Hammir, and the place where history and legend clearly part ways. No Persian chronicle of the Sultanate mentions such a defeat or the capture of a Sultan, and Muhammad bin Tughluq was never anyone's prisoner. Most historians believe the bards have built a great story on a smaller truth. What the inscriptions do show is that Hammir fought hard and successfully against Muslim commanders in the region and kept Chittor against them. The inscriptions of his great-great-grandson Kumbha praise him as having defeated Muslim armies, and give him a proud title: **Vishamaghati Panchanana**, "the lion of the hard passes", a name that remembers exactly the kind of war he fought, in the narrow valleys of the Aravallis where a small army could stop a great one.

The times were in his favour. Muhammad bin Tughluq's reign was full of rebellions, failed projects and costly campaigns, and by the 1330s and 1340s province after province was breaking away from Delhi. A Sultan fighting rebels in the Deccan, Bengal and Gujarat had little strength to spare for a hill kingdom in Rajasthan. Hammir used these years well. He brought back under his rule the chiefs who had scattered after 1303, won the loyalty of the Bhils of the hills as Bappa had done, and steadily widened the territory of Mewar around Chittor.

Mewar's chronicles describe Hammir as a strong and fair ruler who restored order to a land that had suffered years of war. Fields that had been abandoned were farmed again, and travellers and traders returned to the roads below the fort. He rebuilt what he could of the damaged fortress and its shrines.

He was also a devout man. Tradition links him with the goddess, and the temple of **Annapurna** inside Chittor fort is traditionally credited to him; the bards say he honoured a local goddess of the Charans, **Barbadi**, who had blessed his enterprise. Like every ruler of his line, he governed in the name of **Ekalinga**, the lord of Mewar, and counted himself as Shiva's *dewan*, the servant who rules on the god's behalf.

Hammir's reign was long. He ruled for close to four decades, and when he died around **1364 CE** he left behind a kingdom very different from the scattered hill holdings of his youth. Chittor was secure, the Sisodia line was firmly established, and Mewar was once again one of the leading powers of Rajasthan. He was succeeded by his son **Kshetra Singh**, often called **Rana Kheta**, who continued to expand the state, fighting the rulers of Malwa and the neighbouring chiefs.

Later generations never forgot what Hammir had done. When Mewar's greatest builder, Rana Kumbha, recorded the history of his family on the walls of Kumbhalgarh and in the verses of his books, he placed Hammir at the beginning of the line's revival, the man who had taken a fallen house and set it upright again. The story of the boy from the hills who brought Chittor home became one of the foundation stories of Mewar, told and retold for six hundred years.

## Highlights of his life

- **A childhood in the hills.** Born into the Sisoda branch of the Guhilas, he grew up after the fall of Chittor in 1303, when his grandfather Lakshman Singh and father Ari Singh had died in its defence.
- **Recovery of Chittor (c. 1326 CE).** He took the fortress back from the successors of the Songara chief Maldeo, returning it to Bappa Rawal's descendants after more than two decades.
- **Founder of the Sisodia line of rulers.** From his reign the rulers of Mewar were Sisodias who bore the title Rana; every later Maharana descended from him.
- **"Lion of the hard passes."** Kumbha's inscriptions praise him as Vishamaghati Panchanana, a victor over Muslim armies in the passes of the Aravallis.
- **The legend of Singoli.** Mewar's bards say he defeated and captured Muhammad bin Tughluq; no Sultanate source records this, and historians regard the capture as legend.
- **Restorer of the kingdom.** He gathered the scattered chiefs, won over the Bhils, rebuilt the fort's shrines and widened Mewar's lands.
- **A long reign.** He ruled for nearly four decades and died around 1364 CE, succeeded by his son Kshetra Singh.

rana-lakha.name: Rana Lakha
rana-lakha.significance: Mewar king who expanded kingdom and built palaces
rana-lakha.story:
## Rana Lakha — the builder-king of a recovering Mewar

*Rana Lakha's reign is known from later Mewar inscriptions, the Sanskrit and Rajasthani chronicles of the Sisodia house, Muhnot Nainsi's seventeenth-century khyat and James Tod's Annals; the famous story of the coconut and Prince Chunda's renunciation comes from bardic tradition and should be read as such.*

**Rana Lakha** (Lakshasimha), who ruled Mewar from about **1382** to about **1421**, belongs to the generation that turned a recovered kingdom into a prosperous one. His grandfather **Rana Hammir** had won back **Chittor** in the decades after **Alauddin Khilji's** conquest of 1303 and founded the rule of the **Sisodia** branch of the Guhila house. His father, **Rana Kshetra Singh** (Khet Singh), had pushed Mewar's frontiers outwards and fought the neighbouring powers of Malwa and the hill chiefs. Lakha inherited a fortress that was again a capital, but also a land still scarred by war: temples ruined, towns thinned out, revenue uncertain.

### Origins and accession

Lakha came to the throne on his father's death, as an adult and an experienced prince. The chronicles say little about his youth, and the colourful accounts of boyhood training found in popular retellings are not drawn from any source. What the record shows is a ruler whose priorities were consolidation and rebuilding rather than adventure. Mewar under Lakha was not yet the great power it would become under his grandson **Rana Kumbha**, but the foundations Kumbha built on were largely laid in these four decades.

### Wars and frontiers

Lakha's best-attested campaigns were against the **Mer** and Bhil communities of the hill tracts around **Badnor** and the Merwara country, who had remained outside the control of Chittor. Mewar's chronicles credit him with bringing this region under the crown and with taking the stronghold of **Badnor**. Tod also writes of a victory over a Delhi army in the same area; the Delhi Sultanate was weak and divided after the invasion of **Timur** in 1398, and historians treat the details of Tod's account with caution. Lakha also fought the neighbouring Sankhla and other Rajput chiefs on his borders. None of these wars was on the scale of the great sieges of the previous century, and later dramatised accounts of pitched battles with mangonels and named commanders have no basis in the sources.

### Silver, water and stone

The most lasting achievements of the reign were economic and architectural. During Lakha's time the silver and lead (and zinc) workings at **Jawar**, south of the later city of Udaipur, were opened or greatly expanded, and their output gave the Mewar treasury a reliable income. Tradition also places in his reign the building of **Lake Pichola**, said to have been dug by a Banjara grain-carrier, from whom the lake takes its name; the lake later became the heart of Udaipur, founded more than a century and a half afterwards.

Lakha used his revenues to repair Chittor. Temples and palaces damaged in 1303 were restored, and several shrines on the fort are attributed to his patronage. Inscriptions and chronicles also remember him as a generous patron of Brahmins and poets, and as a king who made grants of villages to temples. Tod records a tradition that he spent large sums to free the pilgrimage centre of **Gaya** from a tax levied on Hindu pilgrims; this cannot be confirmed from contemporary evidence.

### The coconut and Chunda's vow

Lakha is remembered above all through a story about his family. His eldest son, **Chunda**, was the heir. The bards tell that an envoy came from **Rao Chunda Rathore** of **Mandore** bearing a coconut, the customary token of a marriage proposal, for the crown prince. Lakha, who was then old, joked that such tokens were surely not meant for a grey-beard like himself. The jest, once spoken in open court, could not be taken back: Chunda refused to accept a bride his father had even playfully claimed, and Lakha himself married the Rathore princess, **Hansa Bai**. Her family was anxious about the status of any son she might bear, and Chunda swore that he would give up his right to the throne in favour of that child.

Whether the coconut exchange happened exactly so cannot be known, but the outcome is historical. Hansa Bai bore a son, **Mokal**, and when Lakha died around 1421 the child succeeded him, with Chunda acting as guardian of the kingdom. Chunda's descendants, the **Chundawats**, received in return the first place among the nobles of Mewar and the right to countersign royal grants, privileges they kept for centuries.

### Death and what followed

Lakha died around 1421. His marriage alliance had brought the Rathores of Marwar into the heart of Mewar's politics, with consequences that unfolded quickly. Hansa Bai grew suspicious of Chunda's power as regent, and he withdrew to the court of Malwa. Her brother **Ranmal Rathore** came to Chittor and gained great influence. After Mokal's murder in 1433 and the rise of the young Kumbha, rivalry between the Sisodia and Rathore nobles ended violently in 1438. These events belong to the next reigns, but they flowed directly from Lakha's last marriage.

### Legacy

In history Lakha stands as a consolidator: a ruler who restored Chittor's buildings, secured its hill frontiers, and found the silver that financed the golden age of Kumbha and his successors. In bardic memory he is the king of the coconut, a man whose careless word cost his eldest son a throne, and whose son's sacrifice became a model of Rajput fidelity to a spoken vow. Both images are part of how Mewar remembers him. The first is supported by inscriptions and later chronicles; the second is a tale shaped by the bards to explain the special standing of the Chundawat clan.

### Key points
- **Reign.** Ruled Mewar from about 1382 to about 1421, son of Kshetra Singh and grandson of Rana Hammir.
- **Frontiers.** Brought the Mer and hill country around Badnor under Mewar's control.
- **Economy.** The silver and lead mines of Jawar were developed in his reign, enriching the treasury.
- **Building.** Repaired temples and palaces at Chittor; tradition links Lake Pichola to his time.
- **Succession.** His marriage to Hansa Bai and Chunda's renunciation made the child Mokal his heir.

kanhad-dev-songara.name: Kanhad Dev Songara
kanhad-dev-songara.significance: Jalore ruler who resisted Alauddin Khilji
kanhad-dev-songara.story:
## Kanhad Dev Songara — the last Chauhan lord of Jalore

*The fall of Jalore is noted in Persian histories (Isami, Firishta and others), while the fullest narrative is the Old Gujarati-Rajasthani poem Kanhadade Prabandh, written by the poet Padmanabha in 1455, nearly a century and a half later; its speeches, numbers and romantic episodes belong to bardic tradition rather than to verified history.*

**Kanhad Dev** (Kanhadadeva) was the ruler of **Jalore** in western Rajasthan at the turn of the fourteenth century and the last independent king of its **Songara Chauhan** line. He is remembered as one of the Rajput rulers who resisted **Alauddin Khilji**, Sultan of Delhi, and as the defender who died when Jalore fell in **1311**.

### The Songaras of Jalore

The Songaras were a branch of the Chahamanas, or **Chauhans**, of **Nadol**. In the later twelfth century **Kirtipala**, a younger son of the Nadol house, established himself at Jalore, whose granite hill was known as **Suvarnagiri**, the "golden mountain"; from Sonagiri came the clan name Songara. Under Kirtipala's successors Jalore became a strong regional kingdom, surviving the Ghurid conquests and the early Delhi Sultans. Kanhad Dev, son of **Samantasimha**, appears in inscriptions as ruling in the closing years of the thirteenth century, sometimes jointly with his father.

The fort he held was among the most formidable in Marwar: walls running along a steep, rocky ridge above the town, with tanks, temples and palaces inside. It commanded the routes between Gujarat and the north, which made it both valuable and exposed.

### First encounters with Delhi

In **1299** Alauddin sent a great army under **Ulugh Khan** and **Nusrat Khan** to invade **Gujarat**; it sacked the temple of **Somnath**. The *Kanhadade Prabandh* says that Kanhad Dev refused the army passage through his lands, and that as the invaders returned laden with plunder, Jalore's forces attacked them and recovered fragments of the Somnath idol, which were installed in temples of the kingdom. This is the poem's central claim for its hero. Persian sources record a mutiny in the returning army near Jalore over the division of spoils, which may lie behind the tradition, but they do not confirm a Rajput victory.

Over the next years Alauddin took the great forts of Rajputana one after another: **Ranthambore** in 1301, **Chittor** in 1303, then Malwa. Persian accounts suggest that Kanhad Dev, seeing this, at one point acknowledged the Sultan's authority and visited his court, and that relations broke down again afterwards. Firishta's version has Kanhad Dev provoked by a boast made at court that no Hindu ruler could stand against the Sultan. Such details are hard to verify, but it is clear that by the end of the decade Jalore was again defiant.

### Siwana and the siege of Jalore

In **1308** the Sultan's army besieged **Siwana**, a nearby fort held by **Sitaladeva** (Satal Dev), who was killed when it fell. Jalore was now isolated. The final campaign, around **1310–1311**, was led by **Kamaluddin Gurg**. The poem describes a long siege, with repeated sallies, the burning of the Sultan's camps and great slaughter on both sides; the scale it gives is clearly exaggerated, but the siege seems to have lasted for some time.

Jalore was finally taken, according to tradition, through betrayal. The *Kanhadade Prabandh* tells of a Dahiya Rajput named **Vika** who showed the besiegers a hidden path into the fort; his own wife, the poem says, was so ashamed that she killed him. Whether or not that episode is literal, treachery opening the gates is a recurring theme in accounts of Jalore's fall.

### Death and the end of the kingdom

When the walls were breached, Kanhad Dev fought among his last followers and was killed. The poem says the women of the fort performed **jauhar**, entering the fire rather than face capture, and that his son **Viramadeva** briefly took the throne before dying in the final fighting. Jalore was annexed to the Delhi Sultanate and placed under Muslim governors; later it passed to other rulers, including the Bihari Pathans and eventually the Rathores of Marwar.

### Memory and legacy

Historically, Kanhad Dev was one of several regional Rajput kings who were destroyed in Alauddin's systematic campaign to reduce the forts of Rajasthan. His kingdom was smaller than Ranthambore or Chittor, and its fall is only briefly noted by Persian chroniclers.

In regional memory, however, he occupies a large place, almost entirely because of Padmanabha's poem. Composed for a fifteenth-century Chauhan patron, **Akhairaj**, who traced his descent from the Jalore house, the *Kanhadade Prabandh* presents Kanhad Dev as a defender of faith and honour who recovered the image of Somnath and refused to bow. It is one of the most important early works of Rajasthani and Gujarati literature, and historians value it for its picture of fifteenth-century attitudes as much as for any facts about 1311.

Today the ruined fort of Jalore, with its later additions, still stands above the town, and Kanhad Dev and Viramadeva are honoured in local songs and commemorations as the last Chauhan defenders of the "golden hill".

### Key points
- **Dynasty.** Ruler of Jalore from the Songara branch of the Chauhans, founded by Kirtipala in the twelfth century.
- **Somnath tradition.** The *Kanhadade Prabandh* credits him with attacking Alauddin's army returning from Gujarat in 1299.
- **Isolation.** Ranthambore, Chittor and neighbouring Siwana fell to Alauddin before Jalore.
- **Fall of Jalore.** The fort fell in about 1311 to Kamaluddin Gurg, by tradition through betrayal; Kanhad Dev died fighting.
- **Memory.** He is remembered mainly through Padmanabha's poem of 1455, a classic of early Rajasthani literature.

viramadeva.name: Viramadeva
viramadeva.significance: Jalore prince who refused Alauddin Khilji's terms and died in the siege of 1311
viramadeva.story:
## Viramadeva — the prince of Jalore who would not bend

*Almost everything told of Viramadeva comes from Padmanabha's poem Kanhadade Prabandh (1455) and later Rajasthani prose tales such as the Viramde Sonigara ri Vat; the Persian chronicles of Alauddin Khilji's reign record the fall of Jalore but do not name him, so his story is best read as cherished regional tradition built around a real siege.*

**Viramadeva**, often called **Viramde** in Rajasthani, was the son of **Kanhad Dev Songara**, the **Chauhan** ruler of **Jalore**. He grew up in the years when **Alauddin Khilji**, Sultan of Delhi, was bringing down the great Rajput fortresses one after another: **Ranthambore** in 1301, **Chittor** in 1303, **Siwana** in 1308. He died in the final siege of Jalore around **1311**, and in the memory of western Rajasthan he became the model of a young prince who chose death beside his father over submission and a royal marriage.

### A prince of the golden hill

Jalore's fort stood on a granite ridge once called **Suvarnagiri**, the golden hill, which gave the **Songara** clan its name. The Songaras had ruled there since the twelfth century, and by Viramadeva's youth they were one of the last independent Rajput houses of Marwar. Nothing is recorded of his birth date, his mother, or his upbringing. The poem presents him as tall, skilled in arms and generous, the conventional portrait of a hero; it is the actions attributed to him that give his story its shape.

### In Delhi: the wrestler and the princess

According to the *Kanhadade Prabandh*, there was a period of uneasy peace between Jalore and Delhi, and Viramadeva was sent to the Sultan's court, as an envoy or as a hostage for his father's good conduct. Such arrangements were common: sons of submitting rulers often spent time at the imperial court. Later prose tales add that he defeated a famous court wrestler, called **Panju** in some versions, winning admiration in Delhi.

The poem's most famous episode follows. The Sultan's daughter, named **Firoza** (Piroja) in the tradition, saw the prince and fell in love with him, declaring that she had been his companion in earlier lives. The Sultan, the poem says, was willing to give her to him in marriage. Viramadeva refused, because accepting would have meant abandoning his faith and his people, and he slipped away back to Jalore. The poem treats this refusal, and the insult the Sultan felt, as one of the causes of the final war.

Historians regard the Firoza story as legend. No Persian source mentions such a daughter or such an offer, and the motif of a Sultan's daughter in love with a Rajput prince appears in several other bardic works. Its value lies in what it says about how fifteenth-century Jalore remembered its prince: as a man who could not be bought, even with love and a throne-side alliance.

### The siege of 1311

The war that ended Jalore's independence was real. After Siwana fell in 1308, its defender **Sitaladeva** killed, Jalore stood alone. Alauddin's army, commanded by **Kamaluddin Gurg**, besieged the fort, and the poem describes many months of fighting, sorties and hardships. In the end, tradition says, a Rajput named **Vika** showed the attackers a secret way in. Kanhad Dev fell fighting.

Here the poem gives Viramadeva his own brief reign. As the fort burned, the surviving nobles crowned him, and he ruled for only **three and a half days**. The women of the fort performed **jauhar**, choosing the fire over capture, an act the sources describe as a terrible necessity of the time rather than something to admire. Viramadeva then led the last defenders out and was killed; some versions say that, gravely wounded and about to be taken, he ended his own life so as not to fall into the Sultan's hands.

### The head and the princess

The poem closes with a scene that has made the story famous. Viramadeva's head was carried to Delhi. Firoza, grieving, asked for it, and when she brought it before her, the head turned its face away, refusing her even in death. She performed the last rites for him and then gave up her own life, in some tellings by entering the **Yamuna**. This ending is pure romance, a bardic resolution in which the lovers are united only by sacrifice. It should not be read as an account of real events.

### Legacy in history and song

In the narrow historical record Viramadeva is barely visible: a son of Kanhad Dev who probably died when Jalore fell. In the literary tradition he is a major figure. The *Kanhadade Prabandh* is one of the founding works of Rajasthani and Gujarati literature, and its portrait of father and son dying together became part of the shared Rajput ideal of honour. Later ballads and prose tales kept his memory alive in Marwar, and in Jalore today he is commemorated together with his father as one of the last Chauhan defenders of the golden hill.

His story also shows how bardic literature worked. It took a real siege and a little-known prince and built around them a drama of love, loyalty and refusal, so that the meaning of the event, rather than its precise facts, would survive.

### Key points
- **Parentage.** Son of Kanhad Dev Songara, the Chauhan ruler of Jalore.
- **Sources.** Known mainly from the *Kanhadade Prabandh* (1455) and later Rajasthani tales, not from contemporary records.
- **Firoza legend.** Tradition says he refused marriage with the Sultan's daughter; historians regard this as legend.
- **Last stand.** By tradition he ruled for three and a half days after his father's death and died in the fall of Jalore around 1311.
- **Memory.** Remembered in Jalore and in Rajasthani literature as the prince who chose death over submission.

kunwar-kanh-singh.name: Kunwar Kanh Singh
kunwar-kanh-singh.significance: Mewar prince who died defending Chittor
kunwar-kanh-singh.story:
## Kunwar Kanh Singh — a prince remembered from the first fall of Chittor

*A Mewar prince named Kanh Singh cannot be securely identified in inscriptions or the major chronicles; the siege of Chittor in 1303 is documented by Amir Khusrau, who accompanied Alauddin Khilji, and by later Persian historians, while the story of the Sisoda princes who died one after another comes from bardic tradition as retold by James Tod. This profile therefore places a traditional figure within the real events of 1303.*

**Kunwar Kanh Singh** is remembered in popular tradition as a young prince of the house of Mewar who died defending **Chittor** when **Alauddin Khilji**, Sultan of Delhi, besieged and took the fortress in **1303**. Unlike Rana Hammir, Rana Ratnasimha or Gora and Badal, he does not appear by this name in the inscriptions of the period or in the main dynastic histories. His story is best understood as one of many memories of the princes and warriors who died in that siege, a memory whose general outline is historical even if the individual is hard to pin down.

### Mewar before the siege

At the beginning of the fourteenth century Mewar was ruled by the **Guhila** dynasty from Chittor, a fortress on a long, high plateau rising above the plains of southern Rajasthan. The senior line, whose rulers bore the title **Rawal**, was then headed by **Ratnasimha** (Ratan Singh), who had come to the throne only around 1302. A junior branch of the same family held the estate of **Sisoda**, and its chief, **Lakshmasimha** (Lakhamsi), was one of the most important nobles of the kingdom. From this Sisoda branch would later come the **Sisodia** Ranas who ruled Mewar for six centuries.

A prince called "Kunwar" in tradition would have belonged to one of these two families. If Kanh Singh was a real person, he was most probably one of the sons of the Sisoda chief, since bardic accounts focus on their deaths.

### The siege of 1303

Alauddin Khilji, who had already taken **Ranthambore** in 1301, marched against Chittor at the end of January 1303. His court poet **Amir Khusrau**, who was present, describes in the *Khaza'in al-Futuh* the camp set up between two rivers below the fort, the siege engines, and the long months of attack. The defenders held out for about eight months. Khusrau writes that the fort fell on **26 August 1303**, that the Rawal came out and submitted, and that the Sultan ordered a great massacre of the population; he gives a figure of thirty thousand, which may be exaggerated but shows the scale of the violence. Alauddin handed the fort to his son **Khizr Khan** and renamed it **Khizrabad**.

The fate of Ratnasimha himself is uncertain. Khusrau implies that he surrendered; later Rajput tradition says he died fighting. The famous story of **Rani Padmini**, which became attached to this siege through **Malik Muhammad Jayasi's** *Padmavat* of 1540, is considered by most historians to be literature rather than history.

### The tradition of the Sisoda princes

The tradition into which a figure like Kanh Singh fits is the one recorded by **James Tod** from Mewar's bards.
