It tells that during the siege Lakshmasimha of Sisoda saw in a vision the goddess of Chittor, who declared that the fort could be held only if twelve princes of royal blood gave their lives for it. One by one his sons were crowned, ruled for a few days, and went out to die. The eldest, **Arisimha** (Ari Singh), was among those killed. The youngest, **Ajayasimha** (Ajay Singh), was sent away so that the line would survive, and the chief himself then fell. Arisimha's son **Hammir**, raised in the hills, would later win back Chittor and found the Sisodia dynasty of Ranas.

The vision and the precise number of sons belong to legend, but the core is credible: the Sisoda chief and several of his sons do seem to have died in 1303, and only a younger branch survived. A prince remembered under the name Kanh Singh may preserve one of these lost sons in local memory, or he may be a later, composite hero standing for all of them. Historians cannot say which.

### What his story means

Popular retellings of Kanh Singh's life describe his training, his speeches in council and his single combats on the walls. None of these details comes from a source, and they should be read as imaginative reconstruction. What can be said honestly is what such a prince would have faced: months of blockade, shortages of water and food, bombardment by stone-throwing engines, and, at the end, a choice between surrender and death in a final sortie. The women of the fort, according to tradition, performed **jauhar** before the last fighting, an act that later generations remembered as tragic resistance; the sources do not allow us to know its scale.

### Legacy

The fall of Chittor in 1303 became one of the defining memories of Mewar, alongside the later sieges of 1535 and 1568. In bardic culture the princes who died in it were remembered collectively as the price of the dynasty's honour, and their sacrifice was used to explain why the surviving Sisodia branch was entitled to rule. Kunwar Kanh Singh, whatever his exact identity, belongs to that collective memory. His story keeps alive the young men of the fortress whose names are mostly lost, and reminds readers that behind the famous names of Hammir and Padmini stood many others who did not survive to be recorded.

### Key points
- **Identity.** A Mewar prince known from tradition; he cannot be securely identified in inscriptions or major chronicles.
- **Context.** Chittor was besieged by Alauddin Khilji from January to 26 August 1303, as recorded by Amir Khusrau.
- **Family.** If historical, he most likely belonged to the Sisoda branch of the Guhilas, whose chief Lakshmasimha died with several sons.
- **Bardic tradition.** Tod records the legend of the princes crowned one after another and sent out to die.
- **Legacy.** He stands for the many unnamed defenders of 1303 whose deaths shaped Mewar's memory.

rao-jodha.name: Rao Jodha
rao-jodha.significance: Founder of Jodhpur city and Mehrangarh Fort
rao-jodha.story:
## Rao Jodha — the exile who built a fort on the Bird Hill

*Rao Jodha's life comes to us through the Marwar khyats, above all the chronicle of Muhnot Nainsi, through the court histories of Jodhpur, and through a few inscriptions such as the one his daughter left at Ghosundi. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

In the early fifteenth century the Rathores were still newcomers to power in the desert country of Marwar. For nearly two hundred years their clan had lived as chiefs of small holdings in the west, around Kher and the Luni valley, descendants of **Rao Siha**, who had come into the region in the thirteenth century. Only in the generation of **Rao Chunda** did they win a real capital. Around the end of the fourteenth century Chunda took **Mandore**, the ancient seat of the Pratiharas, and with it the beginnings of a kingdom.

Jodha was born in **1416**, the son of Chunda's son **Rao Ranmal**. He came into a family that was already restless and divided. Ranmal had been passed over for the throne of Mandore in favour of a younger brother, and like many Rajput princes without a seat of his own, he went to seek his fortune at a greater court. That court was **Chittor**. Ranmal's sister **Hansa Bai** had married **Rana Lakha** of Mewar, and her son **Mokal** became Rana. Through her, Ranmal rose to great power in Mewar, and after Mokal was murdered in 1433, he became the strongest man at the court of the young **Rana Kumbha**.

So Jodha grew up between two worlds: the sand and thorn of Marwar, and the great rock fortress of Chittor with its temples, its intrigues and its proud Sisodia nobility. He learned to ride and fight among his father's Rathore followers, and he learned, too, how quickly favour at a foreign court could turn to suspicion.

Ranmal's power in Mewar made enemies. The Sisodia nobles, and especially the followers of **Chunda Sisodia**, the elder half-brother of Mokal who had given up his own claim to the throne, believed that the Rathore was making Mewar into a Rathore possession. In **1438** the blow fell. Ranmal was killed inside Chittor. The bards tell that he was taken while he slept, that a maidservant had tied him to his cot, and that the old warrior rose with the bed still bound to his back and fought until he fell. Whether every detail is true or not, the murder itself is well remembered in both Mewar and Marwar.

Jodha was in Chittor or close by when his father died. He fled at once with a small band of Rathore horsemen. The Mewar forces pursued them, and many of Jodha's companions were cut down on the long ride west. The Sisodias followed through to **Mandore** itself and occupied it. At about twenty-two years old, the heir of the Rathores had lost his father, his followers and his capital in a single season.

For roughly fifteen years Jodha lived as an exile. He took shelter in the dry country to the north and west, around **Kahuni** and the edges of the Thar, gathering what men he could and raiding when he was strong enough. These were hard years. He had little money, few horses and many enemies, and his kinsmen were scattered.

A famous story belongs to this time, told across Rajasthan as a legend rather than as history. Tired and hungry, Jodha stopped one day at a peasant's hut. The woman of the house set before him a plate of hot *khichri*. Starving, he plunged his hand into the middle of it and burned his fingers. The woman laughed and said: "You are as foolish as Jodha. He attacks the centre of the enemy's land and gets burned, instead of eating from the edges where the food is cool." The prince, the story goes, took the lesson to heart. From then on he began to win back his country piece by piece, from the outside in.

Whether a peasant woman taught him or not, that is how the struggle went. Jodha built up support among the Rathore kinsmen and among neighbouring clans. Tradition remembers the help of **Harbu Sankhla**, a holy man and warrior of the Sankhla Parmar clan, who is still honoured in Marwar as a folk hero. Mewar, meanwhile, had many other concerns. Rana Kumbha was fighting the sultans of **Malwa** and **Gujarat**, and the garrison at Mandore was a distant burden.

Around **1453** Jodha struck. He retook Mandore and drove out the Mewar garrison. Over the next years he recovered the surrounding districts and pressed his raids towards Mewar's own borders. Tradition says it was Hansa Bai, the Rajmata of Mewar and Jodha's own aunt, who pressed for an end to the bloodshed between her two families. A settlement followed. The bards remember a boundary drawn through the countryside, and a saying about which trees grew on which side of it. What matters historically is that Mewar accepted the return of the Rathores to Mandore, and that Marwar and Mewar, for a time, made peace.

Jodha was now master of his inheritance, but he wanted more than to sit again in his grandfather's city. Mandore lay in a low valley, open and hard to defend. A few miles to the south rose a great ridge of rock, steep on every side, called **Bhakurcheeria**, the "hill of birds". On **12 May 1459**, according to the Jodhpur tradition, Jodha laid the foundation of a new fort on its summit. Around its foot he founded a new city and gave it his own name: **Jodhpur**.

Many legends cluster around that foundation. The hill, it is said, was the home of a hermit called **Cheeria Nathji**, the lord of the birds. When Jodha's men moved him from his cave to make way for the fort, the hermit cursed the place with drought. Local people say that Jodhpur's long struggle with water began that day, and that Jodha built a small shrine and a house near the cave to soften the curse. Tradition also says that **Karni Mata**, the warrior-saint of Deshnok who was revered by the Rathores, came to bless the foundation. And there is a darker story, still told with honour in Jodhpur: that a man named **Rajiya Bambhi**, of the Meghwal community, was buried alive in the foundations as an offering, so that the fort would never fall, and that Jodha granted land to his family in return. These are traditions, kept by the people of the city, not facts confirmed by any record of the time.

The fort that rose on the hill became **Mehrangarh**, the "fort of the sun". What Jodha built was smaller and plainer than the vast palace-fortress visitors see today. His successors added to it for four centuries. But the site was his choice, and it was a brilliant one. From the top of its walls a sentry could see far across the plain, and the rock itself was a barrier no army ever easily broke. Jodha brought the image of the goddess **Chamunda**, the patron of his family, from Mandore and installed her in the new fort. His queen **Jasmade**, a Hadi princess, built the tank called **Ranisar** within the walls to store precious rainwater.

From his new capital Jodha set about turning a clan holding into a state. He was a practical ruler. Rather than keep every conquest under his own hand, he sent his sons and brothers out to win and hold lands of their own, bound to Jodhpur by blood. His sons **Duda** and **Varsingh** took **Merta**, which became the seat of the Mertia Rathores. His brother **Kandhal** and his son **Bika** rode north into the dry lands of Jangladesh. Bika's mother was the Sankhla queen **Naurangde**, and the story goes that a jest at court about whether Bika meant to win a kingdom of his own sent him off to do exactly that. Over the following decades he founded the state and city of **Bikaner**, completed in **1488**. Other sons and kinsmen settled at Sojat, Phalodi and elsewhere. The Rathore lands spread across much of western Rajasthan.

This system had its strengths and its dangers. It made the Rathores the masters of a huge region within a single lifetime. It also created powerful branches that would later act as independent states. But in Jodha's own day, it gave the clan room to grow, and it gave his sons something better to do than fight one another for a single throne.

The old enmity with Mewar faded too. Jodha's daughter **Shringar Devi** was married to **Rana Raimal**, Kumbha's son, who ruled Mewar from 1473. Long after her father's death she built a stepwell at **Ghosundi**, near Chittor, and its inscription of **1504** proudly names her as Jodha's daughter. The houses whose quarrel had killed Ranmal were now joined by marriage.

Jodha's character, as the chronicles paint him, was that of a hard, patient and practical man. He had seen what pride and intrigue did at a great court, and he trusted his own kin and his own hills more than any alliance. He was a devotee of the goddess and a patron of the holy men of Marwar. He spent the first half of his adult life losing almost everything and the second half building something that would last for five hundred years.

Rao Jodha died in **1489**, at about seventy-three. He was succeeded by his son **Rao Satal**, who ruled only a few years, and then by another son, **Rao Suja**. The line that later produced **Rao Maldeo**, the great Rathore ruler of the sixteenth century, descended from Suja. The fort Jodha founded on the hill of birds was never taken by storm in all the centuries that followed, and the city at its foot, the blue city of Jodhpur, still carries his name.

## Highlights of his life

- **Survivor of his father's murder (1438).** After Rao Ranmal was killed at Chittor, he escaped with a handful of horsemen and lived for years as an exile.
- **Recovery of Mandore (c. 1453).** He rebuilt Rathore strength in the desert and took back the family capital from the Mewar garrison.
- **Peace with Mewar.** He ended the feud with the Sisodias, and his daughter Shringar Devi later married Rana Raimal.
- **Founder of Jodhpur and Mehrangarh (1459).** He chose the rocky Bhakurcheeria hill for a new fort and founded the city that bears his name.
- **Builder of a wider Rathore realm.** His sons and kinsmen founded or held Merta, Bikaner and other centres across western Rajasthan.
- **Patron of the goddess.** He installed Chamunda in Mehrangarh, and his queen Jasmade built the Ranisar tank within the fort.
- **Death and succession (1489).** He died at about seventy-three and was succeeded by his son Rao Satal.

ranmal-rathore.name: Ranmal Rathore
ranmal-rathore.significance: Rathore king who expanded Marwar territories
ranmal-rathore.story:
When hooves struck the sands of the Thar, they did not merely raise dust—they announced that the desert had awakened. In the late 14th century, in the lap of that same desert, in the courtyard of the Rathore dynasty, a boy was born whose very destiny was expansion—he was Ranmal Rathore.

He was born amid splendour, but the atmosphere was one of struggle. Marwar was strengthening its borders. Small strongholds, scattered power, and the ambitions of neighbouring states—there was challenge in every direction. From childhood Ranmal saw that the throne was not just a right, but a call to war.

With the first light of morning he would reach the stables. Gripping the horse's mane he mastered balance, and practised with the spear on the open plain. The bowstring did not tremble in his fingers. To him the sword's edge was not a weapon, but a resolve. But sharper still was his vision—he read the land, understood the routes, and saw the lines of the future.

By the time he came of age he had decided—Marwar would not remain only on the defensive; it would expand.

The first great clash came near the border. A neighbouring chief challenged the power of Marwar. The ground was flat, but dunes spread far and wide. Ranmal hid his army behind the dunes. The front line offered light resistance and began to fall back.

The enemy advanced—believing victory was easy. Just then horsemen burst out from behind the dunes. The cry of "Rathore!" made the air tremble. Swords met. A cloud of dust spread everywhere. Ranmal himself was in the front line. He parried a chief's blow with his shield and with his counter-stroke pierced his chest. In a short while the enemy fell back.

This was not just a victory—it was a declaration that Marwar's borders would no longer stand still.

The second clash was more complicated. This time the confrontation was with the power of Mewar. Narrow passes among the Aravalli hills, high ramparts and a seasoned army. Ranmal understood that a direct attack could prove costly.

He divided his army into three. The infantry stood in the centre forming a wall of shields, cavalry on both sides. He ordered—"Take control of the mountain roads. Cut the supplies."

The battle began. Arrows rained from the hills. Ranmal signalled his horsemen to spread out. As soon as the enemy tired, he raised his sword—"Marwar!"

The horsemen burst forward like lightning. The Aravallis trembled with the clang of swords. The struggle was fierce. In the end both sides fell back, but Ranmal had proved that Marwar was no longer only a desert power, but a centre of the politics of Rajputana.

The third and decisive battle was fought on the open plain. The sun was overhead. The kettledrums sounded. A cloud of dust was rising. The enemy was greater in number.

Ranmal arranged his army in dense lines. The roar of the guns shook the earth. Many soldiers fell. But he ordered—"Do not break ranks!"

After the next volley of the guns he gave the signal—"Now!"

Horsemen crashed in from both sides. Swords met. An enemy commander challenged him—"Surrender!"

Flames blazed in Ranmal's eyes—"Rathores do not bow!"

The two faced each other. Swords clashed, sparks flew. At last Ranmal's blow prevailed. The commander fell. The enemy lines wavered.

With victory he had forts built. Strong forts rose on the borders. Outposts were built to protect the water sources. Trade routes were secured. Temples were built, where the sound of bells became a symbol of peace. Scholars, poets and learned men began to come to his court. Marwar became not only a battlefield, but a land of culture too.

Once someone in the court asked, "Maharaj, where does expansion end?"

Ranmal replied, "Wherever honour is safe, there lies the border."

With time Marwar's power grew. The influence of the Rathore dynasty spread far and wide. Neighbouring states now regarded him not just as a ruler of the desert, but as an influential leader of Rajputana.

In his final years, when he stood on the ramparts of his fort, he would gaze at the land stretching far away—forts, settlements, temples and safe roads. All of it was the fruit of his resolve.

When his final moment came, the sun was setting. A red glow had spread over the sand. He looked one last time in the direction of Marwar—the land he had expanded and strengthened.

His breath stopped, but Marwar's power lived on.

Ranmal Rathore was not just a ruler. He was the flame of expansion that lifted the Rathore dynasty out of the desert and made it a leader in the politics of Rajputana. He proved that power lies not only in defence, but in expansion and organisation too.

Even today, when the winds of the Thar strike the walls of the forts, a voice echoes in them—
"Marwar is immortal… the Rathores are immortal."

rao-bika.name: Rao Bika
rao-bika.significance: Founder of Bikaner city and kingdom
rao-bika.story:
## Rao Bika — the prince who answered a taunt with a kingdom

*Rao Bika's life comes to us through the Rathore chronicles of Bikaner and Marwar, the khyats of the bards and the traditions kept at the shrine of Karni Mata in Deshnoke. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

In the middle of the fifteenth century the Rathores of Marwar were a rising house. **Rao Jodha**, after years of exile and war, had won back his father's lands, and in **1459** he founded a new capital on a rocky ridge, the city that still bears his name, **Jodhpur**. Around his court gathered a crowd of sons, brothers and kinsmen, each of them a Rajput with a sword, a horse and an ambition. A kingdom can only be divided so many times, and every son of Jodha knew that only one of them would sit on his father's throne.

Bika was one of these sons. The Bikaner chronicles place his birth in **1438**, and name his mother as Rani **Naurangde** of the Sankhla Parmars. He grew up in the hard school of his father's wars, riding with his uncles and cousins, learning how to hold a desert well, how to read a horizon for dust and how to judge a man by the way he kept his word. He was not the heir, and he knew it.

The story of how Bika left Jodhpur is the most famous in Bikaner's memory. Tradition says that one day in **1465**, as Rao Jodha sat in court, he noticed his son Bika whispering with his uncle **Kandhal**, Jodha's own brother. Half in jest, the old Rao asked what the two of them were plotting so earnestly. Were they, he said, planning to conquer some new kingdom for themselves? The court laughed. Kandhal did not. He rose and said that by the grace of his elder brother, that was exactly what they would do. Whether the words were spoken quite like that, the bards cannot say. But the taunt became a vow, and the vow became Bikaner.

The chronicles say Bika set out with Kandhal, a few kinsmen and a small band of horsemen and foot soldiers, numbered in the hundreds rather than the thousands. They rode north-west into the country called **Jangaldesh**, the "land of scrub", the dry tract between Marwar, the Bhati lands of Jaisalmer and the plains of the Punjab. It was not empty. Bhati Rajputs held the forts of the west. Johiya and other clans held the north. And across much of the land lay the cantons of the **Jat** clans, the Godaras, Sarans, Beniwals, Punias and others, each under its own headman, farming where the rain allowed and grazing herds across the sand.

On the way, tradition says, Bika went to **Deshnoke** to seek the blessing of **Karni Mata**, the Charan holy woman revered across the desert as a living goddess. She is said to have foretold that his power would surpass his father's. From that day the Rathores of Bikaner took Karni Mata as the protecting goddess of their house, and her temple at Deshnoke, famous today for the rats that are believed to be her devotees, remained bound to the dynasty ever after.

Bika's first base was at **Kodamdesar**, where he raised a small fort. The early years were a struggle for survival. The Bhatis of **Pugal** and Jaisalmer saw the newcomers as intruders and raided them. Bika answered with arms and with marriage. The chronicles say he married the daughter of **Rao Shekha**, the Bhati chief of Pugal, and the alliance eased the pressure from the west, though quarrels with the Bhatis never quite ended.

The heart of the matter, however, was the Jat country. The Jat cantons were not united. The Godaras and the Sarans in particular were bitter rivals, and the bards tell a story of how that rivalry began over a woman, Malki, the wife of the Saran chief **Pula**, who left him for the Godara chief **Pandu**. Whatever the truth of the tale, the quarrel gave Bika his opening. The Godaras chose to accept him as their overlord, seeking his protection against their enemies. In return, tradition says, the Godara headmen were given the honour of marking the forehead of each new ruler of Bikaner with the *tilak* at his coronation, an honour remembered in the state for centuries.

With the Godaras beside him, Bika turned on those who resisted. The Sarans and other cantons were brought under his rule through years of hard campaigning. These were not great set-piece battles but a slow war of raids, sieges of village strongholds and negotiated surrenders. Bika's skill lay as much in diplomacy as in fighting: he left local headmen in place where they submitted, took revenue rather than land, and offered protection in return for loyalty. Step by step, the scattered Jat country became a Rathore state.

A state needed a capital. Around **1485** Bika began building a fort on a rise of ground called **Rati Ghati**, and in **1488**, on the traditional date of the second day of the bright half of Vaishakh, the city of **Bikaner** was founded around it. Local tradition says the land belonged to a Jat named **Nera**, who agreed to give it only if his name was joined to the new town. So the city became *Bika-Ner*. Historians treat the story with caution, since other explanations of the name exist, but it shows how deeply the founding of the state was tied, in local memory, to agreement with the Jat people of the land.

Bika's small stone fort was modest. The great fort of Bikaner that stands today, Junagarh, was built a century later by his descendant Raja Rai Singh. But the walled town around Bika's fort grew quickly. It stood on routes that carried caravans between the Punjab, Sindh and Gujarat, and merchants were glad of a ruler strong enough to keep the roads safe.

Not every year brought success. Bika's uncle **Kandhal**, the man who had answered Jodha's taunt, continued to carve out lands of his own towards the north-east, on the edge of the territory ruled from **Hisar**. There, around **1490**, he was killed in a clash with **Sarang Khan**, the governor of Hisar. Kandhal's death was a heavy blow to Bika. The chronicles say that Rao Jodha himself joined his son to avenge his brother, and that the Rathores defeated Sarang Khan's forces. The descendants of Kandhal, the **Kandhalots**, remained among the leading nobles of Bikaner.

Jodha died in **1489**, and Bika faced a new kind of struggle, this time with his own family. Tradition says that Jodha had promised Bika certain sacred heirlooms of the Rathore house, among them a royal throne, an umbrella of state, a sword and the family's household deity, in return for Bika's renouncing any claim to the throne of Jodhpur. After Jodha's death, his successor **Rao Suja** would not give them up. Bika marched on Jodhpur to claim what he believed was his. The bards say that bloodshed between brothers was avoided through the mediation of the dowager queen, **Jasmade**, and that the heirlooms were handed over. They were kept at Bikaner ever afterwards as the most precious possessions of the dynasty, and the rulers of Bikaner were proud that the ancestral regalia of the Rathores lay with them.

By the end of his life Bika had built something no one in Jodhpur had expected when he rode out in 1465. His rule stretched across a wide stretch of the northern Thar, from the Bhati frontier towards the edges of the Punjab plains. His kinsmen had also founded their own holdings nearby: his brother **Bida** had established the Bidawat Rathores in the lands of the Mohil Chauhans around Chhapar and Dronpur, a branch that would later be drawn closely into Bikaner's orbit.

Bika was a devout man in the manner of his age. Beyond his devotion to Karni Mata, he is credited with beginning the **Lakshminath temple** in Bikaner, dedicated to Vishnu and Lakshmi, which became the principal temple of the city and was completed by his son Lunkaran. He honoured the Charans and bards who would, in turn, keep his story alive for five centuries.

He is remembered as a ruler of plain habits and great stubbornness, a man who had been given no kingdom and so made one. The chronicles describe him dividing his life between the saddle and the council, settling disputes between clans, receiving merchants, inspecting wells and walls. In a country where water decided everything, the digging and protection of wells and tanks was as important as any war.

Rao Bika died in **1504** at Bikaner. He was succeeded by his eldest son, **Rao Naro**, whose reign would last only a few months, and then by his younger son **Rao Lunkaran**, who would expand what his father had begun. The state Bika founded outlasted the Delhi Sultanate, the Mughal Empire and the British Raj, and remained a princely state until it joined independent India in 1949. Every one of its rulers looked back to the day when a son of Jodha, stung by a joke in his father's court, rode out into the sand to find a kingdom of his own.

## Highlights of his life

- **Departure from Jodhpur (1465).** Tradition says a jest by his father, Rao Jodha, about "conquering a new kingdom" set him and his uncle Kandhal on the road to Jangaldesh.
- **Blessing of Karni Mata.** He sought the blessing of the Charan holy woman at Deshnoke, and she became the protecting goddess of the Bikaner Rathores.
- **Union with the Jat cantons.** Through alliance with the Godaras and campaigns against those who resisted, he brought the scattered Jat country under one rule.
- **Founding of Bikaner (1488).** He built a fort at Rati Ghati and founded the city of Bikaner, which became the capital of a state lasting more than four and a half centuries.
- **Avenging Kandhal.** After his uncle Kandhal was killed by Sarang Khan of Hisar, he and Rao Jodha defeated the governor's forces.
- **Winning the Rathore regalia.** After Jodha's death he secured the sacred heirlooms of the Rathore house from Rao Suja, and they were kept at Bikaner ever after.
- **Founder of a dynasty.** He died in 1504, leaving a state that remained a princely kingdom until 1949.

rao-shekha.name: Rao Shekha
rao-shekha.significance: Founder of Shekhawati region and dynasty
rao-shekha.story:
On that land of Rajputana, where sand and rock seemed to struggle against each other, a boy was born in 1433 CE—a boy who would shape not only his own destiny, but the identity of an entire region. He was Rao Shekha.

He was born into the tradition of the Kachwaha dynasty. There was courage in his blood, but the circumstances were not simple. New strongholds were being founded across Rajputana. Small forts were rising, new chiefs were carving out their territories. Power was being established not by the sword alone, but by foresight.

From childhood the boy Shekha understood that the land of the desert belongs only to those who can water it with their sweat and blood. Balance on horseback, spear practice on the open plain, a firm grip on the shield—this was his daily routine. But he was not only becoming a warrior; he was becoming a builder too.

By the time he came of age his gaze had settled on that stretch of desert where there was as yet no strong authority. There were scattered settlements, unsafe roads and instability. He resolved—a new territory would be born here. A land that would carry his identity.

The beginning was not easy. The surrounding chiefs were busy defending their own borders. Some saw his rise as a challenge. The first clash came on the border. The ground was flat, but dunes spread far and wide. Shekha hid his army behind the dunes. The front line offered light resistance and began to fall back.

The enemy advanced—believing victory was easy. Just then horsemen burst out from behind the dunes. The cry of "Kachwaha!" made the air tremble. Swords met. A cloud of dust and blood spread everywhere. Shekha himself was in the front line. He parried a chief's blow with his shield and with his counter-stroke ripped open his chest. In a short while the enemy fell back.

This was not just a victory—it was a declaration that a new power was being born.

But a territory cannot be established by war alone. With a strategic eye he began building forts. Forts rose on high ground, from where watch could be kept far and wide. Outposts were built near the water sources, to keep supplies safe. Every fort was a symbol not only of defence, but of control.

The second great clash came when a powerful chief attacked the newly established territory. This time the battle was fought on open ground. The kettledrums sounded. Horsemen faced each other. The earth trembled with the clang of swords.

Shekha divided his army into three. The infantry stood in the centre forming a wall of shields, cavalry on both sides. He ordered—"Do not advance until you get the signal."

The enemy attacked fiercely. The wall of shields stopped the first blow. As soon as the enemy tired, Shekha raised his sword—"Now!"

Horsemen crashed in from both sides. The ring closed. Within a few hours the enemy lines broke. The victory was decisive. Now it was no longer easy to challenge his leadership.

Shekha did not only win land; he won the trust of the people. He secured the trade routes. He gave protection to the settlements. He had temples built, where the sound of bells gave a sign of peace. Learning was encouraged. Scholars, poets and learned men began to come to his court.

On one occasion a chief in the court asked, "Maharaj, why are you building so much? The forts are enough."

Shekha replied, "Forts give protection, but culture gives identity. If the identity is strong, the kingdom is unshakeable."

The third and fiercest struggle came when an outside power tried to stop the rise of Shekhawati. This time the enemy was greater in number. The plain was wide. A cloud of dust was rising.

Shekha surveyed the ground. He turned his army towards a narrow way. As soon as the enemy entered, arrows rained from above. Horsemen crashed in from below. The heavy army was trapped in the narrow way. Swords flashed. Blood flowed. The enemy fell back.

From that day Shekhawati became not just a name, but an identity.

With time a chain of forts arose. Temple spires began to touch the sky. Trade flourished. People began to feel safe. Shekha's court became not just a place for planning war, but a centre of culture too.

In his final years, when he stood on the ramparts, he would gaze at the territory stretching far away—forts rising amid the sand, lamps burning in the villages, sounds coming from the temples. All of it was the fruit of his foresight.

When his final moment came, the sun was setting. A red glow had spread over the walls of the forts. He said softly, "The land has been established."

His breath stopped, but Shekhawati lived on.

Rao Shekha was not just a ruler. He was a builder—who gave the Kachwaha dynasty roots in a new land. He proved that valour lies not only on the battlefield, but in building too.

Even today, when the winds of Shekhawati strike the forts, a voice echoes in them—
"The foundation is immortal… the Kachwahas are immortal."

maharani-hansa-bai.name: Maharani Hansa Bai
maharani-hansa-bai.story:
*Historical note: Hansa Bai, the Rathore queen of Rana Lakha and mother of Rana Mokal, is a historical figure, but the battles and acts of government described here are not recorded in the sources.*

When the first light of morning fell on the rocks of the Aravallis, it did not touch only the stones—it touched the soul of Mewar. In the 15th century that same soul took form in a woman who treated the crown not as an ornament, but as a responsibility. She was Maharani Hansa Bai.

She was born amid Rajput splendour, but her personality was not confined to splendour. From childhood she saw that behind the glitter of palaces lay the complexity of politics. Hushed consultations in the council halls, dust rising on the borders, and the balancing of the nobles—all of this was part of her education. She became accomplished not only in the scriptures, but in strategy too.

When she became Maharani of Mewar, the kingdom was struggling not only with outside enemies but with internal imbalance too. Disputes among the nobles, small clashes on the frontier, and the challenges of the revenue system—amid all this she established herself not merely as a queen, but as an administrator.

When a difficult question arose in the court, her voice was calm but decisive. "A kingdom is kept safe by the sword," she would say, "but prosperity comes from justice and order." She had the tax system reformed. The excessive burden on farmers was reduced, so that green would return to the fields and the granaries would stay full. Regular arrangements were made for soldiers' pay and supplies, so that their morale on the battlefield would stay firm.

Once news came from the frontier—the enemy army had camped near a pass. Worry spread through the court. Some chiefs were talking of a direct attack. The Maharani sent for a map. She looked at the lie of the hills and said, "Let them come into the pass. Strike from the heights. When their horses tire, then use the sword."

Following her advice the army laid an ambush in the narrow way. When the enemy came in, arrows and stones rained from above. Horsemen crashed in from below. In a short while the danger passed. The soldiers said among themselves—"The queen's eye can read even the battlefield."

But her contribution was not limited to war. She had the forts repaired and the water sources secured. Temples were built, their walls bearing remarkable craftsmanship. She gave patronage to learning. Gurukuls received grants, manuscripts were collected. Poets, scholars and musicians came to her court. Mewar became not only a land of swords, but a land of culture too.

On one occasion a dispute arose in the court. Some nobles wanted more power. The situation was tense. Maharani Hansa Bai entered the assembly. "If we break from within," she said, "the enemy outside will swallow us. Mewar's strength lies in unity."

Her firmness quieted the dispute. She set out clear responsibilities in the administration. The system of courts was strengthened. Regular accounts began to be kept of the kingdom's income and expenditure. Discipline and balance gave the kingdom stability.

But one more test remained. Suddenly, one night, the enemy stormed the fort. The sound of kettledrums broke the sleep. Chaos broke out on the ramparts. The Maharani herself reached the bastion. In the torchlight her face was calm but radiant.

"Put out the torches," she ordered, "the darkness will confuse them."

In the dark the enemy lost its way. The Mewari soldiers attacked without warning. Swords met. Within a few hours the enemy fell back. There was pride in the soldiers' eyes—their queen was not only the guardian of the palace, but a guide on the battlefield too.

With time Mewar prospered. Green fields, the sound of bells in the temples, and the discussions of scholars in the court—all of it was the fruit of her foresight. She had understood that a kingdom lives not only through its borders, but through culture and order.

Even in her final years she remained active in the court. She taught the heirs—"The weight of the crown is borne more by wisdom than by the sword."

When her final moment came, the sun was setting over the Aravallis. A red glow had spread over the ramparts. She looked one last time at the forts she had strengthened, the temples she had built, and the court where learning and statecraft went hand in hand.

Her eyes closed, but her name was inscribed in the heartbeat of Mewar.

Maharani Hansa Bai was not just a queen. She was the wisdom that gave the sword its direction. She proved that a woman could stand not only behind the curtain, but at the centre of the state. Her legacy lives on today in the ramparts, in the bells of the temples, and in the stability of the administration.

Even today, when the winds of the Aravallis strike the walls of Chittor, a voice echoes in them—
"Mewar is prosperous… Mewar stands unshaken."

rao-nara.name: Rao Nara
rao-nara.story:
*Historical note: The identity of Rao Nara and the battles described here cannot be confirmed from historical sources. Read this story as legend, not history.*

When the sun rose over the golden sands of the Thar, its rays gleamed on the edges of swords. That was the 15th century—when the shadows of forts lay long over the land of Rajputana and war was not only about borders, but about honour. In that age a general was born in the lap of the Rathore dynasty who made his name the echo of the battlefield—he was Rao Nara.

He was born into struggle more than splendour. The land of Marwar was harsh, and its people harsher still. From childhood he saw that the walls of a fort are not just stone—they are vows. As his father placed a sword in his hand he had said, "Rathore blood shines bright only when tempered in war."

The boy Nara would reach the stables as soon as morning came. Mastering balance on horseback, he learned to fall and rise again. The bowstring did not tremble in his fingers. His spear thrust was straight and fast. But sharper still was his vision—he could read the battlefield before the battle began.

It was a time when Mewar's power was at its height. That power was led by Rana Kumbha—a symbol of strategy and valour. The relationship between Marwar and Mewar carried notes of both cooperation and conflict, but one thing was clear—unity was needed against enemies both foreign and internal.

The young Nara was given the responsibility of general. It was not just a post—it was an oath to stand in the front line on the battlefield. He reorganised the army. The horsemen were given light armour, so that they could move like a storm across the desert. The infantry was trained in dense lines of shields. He said, "War is won not by strength alone, but by discipline."

The first great battle took place on the frontier. The enemy army crossed the desert and attacked. The ground was flat, but there were high and low dunes as far as the eye could see. Rao Nara hid his army behind the dunes. The front line offered light resistance and began to fall back.

The enemy advanced—believing victory was easy. Just then arrows and spears rained from behind the dunes. Horsemen crashed in from both sides. The cry of "Rathore!" made the air tremble. Swords met. A cloud of dust and blood spread everywhere. Rao Nara himself was in the front line. He parried an enemy commander's blow with his shield and with his counter-stroke pierced his chest. In a short while the enemy fell back.

This was not just a victory—it was a sign that the desert still burned.

The second clash took place in a mountain pass, where the enemy was greater in number. Rao Nara surveyed the ground. He posted soldiers above and left the narrow way below open.

As soon as the enemy entered, stones and arrows began to rain from above. Horsemen crashed in from below. The heavy army was trapped in the narrow way. The cannon became useless. It was a victory of strategy.

But the decisive battle was still to come.

On the open field the two armies faced each other. The sun overhead, the smell of gunpowder in the air. Rana Kumbha himself was present. The kettledrums sounded. The roar of the guns shook the earth.

Rao Nara signalled his troop—"After the first volley, scatter, then strike together."

The guns were fired. Many soldiers fell. The smoke cleared. He raised his sword—"Marwar!"

The horsemen burst forward like arrows. Swords met. Spears struck home. Blood flowed over the earth. An enemy officer challenged him—"Surrender!"

Flames blazed in Rao Nara's eyes—"Rathores choose death, not slavery!"

The two faced each other. Swords clashed, sparks flew. At last Rao Nara's blow prevailed. The officer fell.

But the enemy's numbers were vast. He began to be surrounded on every side. A spear drove into his shoulder. He pulled it out and flung it away. His sword rose again. A second blow landed on his chest. He staggered, but did not fall back.

Looking towards Rana Kumbha, he called out—"My lord, go forward! We are the wall!"

And he truly became a wall. He held back the enemy line with his own body. His blows were slowing, but the flame in his eyes did not go out.

At last, from many blows, his body gave out. He sank to his knees. His gaze went to the banner flying over the battlefield. A faint smile came to his lips.

He fell to the ground—but his sword still pointed forward.

The battle ended, but Rao Nara's sacrifice became immortal. Rana Kumbha said, "Generals like this are the foundation of a kingdom."

Rao Nara was not just a general. He was the resolve that showed that Rathores do not only rule—they also give their lives on the battlefield. His strategy, his courage, and his final decision—to accept death—were engraved in the sands of the desert.

Even today, when the wind of the Thar blows, the clang of swords can be heard in it.

And in every echo a voice rings out—
"The Rathores are immortal."

rana-raimal.name: Rana Raimal
rana-raimal.story:
## Rana Raimal — the son who avenged Kumbha and rebuilt the house of Ekalinga

*Rana Raimal's reign is recorded in the inscriptions of his own time, above all the great Eklingji inscription of 1488, and in the chronicles and bardic traditions of Mewar, which preserve the story of his family's quarrels. The inscriptions speak in the language of royal praise; the bards add drama and prophecy. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

**Raimal** was a son of **Rana Kumbha**, the greatest builder and one of the greatest warriors in the history of Mewar. He grew up in the most brilliant court Mewar had ever known. In the years of his boyhood his father raised the walls of **Kumbhalgarh** on a mountaintop, set up the **Vijay Stambh**, the Tower of Victory, at **Chittor**, saw the great Jain temple at **Ranakpur** rise under his patronage, and wrote books on music and poetry. Kumbha fought the Sultans of **Malwa** and **Gujarat** for decades and held his kingdom against them both. To be his son was to grow up among architects, poets, musicians and soldiers, and to learn from childhood what a great Rana looked like.

That world ended in murder. In **1468** Kumbha was killed at Kumbhalgarh, and the killer was his own son, Raimal's brother **Udai Singh**, remembered in Mewar as **Uda**. Mewar's tradition says that in his last years Kumbha was troubled by illness of the mind, and that Uda struck him down while he sat at prayer. Whatever the full story, the crime filled Mewar with horror. The bards would never call Uda by his name without adding the word *hatyara*, the murderer.

Uda took the throne, but he could not hold the loyalty of the nobles. To buy support from his neighbours, the chronicles say, he gave away lands that Kumbha had won: territory around **Sambhar** and **Ajmer** to **Rao Jodha** of Marwar, and **Abu** to the Deora Chauhans of Sirohi. The nobles of Mewar grew more angry each year. Raimal, meanwhile, was living away from the court. Tradition says that he had taken refuge at **Idar**, in the hills on the borders of Gujarat, where he had family ties by marriage.

The leading nobles of Mewar sent for him. Around **1473** Raimal returned with his followers, and the chiefs of Mewar gathered under his banner. The chronicles describe several battles between the two brothers, at places such as **Jawar**, **Darimpur** and **Pangarh**, in which Raimal's forces defeated Uda's. Uda fled from Mewar. Raimal entered Chittor and was crowned Rana. The murder of Kumbha had been avenged, and the throne was in the hands of a son the nobles could trust.

Uda went to **Mandu**, the capital of Malwa, to seek help from Sultan **Ghiyath Shah Khalji**, the old enemy of his father. Tradition says that he offered his own daughter to the Sultan in return for an army to win back Mewar, and that as he left the Sultan's presence he was struck by lightning and killed. The bards saw it as the judgement of heaven on a parricide. Whether or not the lightning story is literally true, Uda disappears from history at this point.

Raimal's first years were spent in restoring order. The kingdom had been shaken by the murder and the civil war that followed, and some of the lands Uda had given away were lost for good. The new Rana had to win back the confidence of the nobles, punish those who had supported the murderer, and keep Mewar's powerful neighbours from taking advantage of its weakness.

The most dangerous of those neighbours was Malwa. Ghiyath Shah, despite his reputation as a ruler who preferred his palace and his large household of women to the battlefield, sent his armies against Mewar. Uda's sons, **Sahasmal** and **Surajmal**, came with the Malwa forces, hoping to win their father's throne. Mewar's inscriptions and chronicles record that Raimal defeated these attacks and drove the Malwa army back, and the Eklingji inscription of 1488 praises him as a victor over the Sultan of Malwa. As with all such inscriptions, the language is proud and the details are few, but it is clear that under Raimal Mewar held its frontier against Malwa and kept its independence.

Raimal is remembered above all as a builder of shrines. The temple of **Eklingji**, near Nagda, the seat of Mewar's true lord, had been damaged in the wars of the fifteenth century. Raimal rebuilt it on a grand scale, and much of the temple that stands today, with its great tower and its four-faced image of Shiva, is his work. In **1488** he set up a long inscription there in Sanskrit verse, recording the history of the Guhila and Sisodia rulers from Bappa Rawal to his own time. The Eklingji inscription of Raimal is one of the most important sources for Mewar's history. By rebuilding the shrine, Raimal renewed the bond on which the whole dynasty rested: the Rana as the *dewan*, the servant, of Ekalinga.

His family shared in this work. His queen **Shringar Devi**, a princess of the Rathores of Marwar, built a great stepwell at **Ghosundi**, near Chittor, and her inscription there, dated **1504**, records her gifts and her husband's line. Wells and stepwells were the lifeblood of the dry country, and royal women of Rajasthan often built them as acts of piety.

Raimal's own household, however, was troubled. He had many sons, and three of them were men of great ability and great ambition: **Prithviraj**, the eldest, **Jaimal**, and **Sangram Singh**, who would become famous as **Rana Sanga**. The quarrels among these brothers fill the bardic histories of Raimal's reign.

The bards tell a famous story about how the quarrel began. The three princes, wishing to know which of them would one day rule, went together to the shrine of a Charan priestess at **Nahar Magra**, a holy woman believed to have the gift of prophecy. When she spoke, she said that it was Sangram who would rule Mewar. Prithviraj, hot-tempered and proud, drew his sword and attacked his younger brother on the spot. In the struggle Sangram was wounded and lost the sight of one eye. The tale may have grown in the telling, but it is certain that Sanga lost an eye in his youth and that he fled from the court in fear of his brothers.

Sangram, tradition says, found shelter with a Rathore warrior named **Bida** at **Sevantri**, who defended him against his pursuers and was killed protecting him. Afterwards the prince lived for years in hiding, serving under other chiefs, without revealing who he was.

The other two brothers met tragic ends. Jaimal, the bards say, went to the court of the Solanki chief **Rao Surtan**, who had lost his town of **Toda** to Afghan invaders, and sought the hand of his daughter **Tara Bai**, famed for her beauty and courage. He behaved so insolently that Rao Surtan killed him. When Raimal heard what had happened, he did not seek revenge, saying that his son had earned his death by his own conduct.

Prithviraj, a bold and restless warrior known as **Udna Prithviraj**, "Prithviraj the swift", then won Tara Bai's hand by promising to recover Toda for her father, and the bards say he kept his promise in a daring night attack. He was the hero of many adventures in the songs of Mewar. But his end was sad. His sister had been married to **Jagmal**, the ruler of **Sirohi**, who treated her badly. Prithviraj rode to Sirohi and forced his brother-in-law to promise better behaviour. Jagmal pretended friendship, but tradition says he gave Prithviraj poisoned sweets as he left, and the prince died near **Kumbhalgarh**, within sight of the fortress his grandfather had built. Tara Bai, the bards say, followed him onto the funeral pyre.

So the old Rana lost two of his sons, and the third was living as a fugitive. In his last years Raimal sent for Sangram, the son the prophecy had named. Sanga came home and was recognised as heir. When Raimal died in **1509**, after a reign of about thirty-six years, Sangram Singh succeeded him as **Rana Sanga**.

Raimal's reign is often seen only as the bridge between two giants, his father Kumbha and his son Sanga. But it was a bridge that had to be built. He took a kingdom shamed by a father's murder and torn by civil war, avenged the crime, defended the borders against Malwa, restored the temple of Ekalinga, and handed on to his son a Mewar strong enough for Sanga to make it, for a time, the leading power of northern India.

## Highlights of his life

- **Son of Rana Kumbha.** He grew up in the court of Mewar's greatest builder and warrior king.
- **Avenger of his father (c. 1473).** After Kumbha's murder by Uda in 1468, the nobles called Raimal back from Idar; he defeated Uda in several battles and took the throne.
- **Defender against Malwa.** He repulsed attacks from Ghiyath Shah's Malwa, which came with Uda's sons in its train.
- **Rebuilder of Eklingji.** Much of the present temple of Eklingji is his work, and his inscription of 1488 is a key source for Mewar's history.
- **A family of builders.** His queen Shringar Devi built the stepwell at Ghosundi, recorded in an inscription of 1504.
- **Father of Rana Sanga.** The quarrels of his sons Prithviraj, Jaimal and Sangram fill Mewar's legends; Sangram survived to become his heir.
- **A long reign.** He ruled for about thirty-six years and died in 1509, succeeded by Rana Sanga.

kunwar-prithviraj-mewar.name: Kunwar Prithviraj Mewar
legends: Restored Toda for Tara Bai's father
kunwar-prithviraj-mewar.story:
**Kunwar Prithviraj — the 'flying' prince of Mewar**

Prithviraj was the eldest son of **Rana Raimal** of Mewar and the elder brother of **Sangram Singh**, the future **Rana Sanga**. He was famous for the speed of his raids, and Mewar's tradition calls him **Udana Prithviraj**, the 'flying' Prithviraj.

**The quarrel of the brothers**

Tradition tells that Prithviraj, Sanga and their brother **Jaimal** consulted a priestess to learn which of them would rule Mewar. When she pointed to Sanga, Prithviraj attacked him in anger, and Sanga lost an eye in the fight. Sanga fled, and lived for years in hiding.

**Tara Bai and Toda**

The best-known story of Prithviraj is that of **Tara Bai**, the daughter of **Rao Surtan Solanki**, who had been driven out of **Toda**. She vowed to marry only the man who won back her father's lands. Prithviraj led a daring night attack, recovered Toda, and married Tara Bai. Tradition links her name with **Taragarh**, the fort of Ajmer.

**His death**

Prithviraj did not die in battle. He quarrelled with his brother-in-law, **Jagmal**, the ruler of **Sirohi**, over Jagmal's ill-treatment of Prithviraj's sister. After a reconciliation, Jagmal gave him poisoned sweets as he left, and Prithviraj died on the way home, near **Kumbhalgarh**, in the first years of the 16th century, before his father. Tara Bai is said to have become sati with him.

**Legacy**

Prithviraj's early death opened the way for Sanga, who became one of Mewar's greatest rulers.

maharani-rani-sona.name: Maharani Rani Sona
maharani-rani-sona.story:
## Maharani Rani Sona — the wise queen of the Mewar tradition

*No queen of Mewar named Rani Sona appears in the inscriptions, the Persian histories, the Mewar chronicles or Tod's Annals; "Rani Sona" is best read as a composite, traditional figure, and this story ties her to the real queens and princesses of fifteenth-century Mewar, such as Hansa Bai and Ramabai, whose actions are recorded.*

The bards of Rajasthan remember many queens, and not all of them can be found in the record. **Rani Sona**, the "wise queen of Mewar" who is said to have managed royal affairs and supported the arts in the **fifteenth century**, is one of these. Older retellings give her a full life of council, battle and patronage, but none of it can be confirmed: no inscription, chronicle or Sisodia genealogy names her.

That does not make the figure meaningless. The idea of a capable queen who held a court together is drawn from real women of the period. Looking at them is the honest way to understand what a "Rani Sona" could have been.

### Mewar in the fifteenth century

The fifteenth century was one of the great ages of **Mewar**. **Rana Lakha** (c. 1382–1421) enriched the kingdom with the silver and lead of the **Zawar** mines. His son **Rana Mokal** (1421–1433) rebuilt temples at **Chittor** and **Eklingji**. Then came **Rana Kumbha** (1433–1468), soldier, builder and scholar, who raised **Kumbhalgarh**, built the **Vijay Stambha** at Chittor after his wars with **Malwa** and **Gujarat**, and wrote or sponsored works on music and the arts. His successors, **Udayasimha I** and **Rana Raimal** (1473–1509), held the kingdom together until the rise of **Rana Sanga**.

In such a state the Rana was not the only source of power. The great nobles held their lands in return for military service and often quarrelled over precedence. The royal women lived in the **zenana**, the women's quarters, and rarely appeared in open court, but they were not cut off from politics. A queen could speak for her young son, keep her own household and lands, give gifts to temples, and use the ties of her birth family to bring allies or enemies into the kingdom.

### A real queen in a crisis: Hansa Bai

The clearest example is **Hansa Bai**, a **Rathore** princess, daughter of **Rao Chunda** of **Mandore**. Mewar tradition says she was married to the ageing Rana Lakha on the understanding that her son would inherit the throne. Lakha's eldest son, **Chunda**, gave up his claim, a sacrifice still honoured in the precedence of his descendants, the **Chundawats**.

When Lakha died, Hansa Bai's son **Mokal** was a child. Chunda at first guided the government, but the queen mother came to distrust him, and he withdrew to Malwa. Hansa Bai turned to her brother, **Ranmal Rathore**, who became the dominant figure at the court of Chittor. The chronicles describe the resentment this caused among the Sisodia nobles. After Mokal's murder in **1433** and the accession of Kumbha, the struggle ended violently: Ranmal was killed at Chittor around **1438**, and Chunda returned.

The story shows how much a queen mother could do: she could choose her protectors, shape the regency and bring her brother's house into the centre of power. It also shows the dangers, since every such choice made enemies. The legend of a wise queen calming quarrelling nobles reflects a very real problem of the age.

### Patronage: Ramabai of Zawar

The other side of the legend, a queen who supported temples and learning, also has a historical parallel. **Ramabai**, a daughter of Rana Kumbha, was married to **Mandalika**, the ruler of **Junagadh** in Saurashtra. After her return to Mewar she built a temple and a large water reservoir at **Zawar**, and an inscription of **1497** records her gifts. She is one of the few royal women of the period whose name survives in stone because of what she built.

Step-wells, tanks and reservoirs were a common form of royal women's patronage across Rajasthan, alongside gifts to temples and grants of land to Brahmins. When the bards praise Rani Sona for building temples and gathering scholars, they are describing this tradition.

### Reading the legend

Some episodes in the older story are plainly modern additions, such as novel-style speeches or a queen directing ambushes in the hill passes; no Mewar queen of this century is known to have commanded troops. Others give a queen the duties of a ruler, such as cutting taxes and repairing forts, without any source. The rest, showing a queen who protected her son's interests, managed her household lands and gave generously to temples, matches what is known of royal women of the time.

It is also possible that "Sona" survives from a local tradition, a family memory or a ballad about a real queen whose proper name has been lost. Rajput queens were usually known in the records by their clan or birthplace (**Jhali**, **Rathorni**, **Songari**, **Hadi**) rather than by personal names, and many personal names were never written down. A queen remembered in song as "Sona" could have a different name, or none, in the official genealogies. Without a source, however, nothing more can be said.

### Why the figure endures

Rajasthan's popular memory of royal women has often centred on **jauhar** and sacrifice, as in the stories of **Rani Padmini** and **Rani Karnavati**. The tradition of a "wise queen" offers a different picture: a woman remembered for judgment, patronage and steadiness rather than for death. That picture is supported by Hansa Bai and Ramabai, and later by **Mirabai** in the sixteenth century.

Rani Sona, then, is best understood as a symbol of these women: a name that gathers up the real power and the real patronage of Mewar's queens, even though the life told about her cannot be found in history.

### Key points
- **No record.** No inscription, chronicle or genealogy names a Mewar queen called Rani Sona; the figure is traditional or composite.
- **Real context.** Fifteenth-century Mewar under Lakha, Mokal and Kumbha was rich, powerful and often divided among its nobles.
- **Hansa Bai.** The Rathore queen mother of Rana Mokal shaped the regency and brought her brother Ranmal to power at Chittor.
- **Ramabai.** Kumbha's daughter built a temple and reservoir at Zawar, recorded in an inscription of 1497.
- **Reading the legend.** Tales of a queen leading armies are later additions; her patronage and influence over the court reflect real roles of royal women.

medini-rai.name: Medini Rai
medini-rai.significance: Rajput chief and ally of Rana Sanga
medini-rai.story:
## Medini Rai — the lord of Chanderi

*Medini Rai's career is known from Persian histories of Malwa and Gujarat, from Babur's own memoirs (the Baburnama), and from Mewar's chronicles; the details of his last hours at Chanderi come mainly from Babur, while Rajput bardic tradition adds the colour of loyalty and sacrifice.*

**Medini Rai** was one of the most remarkable figures of early sixteenth-century central India: a Rajput chief who, for a few years, was the real master of the Sultanate of **Malwa**, and who ended his life defending the hill fortress of **Chanderi** against **Babur** in **January 1528**. He belonged to the **Purbiya** Rajputs, the "eastern" Rajput soldiers who had long served the sultanates of Malwa and north India as mercenary cavalry. Very little is known of his birth or early family; he appears in history already as a powerful soldier at the Malwa court.

### Master of Malwa

The Malwa Sultanate, ruled from its splendid capital at **Mandu**, was in disorder by the time **Sultan Mahmud Khalji II** came to the throne in **1511**. Rival nobles and princes of the royal house contested his succession. Mahmud turned to Medini Rai and his Purbiya followers, and with their swords he secured his throne. In return Medini Rai became his chief minister (wazir), and he placed his own kinsmen and followers in key offices and commands across the kingdom.

The Persian historians, who wrote from the point of view of the Muslim nobility, describe this period with alarm: in their account the Rajputs had taken over the state. Whatever the exaggeration, the Sultan himself came to fear the minister who had made him. Around **1517** Mahmud slipped away from Mandu and sought help from **Sultan Muzaffar Shah II of Gujarat**. A Gujarati army marched into Malwa and stormed Mandu in **1518**; many of Medini Rai's Rajputs died in its defence, and the Sultan was restored without his over-mighty minister.

### The alliance with Rana Sanga

Medini Rai still held strong positions in eastern Malwa, centred on **Chanderi** and **Gagron**. He turned to the greatest Rajput ruler of the age, **Rana Sanga** of **Mewar**, who had his own reasons to fight Malwa. In **1519** Mahmud Khalji marched against Gagron. Sanga came to its relief, and at the battle of **Gagron** the Malwa army was routed and the Sultan himself was wounded and taken prisoner. Sanga treated him with chivalry, nursed him and later released him — a gesture still praised in Mewar's chronicles.

From then on Medini Rai was firmly in Sanga's camp. He held Chanderi as the anchor of Mewar's influence in Malwa, and he was counted among the great chiefs of the Rajput confederacy that Sanga built in the 1520s.

### Khanwa, 1527

In **1526** Babur defeated **Ibrahim Lodi** at **Panipat** and took Delhi and Agra. Sanga gathered his allies to drive the newcomer out, and Medini Rai brought a large contingent; Babur himself lists him among Sanga's chief allies. The armies met at **Khanwa**, near Fatehpur Sikri, on **17 March 1527**. Babur's field guns, matchlocks and flanking cavalry broke the Rajput host. Sanga was wounded and carried from the field, and many great chiefs fell. Medini Rai survived and withdrew to Chanderi.

### The siege of Chanderi, 1528

Babur now moved to crush the remaining centres of Rajput power, and Chanderi, a strong fort on a hill commanding the routes between Malwa and the Ganga plain, was the obvious target. He arrived before it in **January 1528**. According to his memoirs, he offered Medini Rai the town of **Shamsabad** in exchange for Chanderi. The offer was refused.

Meanwhile Rana Sanga, though still recovering from his wounds, was marching to Medini Rai's aid. He never arrived. Sanga died at **Kalpi** on **30 January 1528**; later tradition says he was poisoned by nobles who did not want another war with Babur.

At Chanderi, Babur's troops seized the lower town and attacked the citadel. Babur describes how the defenders, seeing that the fort could not be held, put their women and children to death and came out to fight to the last. In Rajput memory this was the **jauhar** of Chanderi, followed by the **saka**, the final charge of men who had resolved to die. The fort fell on **29 January 1528**. Medini Rai is generally held to have died with his men, although the sources are not perfectly clear about the moment of his death. Babur, a frank and often unsparing narrator, records the slaughter and the tower of heads raised after the victory.

### Legacy

Chanderi passed into the hands of Babur's nominees, and with its fall the last major Rajput power in Malwa was gone. A few years later Malwa itself was swallowed by Gujarat and then contested by the Mughals and the Afghans.

Medini Rai's memory is double. To the Persian chroniclers of Malwa he was a usurping minister who turned a Muslim sultanate into a Rajput domain. To Rajput tradition he was the faithful ally who stood with Rana Sanga at Khanwa and, when Sanga was gone, chose death at Chanderi over an exchange of forts. In the local memory of Chanderi, the jauhar site within the fort is still pointed out, and the story of the siege is told alongside the town's famous weavers and its Bundela-era monuments. Historians today see in him a figure typical of an age when Rajput soldiers, Afghan nobles and Turkish sultans served, fought and allied with one another across lines of faith, and when the arrival of gunpowder warfare changed the fate of hill forts like Chanderi.

### Key points
- **Purbiya chief.** Medini Rai rose as a Purbiya Rajput commander at the Malwa court under Mahmud Khalji II.
- **Wazir of Malwa.** He became chief minister and dominated the Sultanate until Gujarat helped the Sultan expel him around 1517–18.
- **Gagron, 1519.** Allied with Rana Sanga, he saw the Sultan defeated and captured at Gagron.
- **Khanwa, 1527.** He fought in Sanga's confederacy against Babur and survived the defeat.
- **Chanderi, 1528.** He refused Babur's offer of Shamsabad; the fort fell on 29 January 1528 after the jauhar, and he is generally held to have died there.

haridas-tomar.significance: Sanganer chief who fought in Mughal wars
haridas-tomar.story:
## Haridas Tomar — a chief of Sanganer in the age of Babur

*No Tomar chief named Haridas of Sanganer appears in the inscriptions, Persian histories, Rajasthani khyats or Tod's Annals; this profile presents him as a figure of local tradition, a composite of the many minor Rajput chiefs who fought in the wars of the 1520s, and sets that tradition against the real history of the Tomars, of Sanganer and of Babur's campaigns.*

The name **Haridas Tomar** survives in this archive with a short outline: a chief of **Sanganer**, a fighter in the wars against the Mughals, a man who died defending his land around **1527**. When historians look for him in the record, however, they find nothing. He is not named in **Babur**'s memoirs, which list the great allies of **Rana Sanga** at **Khanwa**; he is not in the Persian chronicles of the Lodis and the Mughals; and he is not in the genealogies of the Kachhwaha rulers of **Amber**, in whose country Sanganer lay. The honest way to tell his story is therefore as a tale of the kind that bards and village elders told about many local heroes, and to explain the real world that such a tale grows out of.

### The Tomars

The **Tomars** (Tanwars) were one of the old Rajput clans of north India. Tradition credits them with the founding of **Dhillika**, the early city of **Delhi**, in the eleventh century, and inscriptions show Tomar rulers in the Delhi region before the **Chahamanas** (Chauhans) of Ajmer took control in the twelfth century. After the Turkish conquest the clan scattered. Its most famous later branch was the Tomar house of **Gwalior**, whose great king **Man Singh Tomar** (r. 1486–1516) built the Man Mandir palace and patronised the **dhrupad** style of music.

Gwalior was lost to **Ibrahim Lodi** in 1518, and its last Tomar king, **Vikramaditya**, fell fighting on Ibrahim's side at **Panipat** in **1526**. His son **Ram Shah Tomar** later became a wanderer and an ally of Mewar, and died with his sons at **Haldighati** in **1576**. Smaller Tomar families also held lands and village estates across the region between Delhi, Gwalior and the Aravallis, and Tanwar communities are still found in Rajasthan, Haryana and Madhya Pradesh. A local Tomar chief in eastern Rajputana in the 1520s is therefore plausible, even if this particular one is not documented.

### Sanganer

**Sanganer** lies a few miles south of modern **Jaipur**. In the sixteenth century it was part of **Dhundhar**, the country of the **Kachhwaha** Rajputs of Amber. Local tradition links the town's name to a Kachhwaha prince called **Sanga**. Its old **Jain temple** is one of its best-known monuments, and in later centuries Sanganer became famous across India for its **hand-block printed textiles** and its handmade paper. A "chief of Sanganer" in local speech could mean the holder of a fort or estate in the area, a vassal of a greater house rather than an independent king.

### The wars of 1526–1527

The date given for Haridas's death, 1527, places him in the year of **Khanwa**. After Babur's victory at Panipat in April 1526, Rana Sanga of **Mewar** gathered a great confederacy of Rajput and Afghan allies. Among those whom the sources do name are **Prithviraj Kachhwaha** of Amber, **Medini Rai** of Chanderi, **Silhadi** of Raisen, **Hasan Khan Mewati** and **Mahmud Lodi**. Each great chief brought many lesser kinsmen and vassals, and the names of most of these lesser men were never written down. At Khanwa, on **17 March 1527**, Babur's guns and flanking cavalry broke the Rajput army, and countless such men died on the field.

A chief from the Sanganer country who rode in the Amber contingent, or who fought in the skirmishes before and after Khanwa, would fit this history exactly. That is most likely the seed of the Haridas tradition: a real kind of life, remembered locally, even if the individual cannot be confirmed.

### The tale as it is told

The tradition, as it reached this archive, tells of a young chief raised in a small fort, trained from boyhood in riding, swordsmanship and the duties of a ruler, and taught that "the land may be small, but not one's pride." When Mughal forces threatened his country, the story goes, he refused to submit. He is said to have fought a battle at the edge of his land, using low hills to hide part of his force and strike the enemy's flank, and to have harried a besieging camp with night raids. In the end, the tale says, he died in a last battle on the open plain, refusing an offer to surrender.

These episodes cannot be checked, and some look borrowed from the common stock of bardic storytelling: the feigned retreat, the night raid on the powder store, the challenge from an enemy commander. They are better read as the shape that Rajput memory gave to a hero than as a battle report. They do express real values of the age: loyalty to land and lineage, the idea that a Rajput's honour lay in refusing to yield, and respect for the man who dies in the front rank.

### Why such stories matter

Rajasthan's past is full of local heroes like Haridas: men honoured with a memorial stone (**devli** or **paliya**), a song at a village fair, or a few lines in a family genealogy kept by a bard. Most never reached the Persian histories or the court khyats, which concentrated on kings and great nobles. Their stories remind us that the wars of the sixteenth century were fought not only by famous rulers but by hundreds of small chiefs and their followers, whose names survive, if at all, in oral memory.

### Key points
- **Not in the record.** No Haridas Tomar of Sanganer is found in inscriptions, Persian histories, khyats or Tod.
- **The Tomar clan.** The Tomars ruled early Delhi and later Gwalior; their last Gwalior king died at Panipat in 1526.
- **Sanganer.** The town near Jaipur lay in the Kachhwaha country of Dhundhar, later famed for block printing.
- **Year of Khanwa.** The date 1527 links the tradition to Rana Sanga's war against Babur, in which many unnamed chiefs died.
- **A composite hero.** His story is best read as local tradition expressing the values of the age, not as documented history.

silhadi-singh.story:
## Silhadi — the lord of Raisen

*Silhadi's career is recorded in the Persian histories of Malwa and Gujarat (notably the Mirat-i-Sikandari and Firishta), in Babur's memoirs and in Mewar's chronicles; the charge that he deserted Rana Sanga at Khanwa comes from later accounts and is doubted by some historians, while the jauhar of Raisen is remembered in both Persian and Rajput sources.*

**Silhadi** (also written **Salahdi** or **Silhadi Singh**) was one of the most powerful and most controversial Rajput chiefs of early sixteenth-century central India. Described in different sources as a **Tomar** or as a **Purbiya** Rajput, he made himself master of the eastern parts of the Malwa Sultanate, with his seat at the hill fort of **Raisen** near modern Bhopal, and his lands included **Bhilsa** (Vidisha) and **Sarangpur**. His name is joined forever to two events: the battle of **Khanwa** in **1527**, where tradition accuses him of betrayal, and the siege of **Raisen** in **1532**, which ended in jauhar and a last stand.

### Rise in Malwa

Like **Medini Rai** of Chanderi, Silhadi rose in the service of the weakened **Khalji Sultans of Malwa** under **Mahmud Khalji II** (r. 1511–1531). When Mahmud drove out Medini Rai with Gujarat's help, Silhadi kept his own position, and as the Sultanate fell apart he became effectively independent in the east. Raisen, a sandstone hill fort with its own water tanks, was a strong base; Bhilsa and Sarangpur gave him rich farmland and control of routes running between Malwa, Bundelkhand and the Gangetic plain.

He was connected by marriage to the house of **Mewar**: his wife, **Durgavati**, is described as a daughter of **Rana Sanga**. This tie, and Silhadi's own interest in resisting both Malwa and Gujarat, drew him into Sanga's circle of allies.

### Khanwa, 1527

When Rana Sanga gathered his great confederacy against **Babur** in **1527**, Silhadi joined with a large force. Babur's memoirs list him among Sanga's leading allies and credit him with a substantial body of horsemen. At **Khanwa** on **17 March 1527**, the Rajput army was defeated by Babur's artillery, matchlocks and flanking cavalry.

Later accounts, followed by **James Tod** and by much Rajput tradition, say that Silhadi went over to Babur in the course of the battle, or opened negotiations with him beforehand, and that his defection weakened Sanga's line at a critical moment. The story has made his name a byword for treachery in Rajput memory. Modern historians are more cautious. Babur, who would have had every reason to boast of winning over a great Rajput chief, does not clearly describe such a desertion in his own account, and the defeat is fully explained by the Mughal tactics. What can be said is that Silhadi survived Khanwa and returned to his lands, and that he was soon dealing with the new powers of the region on his own terms.

### The siege of Raisen, 1532

The real threat to Silhadi came not from the Mughals but from **Sultan Bahadur Shah of Gujarat**. In **1531** Bahadur Shah conquered Malwa and captured Mandu, ending the Khalji dynasty. Silhadi had at first cooperated with him, but Bahadur Shah was angered by reports that the Rajput chief held Muslim women captive and by his independent power, and in **1532** he turned on him.

According to the Gujarati histories, Silhadi was detained in Bahadur Shah's camp, and under pressure he professed Islam; the sources differ on how sincere or how forced this was. Meanwhile the Gujarat army besieged **Raisen**, held by Silhadi's brother **Lakshman Sen** (Lokhman) and the garrison. Silhadi's son **Bhupat** had gone to seek help from Mewar, and a relief force was expected but did not arrive in time.

When the fort could no longer be held, the women of Raisen, led by **Rani Durgavati**, performed **jauhar**. Silhadi, whom Bahadur Shah had brought to the fort in the hope of persuading the garrison to surrender, joined his brother and kinsmen instead, and they died fighting in the final sally, the **saka**. Raisen passed to Gujarat in **1532**. Bahadur Shah then turned his armies against Chittor, which he besieged in 1533 and again in 1535.

### A divided memory

Silhadi's story is one of the most complex of the age. In Rajput tradition he is remembered first as the man who, it is said, failed Sanga at Khanwa, and bardic verses condemn him. Yet the same tradition honours the jauhar and saka of Raisen, in which his wife, a daughter of Sanga, and his brother and companions died, and in which he himself chose to die with his people. Persian historians, for their part, remembered him as a powerful and troublesome chief whose fall completed Gujarat's conquest of Malwa.

For historians, Silhadi illustrates the shifting loyalties of a time when Malwa, Gujarat, Mewar, the Lodis and the Mughals were all competing for central India, and when a regional chief had to bargain with each in turn to survive. The fort of Raisen still stands above the town, with its palaces, tanks and walls, and local memory continues to point to the place of the jauhar.

### Key points
- **Lord of Raisen.** Silhadi held Raisen, Bhilsa and Sarangpur in eastern Malwa as the Khalji Sultanate declined.
- **Tied to Mewar.** His wife Durgavati is described as a daughter of Rana Sanga.
- **Khanwa, 1527.** He fought in Sanga's confederacy; the tradition that he deserted mid-battle is widely told but doubted by some historians.
- **Gujarat's attack.** Bahadur Shah of Gujarat detained him and besieged Raisen in 1532.
- **Jauhar and saka.** Rani Durgavati led the jauhar, and Silhadi died with his brother Lakshman Sen in the last fight.
