The first battle was fought for a small fort. The Mughal subahdar demanded tribute and submission. Chhatrasal refused.

"Jai Bundela!"
"Har Har Mahadev!"

The hills trembled with the roar of the guns. Dust and smoke spread everywhere. Instead of fighting on open ground, Chhatrasal posted his army behind the cover of the hills.

"Draw them into the pass," his order rang out.

As soon as the Mughal army reached the narrow way, arrows and bullets rained from above. A cavalry charge from below. Swords clashed. Blood flowed over the stones.

A Mughal commander called out—
"Surrender!"
Chhatrasal roared—
"A Bundela does not know surrender!"

There was a duel. His strokes were swift. The enemy fell back.

The second battle was fiercer. This time the Mughal court sent a large army. The aim was clear—to end the Bundela rebellion.

Chhatrasal adopted guerrilla tactics. Raids on Mughal camps in the dark of night. Cutting the supply routes. Constant strikes by small troops.

One night fire blazed up in the Mughal camp. Chaos. By morning the Bundela army struck from the front. The enemy line wavered.

The third and decisive struggle took place on open ground. The two armies faced each other.

"Jai Bundelkhand!"
"Har Har Mahadev!"

The roar of cannon, the flash of swords, the hoofbeats of horses—the sky trembled. A storm of dust rose. Streams of blood began to flow.

A moment came when the Bundela army was surrounded. The soldiers began to fall back.

"Do not fall back!" Chhatrasal himself reached the front line. His sword fell like lightning. Blow after blow. The soldiers' morale returned.

He signalled the reserve. Suddenly the blow came from behind. The Mughal line began to break.

The battle went on long. At last the enemy fell back. Bundelkhand's freedom remained secure.

Chhatrasal did not only fight wars—he laid the foundations of a state. Building forts, reorganising the army, adopting new techniques of war. He turned the geographical strength of the Vindhyas into strategy.

For years the struggle went on. Sometimes open battle, sometimes guerrilla war. Aurangzeb's power was vast, but Chhatrasal's resolve was vaster still.

In the last phase of his life he was gazing at the hills of the Vindhyas. The sun was crimson.

A trusted companion asked—
"Maharaj, will the struggle ever end?"
He said in a low voice—
"As long as the fire of freedom burns, the struggle will go on."

His breath grew still, but his saga became immortal in the land of Bundelkhand.

Rao Chhatrasal Bundela—the founder who established a free kingdom even in the shadow of the Mughal empire, who chose resistance over surrender, who proved that even a land of stone can shake the walls of empire.

Even today a voice echoes in the winds of the Vindhyas—
"Bundelkhand is free."

maharao-shakti-singh-hada.name: Maharao Shakti Singh Hada
maharao-shakti-singh-hada.story:
*Historical note: No ruler of Bundi of this name is known. In Akbar's time Bundi was ruled by Rao Surjan Hada, who made terms with Akbar in 1569 after the siege of Ranthambore. Read this story as legend, not history.*

When the stream of the Chambal struck the hills of Bundi, the ring of swords could be heard in its echo. The fort of Taragarh—cleaving the clouds—was the silent sentinel of that turbulent 16th century. In the north Mughal power was growing. Akbar's armies had fixed their gaze on the states of Rajputana one by one. But Bundi—the land of the Hadas—still held firm to its honour. In that same fiery spirit a name was born—Maharao Shakti Singh Hada.

On the night of his birth rows of lamps were lit inside Taragarh. The roar of kettledrums echoed through the valleys. Weapons were offered at the temple of the clan goddess. An old bard lifted the newborn and said—
"This boy will become strength itself, true to his name."

From childhood Shakti Singh had intensity—firmness in his wrist, fire in his gaze. At five he began riding. On the stony climbs of Bundi he handled his horse as if it were his companion. At seven he drew the bowstring and the arrow flew straight to its mark. At ten the sword came into his hand—and soon became the symbol of his personality.

One day his teacher asked—
"What if the emperor's army stands before you?"
Shakti Singh replied—
"Then the land of Bundi will put it to the test."

While still young he was given the burden of rule. Bundi was under pressure. Envoys came from the Mughal court—bearing terms of treaty and subjection. Some chiefs advised—"Bow and save the kingdom."
But Shakti Singh, gripping the hilt of his sword, said—
"A kingdom saved by bowing is not a kingdom—it is a hostage."

The first great battle was fought on Bundi's border. The Mughal army advanced with heavy cannon and disciplined infantry.

"Jai Bundi!"
"Har Har Mahadev!"

The earth shook with the first roar of the guns. A cloud of dust rose. Shakti Singh spread his army behind the cover of the hills.

"Draw them into the narrow pass!" his order rang out.

As soon as the Mughal army came down into the valley, arrows and bullets rained from above. From below the Hada horsemen crashed in like lightning. Swords clashed. Spears gleamed. Blood flowed over the rocks.

A Mughal commander called out—
"Surrender!"
Shakti Singh roared—
"A Hada does not know surrender!"

There was a duel. His strokes were fast and deadly. The enemy fell back.

The second battle was fiercer. This time the Mughal army was greater in number. They issued a challenge to battle on open ground.

The battlefield filled with dust and smoke. Cannon shot fell. Horses were wounded. Soldiers fell.

Shakti Singh divided his army into three—cannon in the centre, fast cavalry on both wings. As soon as the Mughal army was entangled in the centre, the Hada bands crashed in from both sides.

The roar of "The honour of Taragarh!" rang out.

The earth shook with hoofbeats. The Mughal line wavered. Streams of blood began to flow.

The third and decisive struggle came when a harsh message arrived from the Mughal court—Bundi was to be brought under complete subjection.

Banners flew on the ramparts of Taragarh. Shakti Singh said in the council—
"Today it is a question of honour, greater than life."

The battlefield was wide. The two armies faced each other.

"Har Har Mahadev!"
"Jai Hada!"

The roar of cannon, the clash of swords, the hoofbeats of horses—the sky trembled. A storm of dust covered everything.

A moment came when the Mughal army tightened its ring. Bundi's front line began to fall back.

"Do not fall back!" Shakti Singh himself reached the front line. His sword fell like lightning. Blow after blow. The soldiers' morale returned.

He signalled the reserve. Suddenly the blow came from behind. The Mughal line began to break. The encirclement was reversed.

The battle went on long. But in the final stage a heavy blow tore through his shoulder. Blood flowed. His horse staggered. He fell to the ground, but the sword did not leave his hand.

A Mughal commander called out—
"There is still time—surrender!"
Shakti Singh said, his voice soaked in blood—
"A Hada… does not surrender…"

He raised his sword one last time and struck. Then his arm went slack.

The wind of the Chambal was heavy that day. Bundi lost a lion, but saved its honour.

Maharao Shakti Singh Hada—the ruler who kept Bundi unshaken even before Mughal power, who chose a hero's death over surrender, who proved that freedom beats in Hada blood until the last breath.

Even today the wind echoes over the ramparts of Taragarh—
"Bundi did not bow… and it never will."

kunwar-jagmal.name: Kunwar Jagmal
kunwar-jagmal.significance: Udai Singh II's chosen heir, set aside for Pratap, who joined Akbar and died at Datani
kunwar-jagmal.story:
**Kunwar Jagmal — the heir who was set aside**

Jagmal was a son of **Maharana Udai Singh II** by his favourite queen, **Dheer Bai Bhatiyani**. Under her influence, Udai Singh named Jagmal as his successor, passing over his eldest son, **Pratap**.

**Gogunda, 1572**

When Udai Singh died at **Gogunda** in 1572, Jagmal took his seat on the throne. But the great nobles of Mewar, among them **Krishnadas Chundawat** and **Rawat Sanga**, refused to accept him. Mewar faced the might of Akbar, and they wanted a leader who could stand against it. They led Jagmal from the throne and crowned **Pratap** in his place.

**In Akbar's service**

Humiliated, Jagmal left Mewar and went to **Akbar**, who welcomed a rival claimant to Mewar. He received the jagir of **Jahazpur**, and later Akbar gave him half of the state of **Sirohi**, setting him against its ruler, **Rao Surtan Deora**.

**Datani, 1583**

In **1583**, Jagmal marched with an imperial force against Rao Surtan. At the battle of **Datani**, Surtan's men won a famous victory, and Jagmal was killed fighting on the Mughal side.

**Memory**

Mewar's tradition remembers Jagmal as the prince who chose ambition over his homeland. His story is also a reminder of how the decision of the nobles at Gogunda changed history: without it there would have been no Maharana Pratap.

rao-ratan-singh-rathore.name: Raja Ratan Singh Rathore of Ratlam
rao-ratan-singh-rathore.significance: Founder of Ratlam state, killed at Dharmat fighting for the imperial side
legends: Hero of the Dingal poem Ratan Rasau
rao-ratan-singh-rathore.story:
## Raja Ratan Singh Rathore of Ratlam — the lord who fell at Dharmat

*His grant of Ratlam, his service under Shah Jahan and his death at Dharmat are recorded in Mughal histories and the Ratlam family records; the Dingal "Vachanika" of Khidiya Jaga preserves the bardic memory of his last stand, and the story of the mad elephant belongs to family and popular tradition.*

### A cadet of the house of Jodhpur

**Ratan Singh** was born in about **1618** into the ruling clan of **Marwar**. He was a great-grandson of **Raja Udai Singh** of Jodhpur, the "Mota Raja", and the son of **Mahesh Das**, a Rathore noble who served the Mughal emperors. Because his father was named Mahesh Das, the bards often call him **Ratan Singh Maheshdasot**, "the son of Mahesh Das", following the Rajput custom of naming men by their fathers.

Like many younger branches of the great Rajput houses, Ratan Singh's family had no kingdom of its own to inherit. Their fortunes lay in the service of the empire. A Rajput noble who served the Mughals well could receive a **mansab** (imperial rank) and a **jagir** (revenue land), and a lucky family could turn that jagir into a hereditary state.

### The emperor's servant

Ratan Singh entered the service of **Shah Jahan** (r. 1628–1658) and rose steadily in rank. He served on imperial campaigns and became known as a capable and loyal commander.

Ratlam tradition remembers one episode above all. It tells that an imperial elephant went mad at Agra and ran wild through the streets, and that the young Ratan Singh rode out alone and faced it, striking it until it was brought under control, while the court watched. In the story, Shah Jahan was so impressed that he honoured him on the spot. The tale is told in Ratlam with pride, but it is family and popular tradition; it is not described in the main Persian chronicles, and its details should be read as legend rather than record.

What is recorded is the reward of his service. In about **1652** Shah Jahan granted Ratan Singh lands in **Malwa**, centred on **Ratlam**, a market town on the trade routes between Gujarat and central India. With this grant the **Ratlam state** was founded, and Ratan Singh became its first raja. His house would later give rise to the neighbouring Rathore states of **Sailana** and **Sitamau**, both founded by members of his family.

### The war of succession

In **1657** Shah Jahan fell seriously ill, and his four sons began to fight for the throne. The emperor and his eldest son, **Dara Shikoh**, controlled the court. Against them marched **Aurangzeb** from the Deccan and **Murad Bakhsh** from Gujarat, who joined their armies in Malwa.

To stop them, the court sent an army under **Maharaja Jaswant Singh** of Marwar, the head of the Rathore house, together with the Mughal noble **Qasim Khan**. Among the Rajput chiefs who rode with Jaswant Singh were **Mukund Singh Hada** of Kota and his brothers, **Dayal Das Jhala**, **Arjun Singh Gaur** and Ratan Singh of Ratlam. For Ratan Singh this was a matter of loyalty twice over: he was following the head of his clan, and he was serving the emperor who had made him a raja.

### Dharmat, April 1658

The armies met at **Dharmat**, near **Ujjain**, in **April 1658**. The princes' army was larger and was supported by strong artillery and musketeers, many of them trained in the Deccan wars. The imperial camp was divided; Qasim Khan and many Mughal officers did little fighting.

The Rajputs bore the brunt of the day. They charged across broken ground into the princes' guns and reached the enemy lines, where the fighting was fierce. But they were not supported, and Aurangzeb's commanders brought fresh troops against them. The Hada brothers of Kota fell one after another. When the battle was clearly lost, Jaswant Singh, himself wounded, was led away from the field by his men.

Ratan Singh did not leave. The Persian accounts and Rajput tradition agree that he fell on the field at Dharmat, fighting to the end with his followers, among the many Rajput nobles who died there. Aurangzeb's victory at Dharmat opened the road north, and within weeks he defeated Dara at **Samugarh** and took the throne.

### The Vachanika of Khidiya Jaga

Ratan Singh's death became one of the great subjects of **Dingal**, the literary language of the Charan bards of Rajasthan. The Charan poet **Khidiya Jaga** composed the *Vachanika Rathor Ratan Singh ji ri Maheshdasot ri*, a work in mixed verse and rhythmic prose (a *vachanika*) that describes the preparation for war, the arming of the warriors and the last fight at Dharmat. It is sometimes loosely called the *Ratan Rasau*.

Literary historians count it among the finest works of Dingal. It gives a picture of how the Rajput nobility of the age understood honour: a warrior's duty was to keep faith with the master he served and not to turn his back in battle. Like all bardic works, it heightens and celebrates; its speeches and many of its details are poetry, not a report. But it shows how quickly Ratan Singh's death passed into the memory of Rajasthan.

### Legacy

Ratan Singh was succeeded by his son **Ram Singh**, and his descendants continued to rule Ratlam through the Mughal, Maratha and British periods. Ratlam became a salute state under British paramountcy. In **1948** it merged into the new state of **Madhya Bharat**, later part of **Madhya Pradesh**.

His story is a reminder that Rajput history in the Mughal age was not only a story of resistance; many nobles built their houses through imperial service. At Dharmat, Rathores fought on the side of the reigning emperor against the prince who would become the next one. Ratan Singh chose to keep his oath when the battle was lost, and that choice, more than his grant of land, is what the bards remembered.

### Key points
- **Origins.** A Rathore of the Jodhpur house, great-grandson of Raja Udai Singh and son of Mahesh Das.
- **Founder of Ratlam.** Shah Jahan granted him Ratlam in Malwa in about 1652, founding the state.
- **The elephant tale.** Ratlam tradition says he subdued a mad imperial elephant at Agra; this is family legend, not chronicle.
- **Dharmat, 1658.** He fought under Jaswant Singh for the imperial side and was killed when the battle was lost.
- **Bardic memory.** Khidiya Jaga's Dingal *Vachanika* on his death is a classic of Rajasthani literature.
- **Legacy.** His descendants ruled Ratlam until its merger in 1948.

rawat-kesri-singh.name: Rawat Kesri Singh
rawat-kesri-singh.significance: Mewar warrior who fought at Haldighati
rawat-kesri-singh.story:
## Rawat Kesri Singh — a name from the ranks of Haldighati

*No warrior named Rawat Kesri Singh appears in the contemporary accounts of Haldighati, either in the Persian histories of Badauni and Abul Fazl or in the Mewar chronicles that list Pratap's fallen chiefs; this profile treats him as a figure of local and bardic tradition and sets him against the well-documented history of the battle.*

### What the record says

The battle of **Haldighati**, fought on **18 June 1576** in a narrow pass of the **Aravalli** hills near **Gogunda**, is one of the best documented battles of sixteenth-century Rajasthan. On one side stood **Maharana Pratap** of **Mewar**; on the other, an imperial army sent by **Akbar** under **Raja Man Singh** of Amber, with **Asaf Khan** among its commanders. The historian **Abd al-Qadir Badauni** rode with the Mughal army and wrote an eyewitness account. **Abul Fazl**, Akbar's court historian, described the campaign in the *Akbarnama*. In Mewar, later court chronicles and bardic works kept their own lists of the men who fought and fell.

Those lists include famous names: **Jhala Man Singh** (Bida Jhala), who is said to have taken up the royal insignia to draw the enemy away from Pratap; **Ramshah Tomar**, the exiled ruler of Gwalior, who fell with his sons; **Hakim Khan Sur**, the Afghan commander who fought for Mewar; **Bhim Singh Dodia**; **Rawat Krishnadas Chundawat**; the Bhil chief **Rana Punja**; and **Bhamashah** with his brother **Tarachand**. A Rawat Kesri Singh is not among them.

This does not mean such a man could not have existed. Hundreds of Rajputs fought at Haldighati, and the chronicles name only the leaders. Many lesser chiefs and kinsmen are remembered only in village tradition, family genealogies kept by the **Bhats**, and memorial stones (*devlis*) whose inscriptions are often worn or unpublished. A Rawat Kesri Singh may belong to that unrecorded multitude, or his name may have been shaped later by storytellers. Readers should treat the particular deeds told of him as legend.

### The title "Rawat"

The title **Rawat** in Mewar was borne by many of the great nobles, especially the **Chundawat** chiefs descended from **Chunda**, the elder son of **Rana Lakha**, who gave up his claim to the throne in the fifteenth century. The heads of **Salumbar**, **Deogarh** and **Begun** were Rawats, as were lesser landholders. The name Kesri, meaning "lion" and also "saffron", was common among Rajput men. A Rawat Kesri Singh is therefore a perfectly plausible name for a Mewar noble of the period, and that very plausibility helps explain how such figures enter tradition.

### The tradition

The story told of him follows a familiar pattern of Mewar's heroic tradition. He is said to have been a Sisodia warrior trained from boyhood in riding, archery and the sword, who swore to serve Mewar at a time when Pratap had refused every offer of submission sent by Akbar between 1572 and 1576. At Haldighati, the tradition places him in the front line, leading horsemen who struck the Mughal advance from the cover of the hills, and fighting near Pratap during the crisis of the battle. In the end, the story says, he was wounded by a musket ball and cut down, refusing to surrender.

The speeches given to him in popular retellings, and the details of his charges and his duel with a Mughal officer, are the work of storytellers. They should be read as a portrait of the ideal Mewar warrior, not as a report of a particular man.

### The real battle around the legend

What makes the tradition meaningful is the real course of the battle. The Mewar army, much smaller than the imperial force, opened with a fierce charge that broke the Mughal vanguard; Badauni admits that part of the imperial army fled. The fighting then became a confused hand-to-hand struggle in which, Badauni famously wrote, it was hard to tell friendly Rajputs from enemy ones. The arrival of Mughal reserves, the imperial elephants and the steady fire of the musketeers turned the battle. Pratap, wounded, was led from the field, and his horse **Chetak** became the subject of its own legend. Mewar lost many of its leading men, but Pratap escaped to the hills and continued the war for twenty years, recovering most of Mewar before his death in **1597**.

Haldighati was not a decisive Mughal victory: Man Singh did not capture Pratap, and Akbar was displeased with the result. For Mewar, the battle became a symbol of refusal rather than defeat. That is the setting in which warriors like Kesri Singh, real or remembered, became heroes of song.

### Memory and meaning

Mewar's memory of Haldighati was kept alive by the Charans and Bhats, by ballads sung at fairs, and later by **James Tod**, whose *Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan* (1829–32) called the pass the "Thermopylae of Mewar". In the twentieth century the battle was celebrated in poetry such as **Shyam Narayan Pandey's** *Haldighati*. Each of these retellings added names and scenes.

The figure of Rawat Kesri Singh belongs to this living tradition. He stands for the many Mewar nobles whose names were never written down: men of the Rawat families who followed their Maharana into the pass and did not return. To honour them truthfully is to remember both what is known and what is not.

### Key points
- **Not in the record.** No Rawat Kesri Singh appears in Badauni, Abul Fazl or the Mewar chronicle lists of Haldighati.
- **Plausible name.** Rawat was a common title of Mewar nobles, especially the Chundawats, and Kesri a common name.
- **The tradition.** Popular stories make him a front-line Sisodia warrior who died near Pratap; these details are legend.
- **The real battle.** Haldighati, 18 June 1576, was hard fought; Pratap escaped and continued the war.
- **Unnamed heroes.** His story stands for the many Mewar warriors remembered only in local tradition.

rao-surtan-singh.name: Rao Surtan Deora
rao-surtan-singh.significance: Deora Chauhan ruler of Sirohi who defied Akbar and won the battle of Datani
rao-surtan-singh.story:
## Rao Surtan Deora — the defiant lord of Sirohi

*The outline of Surtan's reign, Mughal intervention in Sirohi and the battle of Datani is recorded in the Akbarnama, Muhnot Nainsi's seventeenth-century Khyat and the Sirohi chronicles used by G. H. Ojha; the tally of his battles and much of his fame come from Charan poetry, above all the verses attributed to Dursa Adha.*

### The Deoras of Sirohi

The **Deoras** are a branch of the **Chauhan** Rajputs who settled in the south-west of Rajasthan in the fourteenth century and founded the state of **Sirohi**, beneath the granite mass of **Mount Abu**. Their country was small, hilly and poor, but it held an important position: it lay between **Mewar**, **Marwar** and **Gujarat**, on the routes that armies and merchants used to move between northern India and the ports of the western coast. Whoever controlled Gujarat wanted the passes of Sirohi secure.

### A boy on a troubled throne

**Surtan** came to the throne in about **1571**, while still a boy. His predecessor, **Rao Man Singh**, had been killed in a feud, and the Sirohi nobility was deeply divided. For years the young Rao had to struggle against powerful kinsmen, above all the noble **Bija Deora**, who held real power at court and at one point tried to take the state for himself. Much of Surtan's early reign was spent winning back authority within his own clan.

These were also the years in which **Akbar** conquered Gujarat (1572–73) and began pressing the Rajput states to accept Mughal supremacy. Most of Rajasthan's rulers did so: Amber, Bikaner, Jaisalmer and, after the death of **Rao Chandrasen**, Marwar. Mewar under **Maharana Pratap** refused. Sirohi, small and exposed, was caught between them.

### Between submission and defiance

Imperial forces entered Sirohi more than once in the years around **Haldighati** (1576), and Surtan's relationship with the empire swung between nominal submission and open resistance. When Mughal armies came in strength he withdrew to the hills of Abu, where cavalry and artillery were of little use; when they left, he reasserted his rule. He never accepted the empire's terms for long, and the Mughals came to see him as an unreliable and troublesome vassal.

Akbar's answer was to use Rajput rivals against him. **Jagmal**, a half-brother of Pratap who had been passed over for the throne of Mewar and had gone over to the Mughals, received a grant of half of Sirohi. Surtan refused to share his country, and conflict followed.

### Datani, 1583

In **October 1583** an army marched against Surtan. Its leaders were Jagmal; **Rai Singh**, a son of Rao Chandrasen of Marwar, then in imperial service; and Surtan's rival kinsmen, supported by imperial troops. Surtan met them at **Datani**, in the Sirohi country, with his Deora clansmen and allies.

The battle was a complete victory for Sirohi. Both **Jagmal** and **Rai Singh** were killed on the field, and the attacking army was broken. Datani became the most celebrated event of Surtan's life and one of the great themes of the bards of south-western Rajasthan. It showed that the empire's policy of setting Rajput against Rajput could fail, and it secured Surtan's hold on his state.

### The poet on the other side

Charan tradition attaches a famous story to Datani. The poet **Dursa Adha**, one of the greatest Dingal poets of the age, is said to have been with the attacking army and to have been wounded and found on the field. Surtan, according to the tradition, treated him with honour, and Dursa afterwards praised the Deora ruler in his verses. Dursa is also famous for his poems in praise of Maharana Pratap, and his work shows how the Charans could admire a ruler's defiance even when they served men on the imperial side. The details of his capture belong to tradition, but the poems associated with Surtan are an important part of Dingal literature.

### The long defiance

Tradition credits Surtan with fighting more than fifty battles in a reign of almost forty years. The number is bardic, but the picture of a ruler constantly at war with neighbours, kinsmen and imperial officers is borne out by the chronicles. Later in his reign, as the empire consolidated its hold on Rajasthan, Surtan came to terms with the Mughals and was confirmed in his state. He died in about **1610**, having kept Sirohi in the hands of his line.

### Legacy

Surtan's descendants ruled Sirohi until it merged into the Indian Union after 1947, and the Deoras remember him as the greatest ruler of their house. His story is often told alongside Pratap's: two rulers in the southern hills who refused to become ordinary imperial vassals. The comparison should not be pushed too far, since Surtan made his peace with the empire in the end, as did Pratap's own son **Amar Singh** in 1615. But at Datani he showed that a small Rajput state, fighting on its own ground, could still defeat the forces sent to divide it.

### Key points
- **House.** Surtan belonged to the Deora branch of the Chauhans, rulers of Sirohi below Mount Abu.
- **A divided state.** He came to the throne as a boy in about 1571 and had to overcome powerful rival kinsmen.
- **Mughal pressure.** Akbar backed his rivals and granted half of Sirohi to Pratap's half-brother Jagmal.
- **Datani, 1583.** Surtan defeated the attacking army; Jagmal and Rai Singh of Marwar were killed.
- **Bardic fame.** Dursa Adha's verses and the tradition of fifty-two battles made him a hero of Dingal poetry.
- **End of reign.** He later reached terms with the Mughals and died in about 1610, still ruling Sirohi.

durgadas-rathore.name: Durgadas Rathore
durgadas-rathore.significance: Legendary Rathore warrior who saved Marwar
durgadas-rathore.story:
## Durgadas Rathore — the guardian of Marwar

*Durgadas's career is well documented in Persian sources such as the Maasir-i-Alamgiri and in Marwar's chronicles, and was studied in detail by Jadunath Sarkar; Rajasthani dohas and folk songs add the heroic colouring, and the dialogue often given to him in popular retellings is legend.*

### Origins

**Durgadas** was born on **13 August 1638** at **Salwa**, near Jodhpur. His father, **Askaran**, was a Rathore noble of the **Karnot** branch and a minister of **Maharaja Jaswant Singh** of Marwar. Tradition says that Askaran was estranged from Durgadas's mother, and that the boy grew up with her in modest circumstances at the village of **Lunawa**, far from the court. The story goes that he first came to Jaswant Singh's notice when he killed a man who had insulted the Maharaja, and that Jaswant Singh took him into his service. The details belong to tradition, but by the 1670s Durgadas was a trusted officer of the Jodhpur house.

### The crisis of 1678–79

On **28 November 1678** Jaswant Singh died at **Jamrud**, near the Khyber Pass, while commanding on the Mughal frontier. He left no living son, and **Aurangzeb** placed Marwar under direct imperial administration. A few weeks later, in February 1679, two of Jaswant Singh's widows gave birth at Lahore to sons, **Ajit Singh** and **Dalthamban**; Dalthamban soon died.

Aurangzeb refused to recognise Ajit Singh as ruler of Marwar. He gave the throne of Jodhpur to **Indra Singh** of Nagaur, a grandson of Jaswant Singh's elder brother, and ordered that the infant be brought up in the imperial harem. Rajput sources add that he would be given Marwar only if he were raised as a Muslim. For the Rathore nobles this was unacceptable.

### The escape from Delhi

In **July 1679**, as imperial troops surrounded the Rathore mansion in **Delhi**, Durgadas and his companions smuggled the infant Ajit Singh out of the city. A rearguard of Rathores, among them **Ranchhordas Jodha** and **Raghunath Bhati**, fought the imperial troops in the streets to cover the escape; many died there. Durgadas and his party rode for Marwar. Ajit Singh was hidden in the hills, in the care of **Mukund Das Khichi** and others, at **Kalindri** in Sirohi territory, where he grew up in secret.

### The thirty-year war

What followed was a long war for Marwar, from **1679** until Aurangzeb's death in **1707**. Durgadas was its chief leader, though never its only one. Imperial armies held Jodhpur and the main towns; the Rathores, unable to win pitched battles, fought a war of raids, ambushes and attacks on supply lines, moving through the deserts and hills they knew.

In 1679–80 **Maharana Raj Singh** of Mewar joined the Rathore cause, and Aurangzeb invaded Mewar. In **1681** Durgadas made his boldest move: he persuaded Aurangzeb's son, **Prince Muhammad Akbar**, to rebel and declare himself emperor. The plot failed when Aurangzeb sowed distrust between the prince and the Rajputs, and Durgadas escorted Akbar across India to the Maratha king **Sambhaji** in the Deccan. He stayed there for several years before returning to Marwar.

### The prince's children

Prince Akbar left his young son **Buland Akhtar** and daughter **Safiyat-un-Nisa** in Marwar. Durgadas kept them safely for many years and arranged for the girl to be taught the Quran by a Muslim tutor. When he finally returned them to Aurangzeb in the **1690s**, the emperor is said to have been surprised to find his granddaughter educated in her own faith. The episode, recorded in the Persian histories, is often cited as an example of Durgadas's honour. It also served his politics: the children gave him leverage, and their return was part of the negotiations that earned Ajit Singh recognition and Durgadas himself an imperial rank.

### Victory and estrangement

When Aurangzeb died in **1707**, Ajit Singh seized Jodhpur. With the support of Mewar and Amber (in the alliance of 1708), he secured his throne. The cause Durgadas had served for nearly three decades had won.

But Ajit Singh, now a grown ruler, grew distrustful of the old guardian whose fame overshadowed him. Durgadas left Marwar. He spent his last years in Mewar, where **Maharana Amar Singh II** gave him honour and a grant of land, and later in Malwa. He died on **22 November 1718** on the banks of the **Shipra** near **Ujjain**, where his memorial (*chhatri*) still stands.

### Legacy

Durgadas is remembered across Rajasthan as the model of the loyal servant: a man who never claimed the throne he saved, who kept faith with an infant he barely knew, and who treated enemies' children with honour. Folk poetry addresses Rajput mothers, urging them to bear sons like Durgadas. Historians see in him a skilled leader of irregular war and a shrewd diplomat whose alliances with Mewar, Prince Akbar and the Marathas kept Marwar's cause alive against the full weight of the empire. Modern India has honoured him with statues, a postage stamp and the name of public institutions.

### Key points
- **Origins.** Born in 1638 at Salwa, son of Askaran, a minister of Jaswant Singh; raised in modest circumstances.
- **The escape of 1679.** He smuggled the infant Ajit Singh out of Delhi while Rathore warriors fought a rearguard.
- **Thirty-year war.** He led Marwar's resistance to direct Mughal rule from 1679 until 1707.
- **Prince Akbar.** In 1681 he backed the prince's rebellion and escorted him to the Maratha court.
- **Honour to enemies.** He protected Akbar's children and had his granddaughter educated in her faith.
- **Death.** Estranged from Ajit Singh, he died near Ujjain in 1718; his chhatri stands on the Shipra.

maharaja-jaswant-singh.name: Maharaja Jaswant Singh
maharaja-jaswant-singh.significance: Rathore ruler of Marwar and senior Mughal mansabdar, scholar and poet
maharaja-jaswant-singh.story:
**Maharaja Jaswant Singh — the Rathore between two worlds**

Jaswant Singh was born on **26 December 1626** at **Burhanpur**, the son of **Maharaja Gaj Singh** of Marwar. He became ruler of Marwar in **1638**, at the age of eleven, and, like his father, served the Mughal emperors as a high-ranking **mansabdar**.

**Dharmat, 1658**

In the war of succession, Shah Jahan sent Jaswant Singh to stop **Aurangzeb** and **Murad**. At **Dharmat**, near Ujjain, in April 1658, the Rathores charged with great courage, but the princes' artillery and numbers carried the day. Jaswant Singh returned to Jodhpur defeated. Tradition says his queen, a Hada princess, closed the gates of the fort against him, saying a Rajput should return victorious or not at all.

**A dangerous game**

After Aurangzeb's victory, Jaswant Singh submitted to him. At **Khajwa** (January 1659), during Aurangzeb's battle against Shuja, he turned against him and plundered the imperial camp. He then promised to join Dara, but was persuaded by **Mirza Raja Jai Singh** to stay away, and Dara was defeated at **Deorai** alone. Aurangzeb forgave him, but never trusted him.

**In imperial service**

Jaswant Singh served in the **Deccan** against Shivaji, as governor of **Gujarat**, and finally on the north-western frontier. He died at **Jamrud**, near the Khyber Pass, on **28 November 1678**.

**Scholar and poet**

Jaswant Singh was also a scholar. His *Bhasha Bhushan* is a classic work on Hindi poetics, and he wrote on Vedanta philosophy.

**After his death**

Aurangzeb took Marwar under direct control. The struggle to save Jaswant Singh's posthumous son, **Ajit Singh**, led by **Durgadas Rathore**, became the great Rathore war of 1679–1707.

maharana-raj-singh.name: Maharana Raj Singh
maharana-raj-singh.story:
The ranges of the Aravallis were not just mountains then—they were a shield. The lakes of Mewar were not just water—they were the eyes of history, which had seen the flames of jauhar, bread made of grass, and battlefields stained with blood. The 17th century… Aurangzeb sat on the throne of Delhi. His empire was vast, his policies harsh, his sword merciless. But Mewar—the land of Sisodia blood—still stood firm. In that same unshaken tradition, in 1629 CE, a boy was born—Maharana Raj Singh.

On the night of his birth rows of lamps were lit in the temple of Eklingnath. The war drum sounded. An old bard looked at the newborn's brow and said—
"In times of crisis this boy will roar like a lion."

From childhood Raj Singh had a unique resolve. When he was put on a horse at five, he held the reins as if he had been a warrior from birth. He raced without fear up the rugged climbs of the Aravallis. The bow at seven, the sword at ten. By his youth his arm had such strength that his strokes were straight and deadly.

One day his teacher asked—
"What if Aurangzeb comes himself with an army?"
Raj Singh replied, calm but firm—
"Then the Aravallis will become his grave."

While still young he received the throne of Mewar. The kingdom was under pressure. Mughal subahdars came with demands of tribute, subjection and humiliating terms. Many states had already bowed. But in the Sisodia tradition, bowing was the last resort—and even then only at the cost of one's life.

The first great battle took place in a frontier pass. The Mughal army advanced with heavy cannon and disciplined infantry.

"Victory to Eklingnath!"
"Mewar is immortal!"

The earth shook with the first roar of the guns. Smoke spread everywhere. Raj Singh withdrew his army from the open ground and posted it in the hills.

"Let them come into the narrow way," his order rang out.

As soon as the enemy entered the pass, arrows and bullets rained from above. A cavalry charge from below. Swords clashed. Blood flowed over the stones.

A Mughal commander called out—
"Bow, and live!"
Raj Singh roared—
"A Sisodia's life is freedom!"

There was a duel. His strokes were swift and unerring. The enemy fell back.

The second battle was fiercer. Aurangzeb sent a harsh order—Mewar was to be brought under complete subjection. This time the army was vast. Cannon, cavalry, infantry—all organised.

The blow fell in the direction of Udaipur. The ramparts of the forts shook. Stones broke. Soldiers inside were wounded.

A general said—
"Maharana, their numbers are double ours."
Raj Singh replied—
"Then our courage will be four times greater."

In the dark of night guerrilla troops went out. Fire suddenly broke out in the Mughal camp. Supply stores burned. Chaos among the horses. By morning the army of Mewar struck from the front. The enemy line wavered.

The third and decisive struggle took place on open ground. The two armies faced each other. Banners flew in the wind.

"Har Har Mahadev!"
"The honour of Mewar!"

The roar of cannon, the flash of swords, the hoofbeats of horses—the sky trembled. A storm of dust rose. Streams of blood began to flow.

A moment came when the Mughal army tightened its ring. Mewar's front line began to fall back.

"Do not fall back!" Raj Singh himself reached the front line. His sword flashed like lightning. Blow after blow. The soldiers' morale returned.

He signalled the reserve. Suddenly the blow came from behind. The Mughal line began to break. The encirclement was reversed.

The battle went on long. By sunset the Mughal army was forced to fall back.

Raj Singh did not only fight wars—he strengthened Mewar from within. Repairing forts, expanding the artillery, training musketeers. Adopting new techniques of war. Organising supply and communications. He made the Aravallis his shield.

For years the struggle went on. Sometimes open battle, sometimes guerrilla raids. Aurangzeb's power was vast, but Mewar's resolve was unshaken.

In the last days of his life Raj Singh stood on the shore of the lake at Udaipur. The sun was crimson. The Aravallis were silent.

A trusted companion asked—
"Maharana, will Aurangzeb ever bow?"
Looking towards the horizon, Raj Singh said—
"Bowing is not his way… but it is not ours either."

Some time later his breath grew still. But his roar still echoes in the valleys of the Aravallis.

Maharana Raj Singh—the Sisodia ruler who kept Mewar unshaken even before Aurangzeb's harsh policies, who chose resistance over surrender, who proved that freedom can live even on the edge of the sword.

Even today a voice rises in the winds of the Aravallis—
"Mewar did not bow… and it never will."

rana-jai-singh-i.name: Mirza Raja Jai Singh I
rana-jai-singh-i.significance: Kachwaha ruler of Amber and one of the greatest Mughal generals
rana-jai-singh-i.story:
**Mirza Raja Jai Singh I — the general of three emperors**

Jai Singh was born on **15 July 1611** into the **Kachwaha** house of **Amber**. He became Raja in **1621**, when he was only about ten years old, and spent the rest of his life in the service of the Mughal empire.

**A soldier of the empire**

Under **Jahangir** and **Shah Jahan** he fought in almost every corner of the empire: in the Deccan, in Central Asia at **Balkh**, and in the campaigns for **Kandahar**. Shah Jahan gave him the title **Mirza Raja**, a mark of the highest favour.

**The war of succession**

In 1658 Jai Singh was sent east with Dara Shikoh's son **Sulaiman Shikoh**, and defeated Prince **Shah Shuja** at **Bahadurpur**. When Dara lost at Samugarh, Jai Singh judged that his cause was finished and went over to **Aurangzeb**. Before the battle of **Deorai** (1659) his letters persuaded **Jaswant Singh of Marwar** not to join Dara.

**Purandar, 1665**

Aurangzeb sent Jai Singh against **Shivaji**. Combining siege-craft and diplomacy, he besieged **Purandar** and made Shivaji accept the **Treaty of Purandar** (June 1665), giving up 23 forts. He persuaded Shivaji to visit Aurangzeb at Agra in 1666, guaranteeing his safety; Shivaji's escape from Agra, under the watch of Jai Singh's son **Ram Singh**, cost the Kachwahas Aurangzeb's trust.

**The end**

Jai Singh's campaign against **Bijapur** in 1666 failed. Recalled and out of favour, he died at **Burhanpur** on **28 August 1667**.

*Note: the "scientist-king" of Amber who built the Jantar Mantar observatories was a later ruler, **Sawai Jai Singh II** (1688–1743).*

kunwar-prithviraj-singh.name: Kunwar Prithviraj Singh
kunwar-prithviraj-singh.story:
## Kunwar Prithviraj Singh — a name from the Kachwaha legend

*No 17th-century Amber prince called Prithviraj Singh who led wars against the Mughals appears in the inscriptions, the Kachwaha vamshavalis, the Persian histories of the Mughal court or Tod's Annals; this profile treats the popular story as bardic legend and sets it against the documented history of Amber in that century.*

Stories of a prince named **Kunwar Prithviraj Singh** of **Amber** circulate in retellings of Kachwaha history. In them he is born to rows of lamps and the booming of kettledrums, rides the stony slopes of the Aravallis at five, and grows up to lead three great battles against the Mughal emperor, ambushing imperial troops in the hills, rallying a wavering line on open ground, and finally refusing submission in open court. These are stirring scenes, but they cannot be matched to any recorded event, and they run against what is known about Amber in the 17th century. The honest approach is to ask where such a story could come from and what the real Kachwaha princes of that age were doing.

### Why the story does not fit the record

The 17th century was the period when the Kachwahas of Amber were most closely tied to the Mughal empire, not at war with it. The alliance began in **1562**, when **Raja Bharmal** gave his daughter in marriage to **Akbar** and entered imperial service. His son **Bhagwant Das** and grandson **Raja Man Singh I** became among the most powerful commanders of the empire. Man Singh led Mughal armies in Kabul, Bihar, Bengal and Odisha, commanded the imperial side at **Haldighati** in **1576**, and built much of the palace complex of **Amber fort**. He died in **1614**.

After a short reign by **Bhao Singh**, the throne passed in **1621** to the boy **Jai Singh I**, later honoured as **Mirza Raja**. Over more than four decades he served Jahangir, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb, fought in Central Asia and the Deccan, and in **1665** negotiated the **Treaty of Purandar** with **Shivaji**. His son **Ram Singh I** (r. **1667–1688**) was the prince in whose custody Shivaji was held at Agra in **1666**, and who was blamed when the Maratha leader escaped. Ram Singh was then posted to **Assam**, where the campaign against the Ahoms ended in the Mughal defeat at **Saraighat** in **1671**. He was followed by **Bishan Singh** (r. **1688–1699**) and then by **Sawai Jai Singh II**, who came to the throne in **1699**.

In such a world, an Amber kunwar who defeated imperial armies in three battles and defied the court would have left a mark in the Persian chronicles, in the Amber records preserved in Jaipur, and in the histories of neighbouring states. No such trace exists. The only serious Kachwaha break with the empire came in **1707–1708**, when Bahadur Shah I seized Amber and Jai Singh II joined Mewar and Marwar to recover it. That episode is well documented and involves the ruler himself, not an unknown prince.

### The weight of the name Prithviraj

The name itself explains much of the legend's appeal. For the Kachwahas, **Prithviraj** recalls **Raja Prithviraj** of Amber, who ruled in the early 16th century (traditionally **1503–1527**). He is remembered as a devotee of the saint **Krishnadas Payohari** of **Galta**, near Jaipur, and Kachwaha tradition holds that the great sub-clans of the family, the **barah kotri** or "twelve chambers," descend from his sons. The name also echoes the far older **Prithviraj Chauhan**, hero of the *Prithviraj Raso*, whose story was retold in every Rajput court.

Bardic composition often borrowed such resonant names and attached them to new heroes, or moved a remembered ancestor into a later age. A "Kunwar Prithviraj Singh" fighting the Mughals in the 17th century may be the product of exactly this blending: the prestige of an old name joined to the theme of resistance to imperial power, a theme that belongs more naturally to Mewar than to Amber.

### What a Kachwaha kunwar's life looked like

The title **kunwar** was used for the sons of a ruler and, in practice, for many young men of the ruling lineage. In the 17th century a Kachwaha kunwar was trained in riding, archery, swordsmanship and the matchlock, and often learned Persian, since a career in imperial service required it. Many held **mansabs**, Mughal ranks that carried pay and the duty to maintain cavalry, and served far from home: in the Deccan, on the north-western frontier, or in the east.

Their dangers were real, but they were the dangers of imperial campaigns. Ram Singh's own son, **Kunwar Kishan Singh**, died before his father, and the succession passed to Kishan Singh's son Bishan Singh. Rivalries between brothers, quarrels over jagirs and the shifting favour of the emperor shaped these lives as much as battle did. The palaces of Amber fort, with their Diwan-i-Am, mirrored Sheesh Mahal and Ganesh Pol, built largely by Man Singh I and Jai Singh I in a blended Rajput-Mughal style, are physical evidence of partnership with the empire, not of the war the legend describes.

### Reading the legend

The story still tells us what later audiences valued: courage before a stronger power, devotion to the clan goddess, refusal to bow, and a prince's duty to stand in the front line. Its war cry of "Har Har Mahadev," its duel with a Mughal commander and its defiant speech in court are stock elements of Rajput heroic poetry. But its battles have no dates, places or named opponents, and its picture of Amber in revolt reverses the real politics of the age. The real Kachwaha story is in some ways more interesting: a lineage that tied its fortunes to the empire, produced some of its greatest generals, and still kept its own identity, which allowed Sawai Jai Singh II to break with Bahadur Shah and later to found **Jaipur** in **1727**.

### Key points
- **Not in the record.** No 17th-century Amber prince named Prithviraj Singh fighting the Mughals is found in Persian, Kachwaha or colonial sources.
- **Amber was an ally.** From 1562 the Kachwahas served the Mughals, producing commanders such as Man Singh I and Mirza Raja Jai Singh I.
- **The name's prestige.** Raja Prithviraj of Amber (early 16th century) and Prithviraj Chauhan lent the name heroic weight.
- **Real kunwars served the empire.** Kachwaha princes held mansabs and fought in distant imperial campaigns.
- **Only real break, 1708.** The one documented Kachwaha clash with the empire involved Jai Singh II himself, allied with Mewar and Marwar.

rao-amar-singh-ii.name: Maharana Amar Singh II
rao-amar-singh-ii.significance: Mewar ruler who reorganised the nobility and allied with Marwar and Amber in 1708
legends: Alliance of 1708 with Marwar and Amber
rao-amar-singh-ii.story:
## Maharana Amar Singh II — the organiser of Mewar

*The main facts of Amar Singh II's life, his dates, his accession, the alliance of 1708 and the marriage settlement with Amber, are recorded in Mewar's court chronicles, Persian accounts of Bahadur Shah's reign and the histories of Jodhpur and Jaipur; the details of his reorganisation of the nobility come chiefly from Mewar tradition as recorded by James Tod, and should be read with some caution.*

**Amar Singh II** ruled **Mewar** for only twelve years, from **1698** to **1710**, and fought no battle that the bards made famous. Yet his reign mattered. He inherited a state worn down by war with **Aurangzeb**, gave its nobility a structure that lasted for generations, and, in the confusion after the emperor's death, brought the three leading Rajput houses together for the last time. The consequences of that alliance reached far beyond his own lifetime.

### A prince in a time of war

Amar Singh was born on **3 October 1672**, the son of **Jai Singh**, then heir to **Maharana Raj Singh I**. He grew up in the most dangerous decade Mewar had known since the days of Pratap. In **1679**, after the death of **Maharaja Jaswant Singh** of Marwar and Aurangzeb's attempt to take control of that kingdom, Raj Singh gave shelter and support to the Rathor cause of the infant **Ajit Singh**. The emperor's reimposition of the **jizya** in the same year deepened the quarrel. Mughal armies entered Mewar, occupied **Udaipur** and **Chittor**, and damaged temples, while the Sisodias withdrew into the hills and fought a war of raids and ambushes.

Raj Singh died in **1680**, and Jai Singh, now Maharana, made peace in **1681**. Mewar ceded the districts of **Mandal**, **Pur** and **Badnor** in place of the jizya, and the Mughal armies withdrew. It was a settlement that saved the state but left it poorer and smaller. Mewar's chronicles also record tension between Jai Singh and his son in the 1690s, when factions at court gathered around the young prince; the quarrel was eventually patched up, and Amar Singh succeeded his father on Jai Singh's death in **1698**.

### Rebuilding from within

The new Maharana's first task was recovery. Years of war and Mughal occupation had disrupted cultivation and revenue, and the great nobles, whose cavalry formed the state's army, held their estates under customs that were often unclear and easily disputed. Amar Singh worked to restore agriculture and the revenues of the khalsa, the crown lands.

His best-remembered measure was the **reorganisation of the nobility**. According to Mewar tradition, recorded by **James Tod** in the *Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan*, Amar Singh fixed the gradations of the chiefs: the first rank, often called the **Solah** ("sixteen"), the second rank or **Battis** ("thirty-two"), and lesser grades below them. He defined their precedence in court, their seats in the durbar and their obligations of service in return for their **jagirs**. Some historians think the system grew over a longer period and that Tod gave Amar Singh credit for a process he only formalised, but it is clear that the classification of Mewar's nobles in later centuries looked back to his reign.
Additions to the **City Palace** of Udaipur, including the garden court known as **Amar Vilas**, are traditionally linked with his name.

### The crisis of 1707–1708

Aurangzeb died in the Deccan in **March 1707**. His sons fought for the throne, and **Bahadur Shah I** emerged as emperor after the battle of **Jajau** in June. He then turned to Rajputana. He wanted to bring **Marwar**, where Ajit Singh had taken **Jodhpur** after Aurangzeb's death, back under imperial control, and he was displeased with **Sawai Jai Singh II** of **Amber**, who had supported his rival **Azam Shah** at Jajau. Bahadur Shah occupied Amber, gave it to Jai Singh's younger brother **Vijay Singh**, and placed Mughal officers in Jodhpur.

Early in **1708**, while the emperor marched south to deal with his brother **Kam Bakhsh**, Ajit Singh and Jai Singh II left the imperial camp and came to **Udaipur**. Amar Singh received them, and the three rulers agreed to act together. Mewar's support, in men and in prestige, allowed the two princes to move against the Mughal officers. Jodhpur was recovered, Jai Singh drove the imperial garrison out of Amber, and the allied Rajputs defeated Mughal forces near **Sambhar** later in 1708. Distracted by Kam Bakhsh and then by the Sikh rising in the Punjab, Bahadur Shah eventually accepted Ajit Singh and Jai Singh in their kingdoms.

### The marriage condition

The alliance was sealed by marriage. Amar Singh gave his daughter **Chandra Kunwar** to Jai Singh II, on the condition, recorded in the histories of both states, that a son born of her would succeed to Amber ahead of Jai Singh's other sons. At the time it seemed a way to bind the houses together and restore Mewar's old pre-eminence. In practice it sowed trouble. When Jai Singh died in **1743**, his eldest son **Ishwari Singh** took the throne of Jaipur, while the Sisodia princess's son **Madho Singh**, backed by Mewar, pressed his claim. The resulting war drew in the **Marathas**, and ended only with Ishwari Singh's death in **1750** and Madho Singh's accession.

### Death and legacy

Amar Singh II died on **10 December 1710**, aged thirty-eight, and was succeeded by his son **Sangram Singh II**, whose long reign was one of relative stability. Amar Singh's achievements were quiet ones: a state put back on its feet, a nobility given order, and a moment of Rajput unity. That unity did not last. Within a generation Marwar, Amber and Mewar were again pursuing separate interests, and the Marathas were exploiting their quarrels. But the meeting at Udaipur in 1708 remains the last occasion when the three great Rajput houses stood together against the empire.

### Key points
- **Dates.** Born 3 October 1672; Maharana 1698–1710; died 10 December 1710.
- **Youth in war.** He grew up during Mewar's war with Aurangzeb (1679–1681), ended by the peace of 1681.
- **Order among the nobles.** Tradition credits him with grading Mewar's chiefs into ranks such as the Solah and Battis.
- **Alliance of 1708.** He united Mewar with Ajit Singh of Marwar and Jai Singh II of Amber, helping both recover their capitals.
- **A costly marriage.** The succession condition attached to his daughter's marriage fuelled the Jaipur succession war after 1743.

## Kunwar Bhim Singh — a Sisodia prince between war and empire

*Mewar's chronicles and Persian accounts of Aurangzeb's reign record a Kunwar Bhim Singh, younger son of Maharana Raj Singh I, as a leader of raids during the Mewar-Mughal war of 1679–1681; the later course of his life, the exact date of his death and the popular claim that he died fighting the Mughals are far less secure, and the heroic death scene of the old story belongs to bardic tradition rather than to the record.*

The popular story of **Kunwar Bhim Singh** of **Mewar** is a simple one. A young Sisodia prince, raised on the edge of the sword, takes his place in the front line against the Mughals, seizes command when his general falls, and dies a hero after cutting down several enemy chiefs. It names no battle, place or opponent. The real history behind the name is more tangled and, in its way, more revealing of the dilemmas Rajput princes faced in the late 17th century.

### Two Bhim Singhs

The name needs care, because Mewar's history knows more than one famous Kunwar Bhim Singh. The earlier was a son of **Maharana Amar Singh I**, a celebrated fighter who joined the rebellion of Prince **Khurram**, the future Shah Jahan, against his father Jahangir. He was killed in **1624** fighting for Khurram against the imperial army in the east. His story is well known, but it does not match a death around **1700**.

The Bhim Singh of the late 17th century was a younger son of **Maharana Raj Singh I** (r. **1652–1680**), the ruler who built the great lake of **Rajsamand** and who defied Aurangzeb in the last years of his reign. Bhim Singh was thus a brother of **Maharana Jai Singh** (r. **1680–1698**) and an uncle of **Amar Singh II**. It is this prince who appears in the record of Mewar's last great war against the empire.

### The war of 1679–1681

The war began over **Marwar**. When **Maharaja Jaswant Singh** died at Jamrud in **1678**, Aurangzeb moved to take control of his kingdom, and after the birth of Jaswant Singh's posthumous son **Ajit Singh**, the Rathor nobles led by **Durgadas** smuggled the infant out of imperial hands. Raj Singh gave the Rathor cause support, and Aurangzeb's reimposition of the **jizya** in **1679** sharpened the conflict. Imperial armies entered Mewar, and the court withdrew from **Udaipur** into the hills, from where the Sisodias fought a war of movement, cutting supply lines and raiding imperial territory.

Kunwar Bhim Singh is remembered as one of the leaders of these raids. Mewar's sources, and Persian reports of the campaign used by historians such as **Jadunath Sarkar**, describe Sisodia forces under the princes striking out of the hills into Mughal-held districts, including raids towards **Gujarat**. The aim was to make the occupation costly and to draw imperial troops away from the Aravallis. Details such as the towns attacked and the size of the forces vary between accounts.

The war widened in **1681** when Aurangzeb's son **Prince Akbar**, commanding in Rajputana, rebelled against his father with Rajput encouragement. The revolt collapsed quickly, and Akbar fled south with Durgadas to the Maratha court of **Sambhaji**. Raj Singh had already died in **1680**, and his successor Jai Singh made peace in **1681**, ceding the districts of **Mandal**, **Pur** and **Badnor** in place of the jizya. Mewar's war was over, though the Rathors fought on for decades.

### After the peace

What became of Bhim Singh afterwards is where the record grows thin and the old story most clearly departs from it. Mewar tradition and later accounts of the state's estates connect him with service under the Mughals after 1681, with the title of **Raja** and with the estate of **Banera**, near present-day Bhilwara, whose chiefs later counted among Mewar's leading nobles and traced their descent from a son of Raj Singh. If this tradition is right, the prince who had raided Mughal lands ended as a Mughal mansabdar, a common path for Rajput nobles once a war had ended in settlement.

The date of his death and its circumstances are not clearly fixed in the sources available. The date of **1700** given in popular summaries cannot be firmly confirmed, and the claim that he "died fighting the Mughals" fits poorly with the tradition of his later imperial service. It is possible that the heroic death scene has been borrowed from the story of the earlier Bhim Singh of 1624, or simply shaped from the stock motifs of Rajput heroic poetry. Readers should treat it as legend unless better evidence appears.

### The world he lived in

Bhim Singh's life illustrates a choice that many Rajput princes faced. Mewar had a long tradition of resistance, rooted in the memory of **Rana Sanga**, **Pratap** and the sieges of **Chittor**, but after the treaty of **1615** between Amar Singh I and Jahangir, it had also accepted a place within the imperial system, while sending princes rather than the Maharana himself to the Mughal court. War in 1679 revived the old pattern of hill warfare; peace in 1681 restored the newer pattern of negotiation and service.

Younger sons especially needed land, rank and a following, and the empire was the largest source of all three. Bards and later retellings tended to remember the fighting and forget the service.

### Remembering Bhim Singh

In Mewar, the name of Kunwar Bhim Singh is still linked with the courage of the hill war against Aurangzeb, and that memory has a real basis. The rest of the story, the command seized on a nameless field and the glorious death, should be held more lightly. The documented prince was a son of Raj Singh who fought in a hard war, lived on into a peace that reshaped his family's position, and left behind a lineage rather than a legend of martyrdom.

### Key points
- **Son of Raj Singh I.** The late 17th-century Kunwar Bhim Singh was a younger son of Maharana Raj Singh I and brother of Jai Singh.
- **Not the Bhim Singh of 1624.** An earlier Bhim Singh, son of Amar Singh I, died fighting for Prince Khurram in 1624.
- **Raids of 1679–1681.** He is recorded as a leader of Sisodia raids during Mewar's war with Aurangzeb.
- **Later imperial service.** Tradition links him after the 1681 peace with Mughal rank, the title of Raja and the estate of Banera.
- **Death uncertain.** The date of 1700 and a death fighting the Mughals are not firmly supported by the record.
